title: Ravens vs Colts: the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly
summary: Another season of Baltimore Ravens football has kicked off, which means it’s time to get back to finding the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly in every matchup! Sunday’s win over the Colts featured plenty to be excited about, but a handful of rough moments, too. Let’s dive in! The Good Lamar Jackson: It had […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball against the Indianapolis Colts during the second quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images Another season of Baltimore Ravens football has kicked off, which means it’s time to get back to finding the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly in every matchup! Sunday’s win over the Colts featured plenty to be excited about, but a handful of rough moments, too. Let’s dive in! The Good Lamar Jackson: It had been 252 days since the world got to see Lamar Jackson play football, and he didn’t disappoint in his return. He had over 300 yards through the air with a 124.2 passer rating. He also added another 40 yards on the ground and answered any questions about his legs with a magical sack escape and scramble to pick up a first down on 3rd and 16 that led to a touchdown. Basically, the MVP is back. The three-headed monster: The Ravens officially have a mythical creature in Baltimore. Pair Lamar Jackson’s performance with Derrick Henry’s 144 yards at 6.0 yards a pop and three touchdowns with Zay Flowers’ 150 yards and a score on five catches, and you have one of the best trios in the NFL. And Flowers’ numbers came in just the first half alone. In offensive coordinator Declan Doyle's first game as a playcaller, the Ravens produced the first game in their 31-year history with this trifecta: 🏈 300-yard passer (Lamar Jackson) 🏈 150-yard receiver (Zay Flowers) 🏈 100-yard rusher (Derrick Henry) Source: ESPN Research — Jamison Hensley (@jamisonhensley) September 14, 2026 Run game: As mentioned above, Henry was able to come in and control this game for Baltimore once they built up a lead. That was massive with Flowers out for the second half, which slowed the passing game. As the Ravens operate from under center more this year, it should open Henry to work in what he was best at in Tennessee, stretch/zone concepts that get him moving on a track. The run game is definitely where the offensive line shined too. According to Next Gen Stats, Henry wasn’t tackled behind the line of scrimmage once during the Colts game. The Ravens' offensive line needs to clean up the penalties and improve in pass protection, but the run blocking was very strong. Derrick Henry finished with 110 yards before contact against the Colts, the third-highest single-game total of his career, per @NextGenStats . Henry… — Ryan Mink (@ryanmink) September 14, 2026 Defense: Since Jesse Minter was hired, the talk around town was how much the Ravens defense would improve after the Zach Orr years. The unit proceeded to get walked down the field on their first drive of the season, and the fear started creeping back in, just slightly. But as expected, Minter adjusted, the players recovered, and Baltimore’s defense dominated the rest of the game. Daniel Jones had fewer than 200 passing yards despite trailing for most of the game. Jonathan Taylor had a solid game, but the Ravens didn’t let him break away for any massive plays. Marlon Humphrey also pried the ball out of his hands after one catch, one of Baltimore’s two turnovers along with a Roquan Smith interception. The pass rush was also very solid, as they finished with two sacks and nine quarterback hits. #Colts QB Daniel Jones was the most pressured quarterback of Week 1, according to @NextGenStats . Jones was pressured on 18 of his 34 dropbacks (52.9%) against the Ravens. — Noah Compton (@nerlens_) September 14, 2026 Special teams: My preseason worries about Tyler Loop were loud, so I’ll make this section just as loud. The second-year kicker had a fantastic day to open the season. He hit all five of his extra points and went 2/2 on his field goal attempts, including a blast from 57 yards for a new career-long that would have been good from 60-plus. Rookie punter Ryan Eckley averaged only 46.7 on his three punts, but all three were beauties that landed inside the 20. He didn’t make any major mistakes, which is a major compliment for the rookie. The Ravens also had good punt and kickoff returns. The Bad Pass protection: While the offensive line was dominant in the run game, they were less consistent in pass protection. There were moments that Lamar Jackson had all day to throw in a clean pocket. There were also moments where Jackson was immediately pressured into a Houdini escape act. Pro Football Focus charted the Ravens with allowing 10 pressures on 33 pass plays, and none of the starters on the line got above a 70.0 pass blocking grade. I am willing to give them some grace with a number of the starters not playing in the preseason, plus Vega Ioane and Jovaughn Gwyn getting their first NFL start against a talent like DeForest Buckner. But they need to improve, and fast. Pass game without Flowers: The Ravens started hot, hunting explosives early and often like they told us they would all offseason. But the pass game got dicey once Flowers went down. He accounted for 150 of Jackson’s 229 first-half passing yards; in the second half, Jackson did not eclipse 100. While some of that can be attributed to the Ravens going run-heavy with the lead, Flowers’ absence was clearly felt. They didn’t have much going through the air until Chris Moore caught a 53-yard deep catch-and-run late in the fourth to seal the game for Baltimore. With Flowers day-to-day and Ja’Kobi Lane down for weeks, guys like Rashod Bateman, Tez Walker, and Elijah Sarratt are going to become the focus of this wide receiver room. They will need to step up. The Ugly Penalties: This made this game closer than it ever should have been. The Ravens went into double-digit territory, totaling 10 penalties for 86 yards. Beyond the sheer amount of penalties the Ravens had, they had multiple penalties that eliminated big plays. Ja’Kobi Lane had his first career touchdown taken away by a hold. Rashod Bateman converted a first down on third and medium on a long catch that was taken away by a hold. Chris Moore had a 49-yard return that turned field position at midfield into starting inside the 20. There’s a chance the Ravens win by 30+ with ease if they don’t commit even half the penalties.
author: Zach Canter

title: Buffalo Bills vs. Detroit Lions: Series history, Josh Allen record
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions have both been around for a long time. A really long time. Yet, somehow, Thursday night will be just the 14th regular-season meeting between the two franchises.  And, because apparently 13 games spread across more than five decades isn’t weird enough, there’s this: The Bills have scored 274 points in those games. The Lions have scored 273. One point […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 15: James Cook #4 of the Buffalo Bills runs with the ball while being chased by Jamal Adams #25 of the Detroit Lions in the third quarter at Ford Field on December 15, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions have both been around for a long time. A really long time. Yet, somehow, Thursday night will be just the 14th regular-season meeting between the two franchises. And, because apparently 13 games spread across more than five decades isn’t weird enough, there’s this: The Bills have scored 274 points in those games. The Lions have scored 273. One point separates two teams that have been playing football for over a combined hundred years. This week’s Time Capsule takes us through a series that hasn’t given us a lot of games but has certainly given us a few worth remembering. _____________________________________________________________________________ The last time: Dec. 15, 2024 This one was supposed to be a potential Super Bowl preview. The Lions entered the afternoon 12-1 and riding an 11-game winning streak. The Bills were 10-3 and coming off a 44-42 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Apparently, Buffalo decided 42 points wasn’t enough. The Bills walked into Ford Field and scored 48. Josh Allen threw for 362 yards and two touchdowns while adding another 68 yards and two scores on the ground. James Cook rushed for 105 yards and two touchdowns as Buffalo piled up 559 yards of offense. And they needed almost all of it. Buffalo jumped out to a 14-0 lead and stretched that advantage to 35-14 in the third quarter, but Jared Goff and the Lions weren’t going quietly. Goff threw for 494 yards and five touchdowns. Detroit scored 21 points in the fourth quarter, and a game Buffalo had seemingly put away turned into one where nobody could really relax until the clock finally hit zero. Bills 48. Lions 42. Potential Super Bowl preview? Well, we know how that part turned out. But Buffalo did leave Detroit with one of its biggest wins of the regular season, and Allen left with another addition to the increasingly ridiculous collection of games on his MVP résumé. _____________________________________________________________________________ Before that: Thanksgiving in Detroit Two years earlier, Allen and the Bills were also in Detroit. Actually, they were there for the second time in five days. A massive snowstorm in Western New York had forced Buffalo’s Week 11 game against the Cleveland Browns to Ford Field. The Bills won that one, flew home, and then turned around and went right back to Detroit for Thanksgiving. Because why make anything easy? This time, the Lions made sure Buffalo had to work until the very end. Detroit tied the game at 25 with just 23 seconds left. Allen hit Stefon Diggs for 36 yards on the first play of the ensuing drive, Buffalo moved into field-goal range, and Tyler Bass connected from 45 yards with two seconds left to give the Bills a 28-25 win. Allen finished with 253 passing yards and two touchdowns while adding 78 yards and another score on the ground. It wasn’t quite the offensive explosion we would see two years later, but the result was the same. _____________________________________________________________________________ The first one: Rookie Josh To find Allen’s first game against Detroit, we have to go all the way back to 2018. Buffalo was 4-9. Detroit was 5-8. Allen was a rookie, and the Bills were still trying to figure out exactly what they had in their first-round quarterback. There were clues. Allen threw for 204 yards and a touchdown and rushed for another score as Buffalo beat Detroit 14-13. It wasn’t 48-42, and it wasn’t a last-second Thanksgiving win, but it started a streak. Allen is now 3-0 against Detroit. Thursday night gives him a chance to make it four. _____________________________________________________________________________ How far back do we have to go? Want to find the last time the Lions beat the Bills? We need to open a slightly older Time Capsule. Oct. 15, 2006. Dick Jauron was Buffalo’s head coach. J.P. Losman was the quarterback. Willis McGahee was carrying the football. For Detroit, it was Jon Kitna at quarterback, Kevin Jones at running back, and Roy Williams catching passes. The Lions won 20-17, and they haven’t beaten Buffalo since. The Bills have won five straight meetings — in 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022, and 2024. Of course, there’s a pretty important qualifier here. Buffalo and Detroit only see each other once every four years under the NFL’s normal scheduling rotation, so a 20-year drought doesn’t exactly mean the Bills have spent two decades tormenting the Lions. But 20 years is 20 years. _____________________________________________________________________________ One stadium closes, another one opens There’s one more piece of history that makes this week’s matchup a little different. Allen’s first game against Detroit, that 14-13 win in 2018, was the last time the Lions played a regular-season game in Orchard Park. It was also their last game in the old Highmark Stadium. Now they’re back, and this time they’re part of something much bigger than the series history. Thursday night’s game will be the first regular-season game played in the new Highmark Stadium. The Bills and Lions have met only 13 times. Buffalo holds an 8-4-1 advantage. One point separates them on the all-time scoreboard. Detroit hasn’t beaten Buffalo since 2006, and Josh Allen has never lost to the Lions. But none of that history happened here. The new stadium doesn’t have a Bills-Lions story yet. Thursday night gets to write the first one.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Penalties were a big factor in Buffalo vs. Houston
summary: For those of you new to the site (and I hope there are many of you), here’s the gist; every week I review the penalties from the Bills game. We talk the rules, what was a big deal. What wasn’t. This week will be a bit shortened just like the game week. Standard and Advanced […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills looks to pass the ball during the first quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images For those of you new to the site (and I hope there are many of you), here’s the gist; every week I review the penalties from the Bills game. We talk the rules, what was a big deal. What wasn’t. This week will be a bit shortened just like the game week. Standard and Advanced Metrics Penalty Counts This is where most traditional penalty analysis lives and breathes. For us it’s just the journey. The league averages are likely a good deal higher now than they will be at the end of the season, but this is where things stand right now. Buffalo was significantly higher than average while Houston was right around it. The easy conclusion is that the Bills had the rougher day, but that’s not necessarily true. Let’s keep going. For yards called on the field, both teams had a very rough go of it. And here the script is flipped. At least on the assessed yards. Here’s where we diverge from traditional analysis. On the right side are “true yards” which count yards impacted/negated by flags as well. And when they’re added in, it’s a dead heat. Penalty harm Buffalo Bills I apologize as I have a time crunch this week so I won’t go through all the flags or have GIFs but look for those next week. The short version for any new readers is that “Harm” factors in not just the assessed yards of a flag, but those negated by penalty as well. It also counts lost downs, points negated, etc. For an example of the calculation, Christian Benford’s defensive pass interference call was assessed for 21 yards which is 2.1 harm (yards x 0.1) but also gave up a free down from second. That adds in 1.0 harm for the total of 3.1. Davison Igbinosun has a “negative” harm on his defensive holding as the Texans had gained seven yards on the play but gave that up for the free five to retain the down. It’s a rare quirk in the formula. It happens, but not enough to drastically revise the whole thing. Overall I felt the penalties were warranted on Buffalo. The too many men on the field which negated what should have been an easy conversion was in my opinion the most egregious one. I know this is brief, so let me know if you have any questions/thoughts/concerns in the comments. The Bills had 13.2 harm for this game total. 10.0 is a good enough divider between a good day and bad, so it’s safe to say the yellow laundry had an impact on Buffalo. Houston Texans The Texans by count looked much better off than Buffalo, but a closer look at impact says otherwise. The Texans had two flags over 4.0 Harm. Kamari Lassiter was called for defensive pass interference and that is all assessed yards. This occurred in the end zone, putting the ball on the one-yard line and was a true field flipper. David Montgomery was called for a chop block and this was more complex. The flag itself was 15 yards. It also wiped out a six-yard gain on 3rd & 5. That negated a first down or, put differently, impacted two downs for another 2.0 Harm. The Texans had 14.2 total harm. While not by much, despite the lower counts compared to the Bills, the Texans had the worse day.

title: 5 Detroit Lions to watch at the Buffalo Bills
summary: The Buffalo Bills are set to take on the Detroit Lions on Thursday night, and they’ll look to open play at the new Highmark Stadium with a win. After slaying their demons down south by beating the Houston Texans in Houston for the first time since 2006, Buffalo is riding high to open the 2026 […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions runs onto the field prior to an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are set to take on the Detroit Lions on Thursday night, and they’ll look to open play at the new Highmark Stadium with a win. After slaying their demons down south by beating the Houston Texans in Houston for the first time since 2006, Buffalo is riding high to open the 2026 NFL season. The Lions also won their first game, though they took a slightly different route to do so. Detroit needed overtime to dispatch the New Orleans Saints, holding on to win 31-30 in a back-and-forth contest. Neither the Bills nor the Lions were able to pull away from their respective opponents, and it’s likely that we’re set for an entertaining game between two of the more exciting offensive clubs in the league this season. If the Bills are going to start this season 2-0, they’ll need to slow some of Detroit’s top players, and they have plenty of weapons to highlight. Here are five Lions to watch against the Bills this week. _____________________________________________________________________________ RB Jahmyr Gibbs Detroit’s top running back might wear number zero, but he’s arguably the best running back in the NFL right now. Equally dangerous as a runner and a receiver, Gibbs can hurt teams in a variety of ways. against New Orleans on Sunday, he totaled 156 rushing yards on a league-leading 29 carries. Nearly half of his rushing attempts resulted in a first down, as he achieved that mark a league-leading 14 times in Week One. As if averaging 5.4 yards per rush wasn’t impressive enough, Gibbs also totaled five receptions for 30 yards on five targets. That was actually a lower-end day for him as a receiver, as he has caught 186 passes for 1,479 yards and ten scores over the course of his career. Now in his fourth year, Gibbs is the bellcow back for the first time, as his former running mate David Montgomery is now playing for Buffalo’s Week One opponent in Houston. Montgomery scored three times in the opener against the Bills, and while Buffalo limited his efficiency by holding him to three yards per carry, he doesn’t have nearly the same burst that Gibbs does. Buffalo needs to be disciplined in its run fits, and the defense needs to be much better overall when it comes to tackling. Otherwise, Gibbs will make them pay. WR Amon-Ra St. Brown The Saints kept St. Brown relatively quiet last week, and he still caught ten passes for 67 yards and two touchdowns on 14 targets in the game. He currently leads the league in targets, receptions, and receiving touchdowns. After Buffalo allowed Nico Collins to catch seven passes for 75 yards and a score last week on ten targets, they’ll face yet another challenge this week in trying to contain St. Brown. He can operate from multiple places on the field, and whether he’s inside or outside, he’s extremely dangerous. Will defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard have top corner Christian Benford travel with him like Benford did with Collins on Sunday? Or, will Leonhard try a different strategy this week? With speedster Jameson Williams on the other side, it’s difficult to commit too many resources to one offensive target, and that’s without even discussing tight end Sam LaPorta. The Benford vs. St. Brown matchup is going to be tremendous on Thursday night. G Ben Bartch After starter Christian Mahogany suffered an injury, which looks likely to keep him out of action this week, Bartch filled in admirably against the Saints. However, with a backup center in Juice Scruggs already starting, the difficulty for Detroit’s offensive line is cranked up a notch this week. Second-year man Deone Walker was a tremendous problem for Houston on Sunday, as was veteran Ed Oliver. Not only is the talent of Buffalo’s interior defensive line something to contend with, but the crowd noise is certainly to be amped up this week. Buffalo’s home crowd is always lively, but with Thursday night being the home opener in a brand-new stadium, I expect the twelfth man to make communication difficult for Detroit. Starting a few backup offensive linemen on the road isn’t ideal, and if Buffalo’s top-line unit can take advantage of some backups up front for the Lions, they can have a huge impact on the game. DE Aiden Hutchinson This guy is a monster. Just four days after having to deal with the combination of Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, Buffalo will have to find a way to deal with Hutchinson, a former No. 2 overall pick. On Sunday against New Orleans, Hutchinson had two sacks, four quarterback hits, and two tackles for loss. That’s how you impact the game up front. Buffalo had a great protection scheme in that they used double-teams, slides, and chips to keep Houston’s edge rushers off balance. They varied who was staying in to chip, and they kept switching who they double teamed, as well. The Bills will have to be just as disciplined in their plan to limit Hutchinson, as he is the kind of player who can single-handedly ruin a game plan. Left tackle Dion Dawkins and right tackle spencer Brown have to bring their A-game. CB Rock Ya-Sin A banged-up Detroit secondary is an area that Buffalo’s explosive passing offense should look to exploit this week. They’re already missing starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who are on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. Reserve safeties Thomas Harper and Christian Izien are also dealing with injuries, so players like Avonte Maddox and Chuck Clark have stepped into larger roles. That kind of unrest at the safety level puts stress on the corners, and Saints quarterback Tyler Shough picked on Ya-Sin last week. On ten targets, Ya-Sin allowed seven catches for 52 yards and a touchdown for a passer rating against of 115.2. Buffalo looked like a completely different team passing the football last week thanks in large part to the addition of DJ Moore on the outside. He opens things up for everyone, as does tight end Dalton Kincaid. If Ya-Sin is one-on-one against anyone on Thursday, I assume that quarterback Josh Allen will take his shots.
author: Sean Murphy

full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 15: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills scores a touchdown in the first quarter against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on December 15, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The last time the Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions squared off, Josh Allen and Buffalo’s offense won a shootout at Ford Field, prevailing 48-42 in Week 15 of the 2024 NFL season. title: Exploring Detroit Lions tendencies ahead of Week 2’s game against Buffalo Bills
summary: The Lions have a clear identity. On both sides of the ball. That’s been the case for the entirety of the Dan Campbell era, the most successful era in Lions football since the Barry Sanders era in the mid-to-late 1990s. Let’s dive into those clear tendencies before the Buffalo Bills host the Lions on Thursday […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - AUGUST 22: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions looks on during warm-ups before a preseason game against the Washington Commanders at Ford Field on August 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Lions have a clear identity. On both sides of the ball. That’s been the case for the entirety of the Dan Campbell era, the most successful era in Lions football since the Barry Sanders era in the mid-to-late 1990s. Let’s dive into those clear tendencies before the Buffalo Bills host the Lions on Thursday Night Football in Week 2. You know, the home-opening prime time game you’ve had circled on the calendar for months now. It’s finally right around the corner. Lions offense Jared Goff vs. pressure Every quarterback experiences a dip in efficiency while under pressure. It’s only natural. BUT, no one has a larger discrepancy in performance from a clean pocket compared to when pressured over the past three seasons. Check this from Fantasy Points’ Scott Barrett, posted right before the season: Jared Goff is literally the worst most pressure-sensitive QB in football @FantasyPtsData https://t.co/g8Vm0sf90n pic.twitter.com/eMa02boPe0 — Scott Barrett (@ScottBarrettDFB) September 3, 2026 So while technically every week “pressure the quarterback” could be key to the game for a defense, it’s really important in this game for the Bills against Goff. He might be the last true drop back quarterback in today’s NFL. Not only does he have the largest EPA per drop back difference in his clean pocket vs. pressured drop backs, his clean pockets amounted to the No. 1 EPA per drop in all of football from 2023 to 2025. Bananas! He was only pressured on 22% of his drop backs against the Saints in Week 1 — a very low number — and went 3-of-7 for 49 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions. But the larger-sample based point remains. Getting to Goff is absolutely paramount. Under center The surge in under center plays across the NFL was one of the fascinating storylines from Week 1, and a reminder of the league’s cyclical nature. NFL league wide under center usage jumped dramatically in Week 1. On normal situation 1st & 10 plays, NFL offenses were under center 66.5% of the time, up from 45.9% in Week 1 of 2025, a 20.6 percentage point jump. That’s higher than every full season rate since 2012. — Ryan Paganetti (@RyanPaganetti) September 14, 2026 The Lions want to live under center. And their narrow victory over the Saints was an indicator of the point of emphasis for Detroit’s offense. Per Football Insights on Twitter , via Fantasy Points Data, the Lions were under center on 75% of their offensive plays in Week 1, second only to the Raiders (75.5%). The third place team in under-center snaps (Ravens) came in at 66.7%. The Bills were under center on 64.3% of their offensive plays in Houston. Jahmyr Gibbs, workhouse In his first two seasons in with the Lions, Gibbs was indisputably in a running back committee with David Montgomery. ‘Tis not the case anymore, especially with Isaiah Pacheco on IR. Gibbs toted the rock 29 times — for 156 yards — against the Saints. Backup Sione Vaki had two carries for seven yards. Gibbs also caught five passes for another 30 yards. His 29 carries were five attempts more than anyone else in the NFL in Week 1. Make no mistake about it — Gibbs is a distinct workhorse in this Lions offense. They want him to touch the ball as frequently as realistically possible, and he’s super explosive, all of which is why he likely went No. 1 overall in your fantasy draft. Play Action I’ll be brief here, because this is straight-forward. Due to their ground-game affinity, the Lions like to first sell the run before passing as much as any club in football. In 2024, Goff led qualifying quarterbacks with 35.7% of his drop backs coming on play action. A season ago his percentage dipped to 28.1% but still ranked in the Top 10 of the NFL. On Sunday against the Saints, Goff utilized play action on 34.1% of his drop backs. This has long been a staple of Detroit’s aerial attack. Lions Defense Blitz happy Detroit defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard — yes, that Kelvin Sheppard — had his unit blitz at the 13th-highest rate in 2025 at 26.6%. In Week 1, he ignited the blitz, sending an extra rusher on 43% of the Saints drop backs, which amounted to the fifth-highest rate among all teams. For the record, Jim Leonhard blitzed C.J. Stroud 24.7% of the time, the 17th-highest in Week 1. Given the Lions don’t have their starting safeties, Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, who, when healthy, might be the best safety tandem in the NFL, if Week 1 is any indication of Sheppard’s philosophy, he simply wants to regularly send the house in hopes of getting the football out of the hands of the opposing quarterback as quickly as possible to limit long-developing routes being targeted downfield. Aidan Hutchinson, workhorse For as much as Gibbs is a one-man show — and a damn good one at that — in the backfield for the Lions, Hutchinson is a one-man wrecking crew on the edge getting after the passer on this Detroit defense. In Week 1, he registered a whopping 10 pressures. The next-highest pressure total came from nose tackle Alim McNeill, who had three. Last season, counting the playoffs, Hutchinson accumulated 100 pressures. Second on the team was Al-Quadin Muhammad, with 53, and he signed with the Buccaneers in free agency. In April, the Lions drafted Derrick Moore in the second round, a rusher I liked quite a bit before the draft, but expectations shouldn’t be astronomically high for him. D.J. Wonnum was the free-agent signee to bookend Hutchinson on the edge. He did muster three pressures against New Orleans yet has only eclipsed the 40-pressure plateau once in his NFL career, and that came back in 2021, his second professional season. The Lions lean on Hutchinson to generate consistent pressure probably more than any other club relies on its No. 1 pass rusher.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bills at Texans Week 1 snap counts: Tight ends take over,  defense logs 79 snaps
summary: The Buffalo Bills opened the 2026 season with a thrilling 36-31 win over the Houston Texans, but the final score only tells part of the story. Buffalo’s offense produced 36 points and 409 total yards on just 58 snaps. The defense, meanwhile, was forced to play 79 snaps as Houston sustained drives and repeatedly tested […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 13: Tight end Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills screams after a first down reception during the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Buffalo Bills on September 13, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX.(Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Buffalo Bills opened the 2026 season with a thrilling 36-31 win over the Houston Texans, but the final score only tells part of the story. Buffalo’s offense produced 36 points and 409 total yards on just 58 snaps. The defense, meanwhile, was forced to play 79 snaps as Houston sustained drives and repeatedly tested Buffalo’s secondary. The Week 1 snap counts give us our first meaningful look at how head coach Joe Brady and his staff plan to divide Buffalo’s roles this season. They also reveal several immediate storylines, including an offense built around multiple tight ends, a surprisingly straightforward running-back rotation and a defensive front that relied heavily on its top four players. Bills offensive snap counts: 58 snaps Offensive line starts with perfect attendance There was no rotation or interruption along Buffalo’s offensive line. Alec Anderson, Dion Dawkins, Connor McGovern, O’Cyrus Torrence and Spencer Brown played all 58 offensive snaps. That continuity helped Buffalo avoid a repeat of last season’s nightmare in Houston, when Allen was sacked eight times and took several additional hits. The Texans still created pressure, but Buffalo’s starting five remained intact and gave Allen enough time to throw for 334 yards and lead the game-winning 96-yard drive. Tackle Tylan Grable was the only reserve offensive lineman to appear, joining the offense for one snap as an extra blocker. The tight ends were everywhere Buffalo’s tight-end usage may be the most revealing number from the entire offensive table. Joe Brady did not simply keep four tight ends on the roster for decoration. Dalton Kincaid played 42 snaps, or 72%, while Dawson Knox was on the field for 39 snaps, or 67%. Jackson Hawes added another 25 snaps, reaching 43%. Even Keleki Latu saw action, playing four offensive snaps. Altogether, Buffalo’s four tight ends accounted for 110 player-snaps across 58 offensive plays. That works out to nearly 2 tight ends per play. Buffalo used 13 personnel, featuring one running back and three tight ends, on 37% of its offensive snaps which strongly suggests that multiple-tight-end formations will serve as a foundation of this offense. James Cook leads a clean running-back rotation Unsurprisingly, James Cook had 42 snaps, 72% of the offensive counts. The more interesting backfield number came behind him. Frank Gore Jr., elevated from the practice squad with Ty Johnson unavailable, played 11 offensive snaps. Ray Davis received only five. Neither had much rushing production, with one carry for three yards apiece. Still, Gore receiving more than twice as many offensive snaps as Davis is something worth following. DJ Moore immediately took over a major role DJ Moore led every Bills skill-position player with 44 offensive snaps, good for a 76% share. He also delivered five receptions for 100 yards and a touchdown in his Buffalo debut. There should be no question about Moore’s place in this offense after one week. He was Buffalo’s most-used wide receiver. Khalil Shakir played 31 snaps, followed closely by Keon Coleman with 29. Joshua Palmer received only 18 offensive snaps below that of Coleman, but one of them produced the biggest play of the afternoon: his 34-yard game-winning touchdown reception. That is an important reminder that snap counts explain opportunity, but they do not always measure impact. Bills defensive snap counts: 79 snaps Buffalo’s defense had a much heavier workload than its offense, playing 21 additional snaps. That helps place some of the individual percentages in context. Several members of the defense were asked to handle enormous workloads in the first game of the season. Three defenders never left the field The Bills had three defenders play all 79 snaps: linebacker Terrel Bernard, cornerback Christian Benford and safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson. Cole Bishop played 72 snaps. Maxwell Hairston played 66 snaps, giving the second year cornerback an 84% share in his first start of the season. Dee Alford handled 48 snaps in the slot. The secondary rotation will be worth monitoring, but the larger concern is how frequently Houston found favorable matchups against it. The defensive front carried a heavy load Ed Oliver led Buffalo’s defensive linemen with 65 snaps, an 82% share. That is a substantial workload for an interior defender. Deone Walker followed with 51 snaps, while Dorian Williams played 53. The snap counts show that Buffalo did not treat Deone Walker as a rotational project. He was one of the defense’s primary players in the opener. The interior rotation existed, but Oliver and Walker carried the overwhelming majority of the workload. Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb each played 63 snaps, or 80% from the EDGE. Like Oliver and Walker inside, Rousseau and Chubb were clearly established as Buffalo’s preferred edge combination. With the defense playing so many snaps, however, managing those workloads on a four-day turnaround will be worth watching. Bernard and Williams form the primary linebacker pairing Terrell Bernard never left the field, while Dorian Williams played 53 snaps, or 67%. Buffalo’s linebacker distribution was fairly straightforward. Bernard handled every-down communication duties, while Williams served as the primary linebacker next to him when the defensive package required it. Bills special-teams snap counts Sam Franklin Jr. led Buffalo with 25 special-teams snaps, or 81%, without appearing on defense. Jordan Hancock was directly behind him with 23 snaps, or 74%. Joe Andreessen and Keleki Latu each played 20, or 65%. Latu’s usage is particularly informative. He played only four offensive snaps but was one of Buffalo’s busiest special-teams players. That role helps explain his value on a tight-end depth chart that already includes Kincaid, Knox and Hawes. What do these numbers tell us? Buffalo’s Week 1 snap counts reveal an offense that wants to use size and versatility. The Bills kept multiple tight ends involved, made Moore their leading receiver by playing time and trusted Kincaid with a much broader role. They also received steady work from an offensive line that did not miss a snap. Defensively, the story was different. Buffalo’s starters were asked to play far too much football. Bernard, Benford and Gardner-Johnson never left the field, while Oliver, Rousseau and Chubb all handled heavy workloads. The Bills have little time to recover or make corrections. Detroit arrives Thursday night for the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium, giving Buffalo only four days between games to determine how the Bills will get their defense off the field.
author: Sara Larson

title: Detroit Lions at Buffalo Bills Week 3 injury tracker
summary: The Buffalo Bills returned from their little field trip to Houston fairly healthy, but now as they prepare to face the Detroit Lions on Thursday Night Football’s Week 2 airing, they aren’t going to have much time to heal up what things bumps and bruises they are dealing with.  The first report of Week 2 is a little […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: DJ Moore #2 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Houston Texans during the second quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills returned from their little field trip to Houston fairly healthy , but now as they prepare to face the Detroit Lions on Thursday Night Football’s Week 2 airing, they aren’t going to have much time to heal up what things bumps and bruises they are dealing with. The first report of Week 2 is a little longer than last week’s, but it’s still not scary. NOTE: This tracker will be updated following each injury report leading up to kickoff. _____________________________________________________________________________ Buffalo Bills injury report Monday It’s important to remember that the Bills did not actually practice on Monday. This list just represents what they estimate participation would have been had they actually done anything much more than film work and rest and recovery exercises. Monday injury report pic.twitter.com/vvOoRtQuKf — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) September 14, 2026 Limited Practice LB Terrel Bernard – Calf RB Ty Johnson – Hamstring DL T.J. Sanders – Knee Full Practice S Cole Bishop – Knee/Groin OLB Bradley Chubb – Thumb DB Jordan Hancock – Quad What we’re watching The good news is that DJ Moore’s quick trip to the medical tent Sunday afternoon, along with Josh Allen’s temporary hand discomfort, didn’t amount to anything. I would expect Ty Johnson to return this week, but if he does, what does that mean for Frank Gore, Jr.? The second-year running back was called up from the practice squad Sunday and out snapped Ray Davis on offense. In fact, the Bills’ fourth running back doubled Davis’s snaps: Gore, Jr. 10, Davis 5. Offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael, Jr. — or Joe Brady depending on how we want to look at the Buffalo offense – seemed very content using Gore, Jr. in a blocking role. It’s unlikely that Bernard will be unavailable, but if he can’t we could see Shaq Thompson called up from the practice squad. Tuesda y Tuesday injury report pic.twitter.com/FteY4KZ9jd — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) September 15, 2026 No Practice DT T.J. Sanders Limited Practice LB Terrel Bernard S Cole Bishop RB Ty Johnson Full Practice OLB Bradley Chubb DB Jordan Hancock What we’re watching Bishop was technically “downgraded” to limited after an estimated full practice on Monday. There’s no serious indication he could miss this game, however. Apparently Sanders was sick, which led to his absence. He did not play in Week 1 against the Texans, remember. I’m mostly zeroing in on Johnson. Despite getting in a practice on Friday before Week 1’s game in Houston, Buffalo decided to keep the veteran on the sidelines as he nurses his hamstring injury back to full health. For as much as it might seem like he should be close to 100% by now — after suffering the injury in the Blue & Red Scrimmage in early August — the Bills could be staring at the 10-day layoff after this game and decide to keep him on the shelf for one more (game) week. Fortunately, DJ Moore did not find himself on the official injury report after this update from Syracuse.com’s Matt Parrino: D.J. Moore left the field after stretch and went back to the locker room. He’s back now with helmet on and rejoined wide receiver group as the Bills finish up individual period. — Matt Parrino (@MattParrino) September 15, 2026 It appears all is well for Moore two days before this Week 2 showdown with Detroit in prime time. _____________________________________________________________________________ Detroit Lions injury report Monday Short, but inconveniently concentrated injury report to open the week. pic.twitter.com/D7wIHC63KG — Justin Rogers | Detroit Football Network (@Justin_Rogers) September 14, 2026 No Practice OG Christian Mahogany OT Blake Miller Limited Practice OL Juice Scruggs Full Practice S Christian Izien What we’re watching Miller and Scruggs are the blockers to monitor on this short week for the Lions. The former was the club’s first-round pick out of Clemson and played 77 snaps in Week 1. Only allowed one pressure. Scruggs is Detroit’s starting center, and he also played on all 77 offensive snaps for Detroit in their Week 1 victory. If Miller can’t go, veteran Larry Borom is the Lions swing tackle. He’s appeared in 64 games with 38 starts in his six seasons to date. As for Scruggs, who, at this point, seems more likely to play than Miller, if he’s unavailable for Thursday night’s game, the Lions would have to do some positional shuffling, as they don’t have a dedicated backup center on the 53-man roster right now. Tuesday #Lions Tuesday (estimated) practice report. No practice for Christian Mahogany (hip) and Blake Miller (knee) for the second day in a row. D.J. Reed was limited with a foot. Juice Scruggs still limited with the knee. Christian Izien looks good to go. pic.twitter.com/8ZVn2qgsee — Nolan Bianchi (@nolanbianchi) September 15, 2026 No Practice (Estimated) OG Christian Mahogany RT Blake Miller Limited Practice CB D.J. Reed OL Juice Scruggs Full Practice S Christian Izien What we’re watching It’s now trending in the direction of the Lions being down both their starting left guard — Mahogany — and first-round pick right tackle — Miller in this game. As would be the case for any team, not having those two starters up front would be rather sizable losses for the Lions in this one. I wonder how much the short week plays in here. The only other notable development from Tuesday’s report is the sudden inclusion of Reed, the veteran (former Jets) cornerback with a foot injury.

title: Buffalo Bills offensive skill positions shined vs. Houston Texans
summary: Let’s start my season of analysis with an apology. First off, the Buffalo Bills are on a short week and everything is very compressed. Second, my youngest plays sports and I was lucky enough to be able to see her play on Monday evening (I will choose supporting my kids every time, but it does […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: DJ Moore #2 of the Buffalo Bills runs after a catch for a touchdown against the Houston Texans in the second quarter of a game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s start my season of analysis with an apology. First off, the Buffalo Bills are on a short week and everything is very compressed. Second, my youngest plays sports and I was lucky enough to be able to see her play on Monday evening (I will choose supporting my kids every time, but it does compress the week further). I’m also on-call for my full time position and they needed my Monday night too. Even worse, I was wholly prepared to highlight D.J. Moore and how awesome he was, but then Dalton Kincaid also had an amazing game. And Khalil Shakir had a steady game too. So what’s a Skare to do with very little time and so many things to cover? Easy, rip through a few highlights and pretend it’s some kind of deep analysis. What the heck, I think we’re all in a celebratory mood anyway. Highlights masquerading as analysis Dalton Kincaid pic.twitter.com/14haAAmiTs — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 15, 2026 If you look at the yardage of 130, it’s hard to believe that Dalton Kincaid only had five receptions on six targets. That’s a preposterous 26-yards per reception. A huge part of that is the route tree with Kincaid being asked to run more like a wide receiver. In just the three clips above, Kincaid is lined up in three different spots with some pretty deep routes. Kincaid delivered on the trust given to him by Joe Brady and Josh Allen. In the first play, expert use of hands leaves Kincaid with space to high point the ball for an incredible catch. On the second one, Kincaid compresses himself to slip by a defender (finesse) then drags some dudes for extra yards like you’d want a tight end to do. On the final play, there’s more of the wiggle to avoid the first tackle, shifts lanes quickly to avoid a second tackle, and is only stopped by the sideline. This is the tight end Bills fans have been dreaming of for quite some time. Fingers crossed this is the new normal. D.J. Moore pic.twitter.com/zRNO9vXHwm — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 15, 2026 It’s pretty amazing that D.J. Moore’s stat line of five catches (eight targets) and 100 yards would be in second place for yards per reception after hitting 20 yards per. It’s arguable he had the better day thanks to a long touchdown, but it’s a true argument hence the dual “analysis.” For D.J. Moore, I’d like to emphasize his capability to protect himself when contact is unavoidable, but also the timing he’s already shown with Josh Allen. Both of the first catches shown have Allen winding up before Moore is even looking and hitting the receiver on his break. Moore also did an incredible job snatching a frozen rope pass from Allen. I’d add that there was a bit of luck on the touchdown. The defender went for the pass breakup rather than the tackle and it cost them big. I would also add that Moore plays the sideline perfectly and manages to maneuver and make the score. Week 1 lies in the NFL, but there’s some hope this is the new look offense for the Bills. It was hard to improve on offense but after a single contest it’s looking quite possible.
author: Skarekrow

title: Josh Allen earns my Week 1 game ball after leading Bills past Texans
summary: Josh Allen accounted for four touchdowns and delivered when the Bills needed him most The Buffalo Bills did not make their first win of the 2026 season easy. Buffalo’s defense struggled to contain the Houston Texans’ passing attack, the secondary appeared to have a target painted on it for much of the afternoon. Yet, when […]
full_text: Josh Allen accounted for four touchdowns and delivered when the Bills needed him most The Buffalo Bills did not make their first win of the 2026 season easy. Buffalo’s defense struggled to contain the Houston Texans’ passing attack, the secondary appeared to have a target painted on it for much of the afternoon. Yet, when the Bills needed someone to take control, Josh Allen once again reminded everyone why the ball belongs in his hands. Allen led Buffalo to a thrilling 36-31 victory, earning my first game ball of the season. Game ball: Josh Allen Allen completed 20-of-29 passes for 334 yards and two touchdowns while adding 23 rushing yards and two more scores. His 357 total yards and four touchdowns were impressive enough, but the situation in which he delivered made the performance even more meaningful. Houston took a 31-30 lead late in the fourth quarter, leaving Buffalo 96 yards away from the end zone with the game hanging in the balance. Allen responded by marching the Bills down the field and connecting with Joshua Palmer for a 34-yard touchdown with 1:36 remaining. It was the decisive score in a game featuring four fourth-quarter lead changes. That drive felt like vintage Allen. He was aggressive, confident and completely unfazed by the circumstances. Even after a potential interception slipped through the hands of Texans cornerback Kamari Lassiter, Allen came right back on the next play and attacked the same part of the field for the go-ahead touchdown. Opening week can produce some uneven football, particularly with a new head coach and several new pieces on offense. Allen provided the stability. Every time Houston appeared ready to take control, he gave Buffalo an answer. It was also Allen’s first win in Houston after entering the afternoon 0-4 there. More importantly, it gave Joe Brady a victory in his regular-season debut as Buffalo’s head coach. There were several deserving candidates, but Allen’s command of the offense and his work on the final drive made him the clear choice for Week 1. Honorable mention: Dalton Kincaid A healthy Dalton Kincaid looked ready to become one of the most dangerous pieces of Buffalo’s offense. Kincaid caught five of his six targets for 130 yards, averaging an incredible 26 yards per reception. His afternoon included gains of 35 and 40 yards as Allen repeatedly found him attacking Houston’s defense downfield. Kincaid in 2026, fantasy managers and Bills fans should both be paying attention. Honorable mention: DJ Moore DJ Moore’s first regular-season game in a Bills uniform provided exactly the type of performance Buffalo hoped it was adding to the offense. Moore caught five passes for 100 yards and a touchdown, giving Buffalo two 100-yard receivers in the same game. He showed an immediate connection with Allen and provided the offense with another dependable playmaker capable of creating yards after the catch. Buffalo spent much of the offseason talking about how Moore could expand the passing attack. It took only one game for him to demonstrate why. Honorable mention: Tyler Bass Tyler Bass quietly supplied 12 crucial points in a five-point victory. Bass was perfect against Houston, connecting on all three of his field-goal attempts and all three extra points. His kicks included a 46-yard field goal following Buffalo’s takeaway on Houston’s opening possession and a 33-yarder that tied the game at 20. After everything surrounding Buffalo’s kicking situation over the past year, a perfect opening performance deserves recognition. The defense delivered when it mattered Buffalo’s defense will have plenty to correct before Thursday night. Houston found favorable matchups against the secondary throughout the game, and C.J. Stroud threw for 274 yards and two touchdowns. Terrel Bernard finished with 12 total tackles, while Deone Walker and Greg Rousseau each recorded two tackles for loss. The run defense also settled down and performed better in the second half. For all the problems, the defense produced the game’s final answer. Rousseau recorded his second strip-sack of Stroud on Houston’s last possession, and Bernard recovered the fumble to secure the victory. The same combination had helped create Buffalo’s first points when Rousseau forced a fumble on Houston’s opening drive and Ed Oliver recovered it. It was far from a complete defensive performance, but the Bills made the decisive play when they absolutely needed one. A game ball that meant more The most meaningful moment may have happened after the clock reached zero. Inside the locker room, Allen presented Brady with the game ball from his first regular-season victory as an NFL head coach. Brady accepted it, but immediately redirected the recognition. “Only one person deserves this more than anyone else, and that’s Ed Oliver,” Brady told the team. Oliver has endured unimaginable personal loss during the offseason, making Brady’s gesture much larger than football. It was a heartfelt reminder of how closely this team has rallied around him. Allen earned my Week 1 game ball for carrying Buffalo to the finish line. Inside the Bills’ locker room, however, the most important game ball went exactly where it belonged. Buffalo is 1-0, Allen finally has his victory in Houston, and Brady has his first win as a head coach. Now the Bills have a short turnaround to prepare for the Detroit Lions and the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium.
author: Sara Larson

title: Josh Allen is not a reckless, YOLO, turnover-prone quarterback
summary: I’ll admit, it feels bizarre to be compelled to write this about Josh Allen in Year 9, especially after a 36-point eruption against that Houston Texans defense in the Buffalo Bills’ Week 1 win. Allen is not an overly reckless, YOLO, sugar-high quarterback bound to put the ball in precarious situations in critical moments of […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills runs off the field after 36-31 win against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’ll admit, it feels bizarre to be compelled to write this about Josh Allen in Year 9, especially after a 36-point eruption against that Houston Texans defense in the Buffalo Bills’ Week 1 win. Allen is not an overly reckless, YOLO, sugar-high quarterback bound to put the ball in precarious situations in critical moments of every game. But is he ultra conservative? Ab-so-lutely not. I’m letting recency bias get the best of me here, because on Sunday, Allen certainly did make a poor throw the play before he ripped one of the best throws of his career to date to Josh Palmer on the eventual game-winning touchdown. And for as much praise as he’s rightfully received for the 34-yard touchdown — which was a 45 air-yard strike without room to step into the throw — the specific criticism for the jump ball the play before was out of control. Allen saw single coverage on Palmer with a chance for a go-ahead touchdown. The decision wasn’t brutal. The pass was simply underthrown and too far to the inside. Allen would undoubtedly admit that himself. The bad throw deserved to be shown. Without question. But to suggest “this is what you get from Allen every week,” is flat-out incorrect. My gameday column before Week 1 focused on first impressions, and how powerful they can be. And even after an MVP and an incredibly long stay in the NFL’s elite realm of quarterbacks, Allen still can’t shake the first impressions he made in this league. As a rookie, Allen’s 5.1% turnover-worthy play rate (a self-explanatory advanced metric) was the third-highest out of 39 qualifiers. Bad. And the first impression was made. The next season, when he did show clear signs of improvement, Allen’s 4.3% TWP rate was the ninth-highest out of 39 qualifying quarterbacks. That sophomore NFL season cemented the first impression in the minds of many. Heck, I remember going on radio shows after Buffalo’s Week 1 loss to the Jets to begin the 2023 season — in which Allen threw three interceptions and had a fumble — and having to ward off suggestions that he might be Jameis Winston. Check the following chart, and tell me if it reads like a super-careless quarterback. *lower rank is better Josh Allen Turnover-Worthy Play Rate (rank) 4th Q / OT Turnover-Worthy Throw Rate 2025 2.4% (7th / 43) 2.2% (8th) 2024 2.6% (15th / 44) 1.1% (4th) 2023 3.0% (20th / 41) 3.3% (12th) 2022 4.0% (31st / 41) 6.7% (30th) 2021 3.2% (19th / 38) 2.2% (2nd) 2020 3.4% (23rd / 38) Data unavailable Allen was the YOLO, sugar-high quarterback in his first two seasons. Since then, hardly. And he’s gradually improved how well he protects the football in each of the last four seasons. Four seasons is an eternity in the NFL! But it’s like many haven’t caught on to said vital advancement in Allen’s game. Maybe it’s because of the 18-interception 2023 campaign? Probably. Allen threw the second-most picks that year, but as you can see above, his Turnover-Worthy Play Rate ranked smack dab in the middle of all quarterbacks. Despite this clearly being a persuasive piece, it’s alright with me if you want to ignore the numbers because of your inherent faith in the old-fashion eyeball test. Because even if in your mind Allen is still a reckless, YOLO, sugar-high quarterback who puts the ball in danger every game in key moments, it is precisely what makes him such a daunting matchup for any defense. And, sure, you’ve heard about that dynamic before, but it’s probably not explored deeply enough. Here are Allen’s Big-Time Throw Rates — a metric that counts the most challenging, high-degree of difficulty throws, typically further downfield / through tight windows — and rank among quarterbacks with 200+ attempts since the beginning of 2020. Josh Allen Big-Time Throw Rate (rank) 2025 5.1% (9th) 2024 7.0% (1st) 2023 6.2% (2rd) 2022 7.6% (1st) 2021 5.9% (6th) 2020 6.1% (8th) Ridiculous, right? As you can probably imagine, Allen is the only quarterback in the NFL to finish in the Top 10 of that metric in each of the last six seasons. And it speaks directly to Allen squeezing everything humanly possible out of his offensive scheme and skill-position talent. He’s often had to make those challenging throws because the easy, wide-open tosses haven’t been available to him as frequently as the other top quarterbacks in football. Allen operating as the most full-throttle, all-gas, no-brakes quarterback in the NFL is the best possible scenario for the Bills offense and the worst possible scenario for each defense it faces. Allen’s bad plays may — see: probably — look different than other quarterbacks. Does that really matter? All interceptions and turnovers count the same. In golf, if you hit the ball one foot out of bounds or 20 yards out of bounds, you’re still taking the same penalty. I get it though — the ball that sails way right has more of a visceral impact on our brains. It’s a cognitive bias we naturally suffer from. The distinction between the psychological influence and real-life result of those occurrences needs to be acknowledged. And with any quarterback, I’d much rather chances being taken at a ferocious clip than essentially never looking for the big play, routinely erring on the side of caution. The timid, risk-averse quarterbacks are available in the undrafted ranks every April. And, heck, there are many passers who have the desire to play aggressively but lack the physical talent to match. Without being in defensive game plan meetings, I’m going to venture a guess that Allen’s willingness and ability to make big-time throws stresses a defense significantly more than his occasional tendency to give the ball away. There’s just no way a defensive coordinator fires up the film before playing the Bills and is giddy about his unit’s chances to force an Allen turnover. He’s almost assuredly far more unsettled about what Allen is capable of doing to his defense with his arm… and that’s before you factor in any of the quarterback’s legendary running talent. How do I stick the landing on this column? Maybe just with my take that Allen is absolutely not a reckless quarterback. In fact, he’s long been a player who understands, is comfortable with, and confident in his seismic talent, which has made him the best player in the NFL, in my opinion .

title: Cat Scratch Reader Reacts Survey: Week 2 brings more questions than answers
summary: We try every year not to overreact to Week 1 for any team in the NFL. Are the Chicago Bears going to average 59 points a game? No. Are the Carolina Panthers going to give up 59 points a game? No. Can I think of more ways to remind you that the Panthers lost Week […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA JANUARY 05: Carolina offensive coordinator Brad Idzik embraces quarterback Bryce Young (9) during the NFL game between the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons on January 5th, 2025 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We try every year not to overreact to Week 1 for any team in the NFL. Are the Chicago Bears going to average 59 points a game? No. Are the Carolina Panthers going to give up 59 points a game? No. Can I think of more ways to remind you that the Panthers lost Week 1 by surrendering a franchise record 59 points in a single game? Probably later. For now, I want to focus on the positives. The Panthers scored 37 points of their own, including staying tied with the Bears at 31 points through about the middle of the third quarter. That’s an offensive output well beyond expectations against a defense that was not playing with an aggressive lead until the fourth quarter. This is not what we have come to expect from a team led by Dave Canales and Bryce Young. Whether or not that can be attributed to a level up from Young or the influence of Brad Idzik calling plays is yet to be determined. Whether or not that was simply a flash in the pan or the sign of things to come is the first question to assess. So that’s where we are starting with y’all this week. Do you think what we saw on Sunday was above, below, or right about the average effort we’ll see from the Panthers offense this season? Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Panthers fans and fans across the country. Was Week 1 emblematic of the Panthers offense? Are you feeling confident in the Panthers? title: Ask Brian: Week 1 fallout
summary: Hello CSR! Welcome to Ask Brian, part one of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! They have signed linebacker Tyrel Dodson off the practice squad in a corresponded roster move. This is a two-for-one response to failures from both […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - January 4: New England Patriots tight end Hunter Henry is tackled by Miami Dolphins linebacker Tyrel Dodson in the fourth quarter. The Patriots played the Dolphins at Gillette Stadium on January 4, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have waived their primary returner and second-year wide receiver Jimmy Horn Jr just a couple days after an abysmal performance in their season opener against the Chicago Bears. They have signed linebacker Tyrel Dodson off the practice squad in a corresponded roster move. This is a two-for-one response to failures from both the special teams unit and the defense from Sunday’s surrender of 59 points. Horn routinely struggled to field punts and kicks and has not provided positive value in a crowded receiver room to date. Meanwhile, on defense, the Panthers gave up 291 rushing yards on 39 attempts (7.5 yards per attempt) and four rushing touchdowns to the Bears. Clearly they need some additional help. Enter Tyrel Dodson. He had 129 tackles, ten for loss, and five sacks last season in 16 starts for the Miami Dolphins. The 28-year old linebacker has long been seen as more of a run defender than a true coverage linebacker, but that seems to fit the Panthers weakness right now. In the return game, look for Chuba Hubbard and Xavier Legette to take the majority of punts and kicks.

title: Panthers vs Bears Game Review: Hasty generalizations
summary: The full story of an NFL season is not written after a single game. Even one where you are force fed a 50-burger in your own stadium. It was a hard one to stomach for anyone rooting for the Carolina Panthers, but despite a lopsided final score and number of concerning takeaways, it’s probably the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates touchdown with Jalen Coker #18 against the Chicago Bears during the third quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The full story of an NFL season is not written after a single game. Even one where you are force fed a 50-burger in your own stadium . It was a hard one to stomach for anyone rooting for the Carolina Panthers, but despite a lopsided final score and number of concerning takeaways, it’s probably the best start to a season in the last 5 years. If I had to sum up the reason why, it’s that even when things looked bad, they still looked competitive. We are all mindful that that is a shamefully low bar, but the point remains that it’s a vast improvement over what has been the recent quality of football coming out of Charlotte, North Carolina. So, let us all not jump to the conclusions that we may want to after a single week. Even if this one week stirs up some still unresolved trauma from the 2024 Panthers defense that allowed almost 32 points per game. Let us look on the bright side and decide that even if the Panthers defense is that bad, scoring 37 points a game means the Panthers will still win an average football game. Feel better yet? No? Then in the spirit of overreacting to Week 1, let’s make some hasty generalizations based on what we saw on Sunday afternoon. Jalen Coker will be the best Panthers receiver of all time A receiver putting up 8 receptions for 138 yards and 2 touchdowns a game? That’s 136 catches for 2,346 yards and 34 touchdowns in a whole season. Make room Steve Smith, there’s another triple-crown winner coming through. He doesn’t even need separation to make it happen, either. According to NFL’s NextGenStats, Coker only had an average 1.9 yards of separation at the time of catch or incompletion – 8th worst total in the league. The Offensive Line is the most consistent in the entire NFL If you thought that both tackles being out for Week 1 and starting a new budget free agent acquisition at center was going to be a problem, you were wrong. In fact, the Panthers offense line looked about as good as it possibly could have given the circumstances as no starter had a run blocking or pass blocking grade considered below average. Hats off to the winners of PFF’s Offensive Line of the Week . Give Bryce Young all of the money If Baker Mayfield is going to sign for 3 years, $165 million to only put up 217 yards and 0 touchdowns, surely Bryce Young’s 361 passing yards and 4 total touchdowns must be worth $60 million a year? Young is currently 3rd in the NFL in passing yards, tied for 2nd in passing touchdowns and top 10 in a bevy of other important stats including EPA/Play (9th – +0.27), completion % over expected (9th – 6.6%), yards per attempt (4th – 9.3) and average depth of target (10th – 9.8 yards). Strip Derrick Brown of his captaincy The Bears scored 8 touchdowns, but 2 of them came on the back of some rough decisions from one of the purported team stalwarts. Mistake number one was leveling Caleb William’s on cheap shot that was flagged for unnecessary roughness after a throwaway that ultimately turned a 3rd and 20 into 1st and goal. I can almost forgive that one as William’s must have been immensely frustrating to deal with the entire afternoon. Williams had nearly a 20% completion percentage over expected and had 10 scrambles for 65 yards and 2 rushing touchdowns. Every time they though they had him, he pulled a Houdini act to get away. But you know what is unforgivable? Taking away a big man interception because you lined up offsides. Do you know how rare it is for a 332 lb defensive lineman to intercept a football? Neither do I, but I know it’s not often, much less from the literal 1 yard line. A big man shows soft hands and a hero’s heart to pluck a ball right out of the air in the Panther’s time of most dire need – and it’s called back because your helmet was over the line? Derrick Brown deserves a lot of love for what he has done for the Panthers, but this is an outrage that cannot be tolerated. It’s not all over yet and there is still plenty of road ahead on this journey. We’ll see you next week after the Panthers take on the Atlanta Falcons. Until then, Keep Pounding

title: Bears-Panthers Upon Further Review: A Closer Look at the Referees
summary: Hello Chicago Bears Fans!  Welcome to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag, that’s right – the refs.  Every week when the Bears end up in the loss column, Bears fans leave Soldier Field (or the living room) with the same two questions: Did we actually lose that game, or did […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 6: A detail view of a flag on the field during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game between the Carolina Panthers and the Chicago Bears, at Soldier Field on October 6, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello Chicago Bears Fans! Welcome to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag, that’s right – the refs. Every week when the Bears end up in the loss column, Bears fans leave Soldier Field (or the living room) with the same two questions: Did we actually lose that game, or did the officials take it from us? And when we are in the win column, we will inevitably hear from opponents’ fans that they were robbed by the refs. Well, were they? Upon Further Review exists to answer these questions with film, the rulebook, and a consistent grading scale: Each week I’ll isolate the flags and no-calls that went against Chicago and against the opponent, grade every one as Correct, Arguable, Incorrect, or Horrible, then roll those grades into four numbers: a Calls-Against-Bears rating, a Calls-Against-Opponent rating, an overall referee performance score, and a differential that shows which sideline got the better of the crew. I’ll also pull the most controversial calls from around the league so we can see what call this year will have NFL fans screaming, “wait, what?” and NFL rules analysts assuring us, “always has been.” Chicago beat Carolina 59–37 on Sunday in Charlotte. Official totals: Bears 12 penalties for 57 yards, Panthers 11 for 84 yards. Below are all accepted flags, in order, with the player named, the yardage, the game clock, and the score when the penalty was enforced. First Quarter CHI 0, CAR 0 Rome Odunze (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 15:00, first play from scrimmage. Swift’s 17-yard run came back; ball spotted at the CHI 19. Dayo Odeyingbo (CHI), roughing the passer, 1 yard — 12:54. After Young’s 26-yard completion to Coker at the CHI 2. Half-the-distance; first-and-goal at the 1. Montez Sweat (CHI), defensive offside, 0 yards — 12:44. Already at the 1; replay first-and-goal. Darren Waller (CAR), offensive pass interference, 9 yards — 12:29. Waller’s 1-yard TD catch wiped off. First-and-goal from the 10. CHI 0, CAR 7 Garrett Bradbury (CHI), offensive holding, 9 yards — 10:09. Swift’s 9-yard run on 3rd-and-1 nullified. Cairo Santos (CHI), kickoff short of landing zone — 5:52. Ball placed at the CAR 40 (no yardage in the official 57-yard total). CHI 14, CAR 7 Isaiah Simmons (CAR), offensive holding, 10 yards — 1:59, on the kickoff return. Carolina started at its 17. M. Freeling (CAR), false start, 5 yards — 1:27. Second Q uarter CHI 14, CAR 7 Mitchell Evans (CAR), unnecessary roughness, 15 yards — 15:00. After Raymond’s 23-yard punt return to the CHI 44; Bears started at the CAR 41 and scored two plays later (Kmet 22-yard TD). CHI 21, CAR 14 S. Thomas (CHI), illegal block above the waist, 10 yards — 12:40, on the kickoff return. Bears started at their 12. Dayo Odeyingbo (CHI), illegal use of hands, 2 yards — 9:21. Half-the-distance; first-and-goal at the 2. Carolina later scored on Young’s 7-yard scramble. Carolina, illegal shift, 5 yards — 9:09. Wiped a 1-yard Hubbard run at the goal line. CHI 24, CAR 21 James Lynch (CHI), defensive offside, 5 yards — 5:16. Robert Hunt (CAR), offensive holding, 10 yards — 4:11. Brooks’ 12-yard run came back. CHI 24, CAR 24 Chicago, delay of game, 5 yards — 0:38. Williams still converted and scored on a 29-yard scramble two plays later (31–24 at half). Third Quarter CHI 31, CAR 31 Colston Loveland (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 4:55. Created 2nd-and-20 at the CAR 21. Derrick Brown (CAR), roughing the passer, 10 yards — 4:31. After Williams threw the ball away on that 2nd-and-20. Automatic first down at the CAR 11; Swift scored from the 1 three plays later (38–31). CHI 38, CAR 31 Cairo Santos (CHI), kickoff short of landing zone — 3:05. Again spotted at the CAR 40. R. Walker (CAR), false start, 5 yards — 2:33. Carolina then failed on 4th-and-3; Monangai ripped the 61-yard TD on the next snap (45–31). Fourth Quarter CHI 45, CAR 31 Chicago, illegal formation, 5 yards — 12:48. Derrick Brown (CAR), defensive offside, 0 yards — 7:21. Nullified Bobby Brown III’s interception in the end zone. Williams threw a 1-yard TD to Jahdae Walker two plays later (52–31). CHI 52, CAR 31 Jalen Coker (CAR), offensive pass interference, 10 yards — 4:38. Wiped a 1-yard TD pass to Mitchell Evans. Carolina still scored on Coker’s 8-yard catch; PAT blocked (52–37). T. Gipson (CAR), neutral zone infraction, 5 yards — 3:52. Gifted Chicago a first down; Swift scored from 28 yards on the next play (59–37). Snapshot: Flags For and Against In our inaugural UFR, I’m glad I’m not in a position to analyze the flags that cost us the game. In fact, it was flags against the Carolina Panthers that were pivotal – the first-ever “roughing the passer” call for Caleb Williams, erasing a 2 nd and 20 near the red zone, and an interception at the goal line that was erased by an offside. Both of those flags were on Carolina Panthers defensive lineman, Derrick Brown. Carolina also had two touchdowns called back for offensive pass interference (Waller in Q1, Coker/Evans in Q4). That said, while those penalties were certainly the most impactful, in my evaluation none of them were incorrect calls. Chicago’s flags were more volume than impact—two landing-zone kickoffs, two holdings that were overcome, and a pair of small defensive infractions near the goal line—except Odeyingbo’s first-quarter roughing, which put Carolina at the 1, and arguably Rome Odunze’s holding call on the first snap of the game, which killed a first down run, and on the next play Luther Burden would fumble the football, leading to a Carolina touchdown. Flag of the Game: The “Roughing the Passer” on Derrick Brown Panthers called for roughing the passer for this hit to Caleb Williams pic.twitter.com/I8GD65igAT — Rate the Refs (@Rate_the_Refs) September 13, 2026 Rule that matters: once the passer leaves the pocket and throws on the run, he loses the one-step protection. He still cannot be hit late with no attempt to avoid, stuffed, or driven through. Williams is outside the pocket, retreating, then dumps the ball toward the sideline. Brown (#95) is still coming. Contact is after the release. Williams goes down hard. Brown said he thought it was one step. Canales called it the two-step rule and “tight.” From video review, it is more than one step. Both from a forcible contact perspective (forearm to Caleb’s sternum) and from the differential between when the pass left Caleb’s hand and when Brown made contact (close to two full steps) – this is classic RTP. I rate this call correct. Brown had plenty of time to pull up and instead he delivers a blow to the quarterback. Upon Further Review — Week 1: Bears 59, Panthers 37 Crew: Brad Allen . Official totals: Chicago 12–57 , Carolina 11–84 . Scale: Correct / Arguable / Incorrect / Horrible . Weight is impact, not whether the flag was right: 1 housekeeping, 2 drive-changer, 3 scoring-situation / automatic first down that feeds points, 4 wiped score, wiped takeaway, or a dead drive flipped into a touchdown. Calls Against Chicago # Play Grade Wt Why 1 Odunze holding, Q1 15:00, 0-0, 10 yds Arguable 2 First-snap hold on a 17-yard Swift run. Typical Week 1 grab; no isolated replay. 2 Odeyingbo RTP, Q1 12:54, 0-0, 1 yd to the 1 Arguable 3 Automatic first down at the 1 after Coker’s 26-yard catch. League already has it in the fine pile. No public isolate. 3 Sweat offside, Q1 12:44, 0-0 0 yds Correct 1 Neutral-zone foul at the 1. Bright line. 4 Bradbury holding, Q1 10:09, 0-7, 9 yds Arguable 2 Killed 3rd-and-1. Chicago still converted the next snap. 5 Santos short of landing zone, Q1 5:52, 7-7 Correct 2 Kick landed at the CAR 22. Rule is automatic: ball at the 40. 6 S. Thomas illegal block above waist, Q2 12:40, 21-14, 10 yds…
