title: Midweek Musings: Buckle Up, Bears Fans
summary: Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: The summer of 2026 was mostly a hot and humid mess in the Midwest. It rained a lot, the temps got uncomfortable early, and we were offered […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Head Coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears looks on against the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: The summer of 2026 was mostly a hot and humid mess in the Midwest. It rained a lot, the temps got uncomfortable early, and we were offered few reprieves. Then football started, and cooler weather arrived. We’re close to hoodie season. You can almost taste the apple cider. I love autumn, mainly for the football, but give me all the other good stuff that comes with it too. I’ve never correctly advocated for a Chicago Bears head coach candidate before Chicago landed Ben Johnson – and I was extremely early. It was early in the 2023 season I started pushing it and when I dropped the idea on a Lions podcast, the hosts about kicked me off the show. I knew I had something at that moment. It’s given me an added layer of enjoyment to this new era of Bears football. I was extremely confident the Bears would be getting an offensive mastermind. I had no idea he’d be such a badass. The new Nike Bears logo is incredible. I love this thing so freaking much . I might need to get another writing gig to help pay off all the gear I’m going to buy. Don’t tell my wife. I was wrong about D’Andre Swift. I said he was a supercharged RB2 or a decent lead in a committee but he wasn’t a guy who could dominate in the run game. While that was the book on Swift before he landed in Chicago – and a fair representation of his work in 2024 – he’s been a much improved back under the Ben Johnson regime. It’s not often you see this type of growth this deep into a player’s career. Kudos to him for making it work. I liked the Panthers jerseys – the black and Carolina Blue (or whatever they’re calling it) is a fun look. I just can’t understand choosing to wear dark colors on a hot day in September while letting your opponent where the traditional away whites. The temps were brutal. I wonder if they regret their uniform choice. Speaking of the hot Carolina temps – did you catch Caleb Williams wiping his hand off mid-play to get a better grip on the football? I don’t think I’ve ever seen that before. Caleb wipes his throwing hand mid-play pic.twitter.com/u3rIOUC44h — Adam Hoge (@AdamHoge) September 15, 2026 PFF put out a grade on Caleb Williams that sure looked like they didn’t watch the same game the rest of the world saw on Sunday. Really good reminder that the grades are an invention for engagement, as explained by their founder years ago. Engage in those grades at your own risk, positive or negative. I said on Bear & Balanced this week that I thought that might’ve been one of Caleb’s best games as a pro. He looked completely in charge and had a steady, high-level performance. There are a couple of throws and runs that will make his end of season highlight reel, yes, but there were so many smart decisions on when to run, when to throw away, and when to check the ball down that were a work in progress last season. This is big trouble for the rest of the league and for those Caleb haters in your group chats. If you’re just coming back to the site and missed my story on the history of the Chicago Bears mascots , I promise you it’s worth your time. These niche history dives are fun but always take more time than I think they will. I thought the TD pass to Jahdae Walker was beautiful. The pass itself was a nice little schematic win, but the fact that Ben Johnson schemed up Walker after he did all the dirty work all game was one of those football moments where you know that guys are buying in and Johnson understands how to reward hard work. Football euphoria. Did you notice that Carolina wanted nothing to do with Zavion Thomas on their kickoffs? I’m curious if that’s a trend we’ll see and, if so, whether there’s a way to call a better return play knowing they’ll be targeting the non-Zavion returner. Plenty of hand-wringing over the defense, and I get it; we’ve come to expect a certain standard of living on the defensive side of the ball over the years. Let’s see where it goes over the next few weeks, but I want those of you who can’t help but lead with the negative to do me a favor and look up at the scoreboard once in a while. This is fun if you’re willing to join the rest of us. I’m eager to get to the Vikings game. I have a lot of Vikings fans in my general orbit, and while we can all be happy for them reveling in their big win against Green Bay last week, it’s time to start making a statement with a divisional victory. I don’t really care who is playing quarterback; jump on this team early and dare them to play in the track meet with you. Pushing teams to get out of their comfort zone puts the ball in harm’s way and will allow the Bears to continue their dominance in the turnover differential. Only 548 more points to break the 2013 Broncos mark…

Beyond surprising results like the Chargers losing to the Cardinals or the Giants beating the Cowboys, bigger storylines emerged. Scoring was way, way up. And the Bears were part of it. We know the Bears are going to move up the ranks after such a headline-grabbing performance. And they were assisted by the likes of some of the week one national darling teams laying eggs (shoutout Green Bay!). Let’s see where Chicago lands this week. WCG – Aaron Leming 7. Chicago Bears (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: The offense’s Year 2 jump under Ben Johnson is evident, but the defense might keep them from being a legitimate Super Bowl contender. The Bears must find some defensive balance, and it must happen in a hurry. Better health will help, but for now, the offense will face continued pressure to produce 30-plus points per game. The Athletic – Josh Kendall and Chad Graff 4. Chicago Bears (1-0) Last week: 10 Sunday: Beat Panthers 59-37 What we learned: Best offense in the NFL? Ben Johnson told our Dan Pompei this offseason that he wanted to build the highest-scoring offense in league history. It seemed outlandish at the time. Then the Bears hung 59 on the Panthers in Week 1, and suddenly anything seems possible. The defense carries plenty of questions, but that offense was unbelievable. Yahoo Sports – Frank Schwab 10. Chicago Bears (1-0, LW: 11) The Bears are going to be fun to watch. The offense was fantastic against a Panthers defense that isn’t great but not that bad (22nd in defensive DVOA last season). They put up 59 points, a franchise record for a season opener, and 552 yards. That’s great. They also allowed 37 points and 478 yards against a Panthers offense that was 25th in DVOA last season. Every game might be a pinball machine. And the Bears’ offense might be so good it doesn’t matter how much the defense allows. It’s why they’re not higher in the top 10. NFL.com – Nick Shook 8. Chicago Bears (11) Ben Johnson stated his intent to rewrite the offensive record books with his team in 2026. After one week, the Bears are on pace to do so. They detonated the Panthers in a style that mirrored their 2025 success, running the ball authoritatively and letting Caleb Williams make superstar plays in an incredible offensive explosion. The one drawback: They gave up 37 points, a concern tied to a defense that still might be a persistent weakness. CBS Sports – Pete Prisco 9. Chicago Bears (15) Maybe Ben Johnson is right and this team will break the single-season scoring record. They looked unstoppable in rolling up 59 points against the Panthers. USAToday – Nate Davis 4. Chicago Bears (5): The Windy City Cowboys? The Bears barely played a lick of defense Sunday in Charlotte but nevertheless looked like a team very much capable of making a run to Super Bowl 61 − especially with Caleb Williams, fresh off his first game with multiple TD passes and runs (even he’s not Allen-esque … yet), at the helm. What do you think of this week’s rankings? Are the Bears getting the respect they deserve following their win?

title: Hot Take Tuesday: Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson have put everyone on notice
summary: Holy Bleep. We will keep it PG today for the kiddos, but my oh my, what a difference a coach and a quarterback make. What the Chicago Bears did on Sunday was historic. The Bears put up numbers never seen in week one of the NFL season. It was the 12th highest-scoring game of all-time. […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after their 59-37 win against the Carolina Panthers of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Holy Bleep. We will keep it PG today for the kiddos, but my oh my, what a difference a coach and a quarterback make. What the Chicago Bears did on Sunday was historic. The Bears put up numbers never seen in week one of the NFL season. It was the 12th highest-scoring game of all-time. The Bears scored the 23rd-highest points by a single team of all-time, and if you go over the last 50 years, that number moves up to 7th. In short, it was bananas. Yes, we could criticize the defense, and it deserves criticism. But we will save that for another time when the defense costs them a victory, because no matter how bad the defense was, it simply didn’t matter. The Bears offense was that good. Think about the growth of Caleb Williams. Don’t think about it from where it was last year in the playoffs. Roll the clock back 365 days and think about where it was when last season started. Do you remember the frantic pace of Caleb’s play against the Vikings? Look at how much more relaxed and in control he is one year later. Look at the growth of Ben Johnson as a head coach. In week one, he made a special teams decision that might have cost the Bears a victory. In week two, he got smashed by his former team. A year later, he’s the one doing the smashing. Look at the buy-in from this team. Did you see the receivers? Jahdae Walker was blocking everyone. D’Andre Swift was an animal in pass protection. Luther Burden and Rome Odunze were putting bodies on everyone. No block, no rock. It’s a full buy-in. Ben Johnson has the beautiful tape to back it up now. You want to have explosive plays when the ball is in your hand? Your teammates will block for you and make that happen. But if you want them to block for you, you need to block for them. I can’t remember a skill position group, as a whole, blocking like this. That is a group of bad mother, you know what. They are a tough group that is going to make secondaries sore on Monday morning. Think about the offensive line. No Drew Dalman, no problem. This line didn’t skip a beat; it controlled the line of scrimmage and allowed the Bears to rush for nearly 300 yards on the ground. D’Andre Swift is now an animal. He’s one of the top 10 backs in the league. He isn’t the same guy who played soft in Detroit. You know what’s amazing? The Bears gained almost 600 yards on offense, and their big three of Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, and Rome Odunze averaged about 35 yards each. They weren’t the focal parts of the offense. They didn’t need to be. The ground game dominated. Caleb Williams dominated. Cole Kmet scored. Jahdae Walker scored. Kaliff Raymond led the receivers on Sunday. It was a full team effort, and their big offensive weapons barely had to carry a load. They scored 59 points anyway. Their time will come. Ben Johnson is a Madman. I say that in every complimentary way possible. He says he wants this offense to be the highest-scoring one of all time, and I believe him. Will they get there? Probably not, but it’ll be fun watching them try. The highest-scoring Bears team is the 1985 Bears. They scored 456 points. They scored 7 defensive TDs and Special Teams TDs that year (not to mention the number of short fields the offense got on turnovers). That offense scored 407 points without the defensive TDs. The 2013 Bears scored 445. This offense will destroy both those teams. They will easily surpass 500 points this season. 540 points would make them one of the 10 greatest offenses of all time. Who would they be with? Peyton Manning’s 2013 Denver Broncos, two Tom Brady Patriots teams (including the 2007 team that went undefeated in the regular season), Ben Johnson’s 2024 Lions offense, Patrick Mahomes 2018 Chiefs offense, Aaron Rodgers and the 2011 Packers, the 2011 Saints with Drew Brees, the 1998 Vikings with Randall Cunningham launching bombs to Randy Moss, and Washington in 1983, that was a ferocious ground attack led by John Riggins. Of those nine teams listed, six of them have all-time QBs. That’s not bad company for Caleb Williams to be in if they can get there, and I think they just might. The Bears offense has arrived. Defensive coordinators around the league are about to see how good Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams are. Get ready for a wild ride this year, Bears fans, and guess what? Get used to this. For the next decade, the Bears are going to be an elite offensive team, something that no one has said about the Bears since FDR was President. Holy Bleep.
author: Bill Zimmerman

title: Bears-Panthers Stock Watch: Swift & Walker up, Stevenson down
summary: With an opening weekend 50-burger, the Chicago Bears have announced they are not going to let regression come to them. A record-setting 59-37 victory sets the tone for the 2026 Bears. For better or worse, the game sets the tone for this team and what the league and the fans are going to expect the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the first quarter against the Carolina Panthers of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images With an opening weekend 50-burger, the Chicago Bears have announced they are not going to let regression come to them. A record-setting 59-37 victory sets the tone for the 2026 Bears. For better or worse, the game sets the tone for this team and what the league and the fans are going to expect the rest of the way. But it wasn’t all good. It rarely is in football. However, there was plenty worth revisiting, too. If you’re new to this piece, I pick three players I see as rising and three I see as falling. It’s a week-to-week exercise, but the performance over multiple games plays a part, too. With that said, let’s get to this week’s stock watch. Stock up Ben Johnson, coach – I wasn’t sure my stock in this man could go up, but here we are. The man crush is deep. I knew he was the real deal as a coach and coordinator. But seeing the team put up 59 points , all on offense, is mind-boggling to me as a longtime fan of this team. Johnson is an incredible play designer and caller. D’Andre Swift, RB – Fresh off his contract extension, Swift scored three TDs to start the season with a bang. On his way to 124 yards and three rushing touchdowns. His yards matched his Bears career high and the touchdowns were a new high for his entire career. Jahdae Walker, WR – Walker was a three-phase contributor on Sunday. He had a highlight block on special teams, multiple great blocks on offense and Ben Johnson rewarded him with a 1-yard touchdown later in the game. With the receiver shuffling that was done in the offseason, there was some question about what kind of role Walker might have. But if this week was any indication, the Bears will be asking him to be a role player a lot this season. Stock down Tyrique Stevenson, CB – Stevenson enters a contract season with the opportunity to really carve out a role and earn his future in Chicago. But his first game felt like a lot of what we’ve seen over his first three seasons. Moments of flash, moments of getting beat and moments of getting banged up. Stevenson has to be more consistent to earn that second deal. Luther Burden, WR – Burden’s game was solid overall. He made good catches and even had a couple of big pass plays. But his fumble on the opening drive set up a Carolina touchdown and was a terrible way to start the game and his season. I’m not worried long term, but this is still a mistake that has to be cleaned up. Colston Loveland, TE – I think this was a one week blip. He had two targets and one of them was a miss by Caleb, so it’s hard to even get down on Loveland too much. But finishing the game with zero catches is surprising. And he was flagged for a holding penalty, too. Again, this isn’t one to be worried about, but someone has to land here. Who’s stock do you think is up or down after week one? Let us know in the comments.
author: Sam Householder

title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Beat the Carolina Panthers
summary: Welcome to the first rendition of my new series for the 2026 season, where I recap what I believe to be the three reasons the Chicago Bears won or lost the previous game. In week 1, the Bears went on the road against the Carolina Panthers – a playoff team from a year ago – […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a touchdown with D'Andre Swift #4 during the second half of the game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to the first rendition of my new series for the 2026 season, where I recap what I believe to be the three reasons the Chicago Bears won or lost the previous game. In week 1, the Bears went on the road against the Carolina Panthers – a playoff team from a year ago – and both teams came away with the most week 1 points scored in their respective franchises history in the 59-37 Bears victory. The 96 combined points were the most ever in a Week 1 contest in NFL history! Ben Johnson’s offense also had the most total yards (552) in a season opener in franchise history. But it was not all good, as Chicago fumbled on their opening drive, which led to 7 quick points for Carolina. The Bears failed to get 2nd-year stud Colston Loveland involved in the passing game, and he ended up with 0 catches for the first time since week 2 of his rookie season. Chicago committed 12 penalties – their most since week 1 of last season and Ben’s first ever as a head coach. To top it off, the Bears gave up 361 yards passing and 3 TDs to Bryce Young. With all that said, Chicago still got the W. And here are my three reasons why. 1. Caleb Williams It would be easy to point to Caleb’s success with his legs in this one. After all, it was his first time as a pro rushing for two scores (should have been three were it not for some bogus officiating, but I digress), and his 65 yards on the ground were his most ever to this point in his career. One could also point to his latest array of highlight reel throws like the TD to Kmet or the “Air Jordan” dime to Kalif Raymond on the run or the 30 yard bomb to Randy Moss Rome Odunze, but I was most impressed by his control of the game and decision making. Apparently, he took some advice from Hall of Famer Drew Brees in the production meeting leading up to game day. No matter what it was, Caleb was dialed in and played within himself, keeping the chains moving and maintaining control of the game. Without Caleb, Chicago might not win this game. But probably still does because of… 2. The Run Game According to ESPN Insights, Bears RBs D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai are the first teammates to each eclipse 100 yards on the ground in a season-opening game since 1980, when the Detroit Lions tandem of Billy Sims and Dexter Bussey accomplished the incredible feat. And while those two played their tails off and ran with quickness, power, and purpose, the run blocking by the offensive line, tight ends, and wide receivers was on point in this one. The 291 rushing yards were the second most in Ben Johnson’s tenure as head coach of the Bears. To do that in week 1, on the road, against a stout Carolina defense was insanely impressive. Some people might believe the Panthers’ defense is just that bad this year, but time will reveal if it was more them being putrid or the Bears’ offense being that good. 3. Rookie DBs Throughout the game, I only noticed two players on defense who showed up more than once to make a play. And both rookies. First-round safety Dillon Thieneman and fourth-round corner Malik Muhammad. Thieneman was all over the field and ended up leading the team in total tackles. Granted, you never want your safety to lead your team in tackles, but the Panthers rushing offense is good-to-great and they have some big WRs to bring down. Aside from one physical error on the first Panthers drive where the former Oregon Duck failed to get his head across and possibly another play where he may have made the wrong run gap fill, Thieneman played lights out. His physical collision with Panthers 2025 first-rounder Tetairoa McMillan may not have officially caused the fumble, but it absolutely helped. Muhammad, meanwhile, was likely my surprise of the whole game. His stickiness in coverage, including against the aforementioned McMillan, who was Offensive Rookie of the Year, mind you, was huge. Muhammad nabbed his first career INT, recorded 3 tackles, and had 2 passes defensed. More of that, please. Especially with so many others struggling on the defensive side of the ball! What about you? Was there another reason you felt was more integral to the teams week 1 win? Let us know below!
author: Bryan Orenchuk

title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL: Chicago Bears put the League on notice, plus much more
summary: 1. You know what? I’m glad Pro Football Focus gave Caleb Williams a hilariously low grade for his explosive and efficient Week 1 performance against the Carolina Panthers, in which he accounted for four touchdowns. I actually love the idea of Ben Johnson walking up to him at Halas Hall and being like, “You know […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) scores a touchdown in the first quarter against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Bob Donnan-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect 1. You know what? I’m glad Pro Football Focus gave Caleb Williams a hilariously low grade for his explosive and efficient Week 1 performance against the Carolina Panthers, in which he accounted for four touchdowns. I actually love the idea of Ben Johnson walking up to him at Halas Hall and being like, “You know they gave you a ‘D’ for that, right?” Let him go ahead and think that’s a bad game he has to get better from. Because if that was just “meh” from him, I can’t wait to see what the rest of this year looks like. 2. If there’s one thing Jacoby Brissett is going to do, it’s win a Week 1 start against a team he has absolutely no business beating. Seriously, I’ve seen him do it twice now in the last three seasons: first with the Patriots against the Joe Burrow-led Bengals in 2024 and now against the Justin Herbert-led Chargers this year as a member of the Cardinals. Now, you can count on that being one of just a handful of wins for Arizona this year. They simply do not have the horses to be good this year. But if you’re wondering why really good backup quarterbacks stay employed forever and occasionally get extended looks as starters, Brissett is a perfect example of why. For one game, he can do stuff like that. 3. Speaking of…I thought the Minnesota Vikings were completely screwed when Kyler Murray went down with a concussion against Green Bay, but Carson Wentz proved me extremely wrong. My most recent memory of Wentz is him playing (poorly) with one arm hanging from its socket by one strip of duct tape, so perhaps I just didn’t have the measure of what he can still do. But watching him lead that second-half comeback against the Packers (and hearing my Wisconsin friend being so pissed about it he could barely discuss it) was almost as satisfying as watching the U.S. Women’s FIBA team put belt to some baguette-eating ass in Berlin. Apparently, GB hasn’t left division-losing choke jobs in 2025. 4. We won’t know for a while if this iteration of the Kansas City Chiefs is truly a contender again with this version of Patrick Mahomes. (Maybe Bo Nix just felt like crapping the bed tonight. Who knows?) But something about watching Mahomes scamper to the end zone, Travis Kelce put up 71 receiving yards at age 72, and Kenneth Walker eat the Broncos defense for lunch made it feel like they’re at least ready to make the playoffs again—even if just for one week. Which…don’t know how to feel about that. Giving Mahomes a run game opponents have to respect is kind of unfair. If he gets back to completing passes again—and he will—things might get uncomfortable in that division. 5. My question of the week for y’all to answer below: how old would Derrick Henry have to be before you felt comfortable enough to step in front of him when he has a full head of steam? I’m not sure if the answer can realistically be younger than 60. Every time you think he’s lost a step, he pops out with 130 yards and three TDs to remind you who the king is. The only question is whether he plays long enough to go for all the records or not. Wouldn’t put it past him. That dude is made of vibranium. Oh yeah, his teammate is pretty good, too. One week into the Declan Doyle experience, one wonders if the Ravens’ offense with Lamar Jackson has a chance to be as electric as Chicago’s. (Did I just type that sentence?) 6. I originally thought the Cleveland Browns would give Deshaun Watson five games or so before giving way to Shedeur Sanders purely for financial reasons. And yes, Browns head coach Todd Monken has committed to Watson for Week 2 against Tampa Bay. But after that drubbing at the hands of the Jacksonville Jaguars, that clock is ticking. I don’t care what the counting stats (205 yards on 72% completions, 1 TD, 1 INT) say. Oh brother, this guy STINKS. 7. That Rams talk went from “super team” to “sucks to be y’all” real fast. I love Myles Garrett and respect his desire to tough things out and play through whatever was ailing him. But sometimes, you have to protect a player from himself—especially you invested that much in to bring him here. Now, Garrett’s out for at least four weeks as he gets his knee cleaned up, and you wonder how long it’ll take before he’s back to being himself. But at least you have Aaron Donald ready to turn it up in his absence, right? Well…maybe not yet. (Understandable, by the way. Don’t make the same mistake you just made with Garrett.) Also, asking a recently un-retired Donald to play a huge role on defense right off the bat wasn’t the plan. Ultimately, the Rams will likely be okay. They still have Matthew Stafford, Puka Nacua, Davante Adams, and Kobie Turner, among other things. But getting washed by the 49ers in Week 1 and immediately losing their best player in the process was not the plan. Then again, that’s never the plan in the NFL. 8. Took me a while to get to this, but let’s talk about just how big an aberration the 791 points per game scored across all NFL season openers is as far as recency goes. The league hadn’t seen an opening weekend with that many points scored since 2021, the first year the season expanded to 17 games. Before then, 700+ points was a common occurrence. From 2022 to now, though? The league hasn’t seen more than 668 points in its first slate of games until Week 1 of this year. Such an interesting data point to add to the discussion about how teams handle having three preseason games, especially given that most teams don’t play their starting offenses much at all these days. Is the offensive element of surprise finally overtaking the rust? Is practice proving itself king over preseason games? Will that momentum continue once the season expands to 18 games? 9. I really hate to say. I really do. But I think the refs ultimately got the call on the overturned New Orleans Saints walk-off strip sack right. Chase Young makes contact with Jared Goff before he throws the football, but he doesn’t lose it until his arm moves forward as part of his throwing motion. By the letter of the law , that’s enough to constitute an attempted forward pass. Would’ve been great to see the Lions drop that one to the upstart Saints, but alas. Also, I respect Kellen Moore going for the win at the end rather than hoping for the tie. You’re a young team with a young quarterback against a good team. Screw going for the tie. You play to win the game. That decision gives your team more information and experience than simply trying not to lose. We’ll see if New Orleans keeps it up, but they might just have made the NFC South far more interesting. 10. His team might have won their first game of the season. But you’ll be hard-pressed to find many bigger losers in the NFL world over the past few weeks than Aaron Rodgers. I will not be elaborating. IYKYK.
author: Khari Thompson

title: Do the Chicago Bears need to aggressively add to their defense?
summary: Soak it in. The Bears’ offense is what everyone has been asking for since Rex Grossman laid a 2006-sized egg. A modern offense capable of scoring at any time and in any manner. And yet, this roster does not look ready to compete for a championship. Why? The defense remains flawed. While there were still […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers runs with the ball during the second quarter against the Chicago Bears of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Soak it in. The Bears’ offense is what everyone has been asking for since Rex Grossman laid a 2006-sized egg. A modern offense capable of scoring at any time and in any manner. And yet, this roster does not look ready to compete for a championship. Why? The defense remains flawed. While there were still some standout performances, namely from rookies Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad, the defensive line and defensive backfield have major holes. Do the Bears need to make a trade and add to their defense? I’m 95% there. There are only a few remaining reasons to be optimistic that the Bears defense can still improve. First, they are still missing some key players in Kyler Gordon and Coby Bryant. However, the severity of Bryant’s injury and lack of clarity around Gordon means that you can’t necessarily count on either of them. If (very big if) Gordon can return and make the impact he is capable of, that could help lock up the middle of the field and push someone like Muhammad outside where he might be more comfortable. If (another big if) Bryant can return 3/4 of the way through the season, he can bring some range and playmaking to the back end. Hard to rely on either of those realities, but neither are impossible. Another reason for tepid optimism is the early returns on the young players. Both Thieneman and Muhammad had standout performances. Still, there were things that need cleaning up, particularly Muhammad’s coverage in the slot. He was beaten a few times on quick crossers — proof that he still needs time to get better at this new position. Add in preseason stars Jordan van den Berg and Jayden Loving, and there is still potential for some real growth along the defensive front. My final plea for patience is simply that the Bears defense was put in a few bad situations, giving the Panthers short fields. The Panthers had drives start at the Bears 42, Panthers 40, Bears 21, and Panthers 42. This is unsustainable for any defense — and a sticking point I am sure Head Coach Ben Johnson will make during the upcoming week. Still, the Bears surrendered 24 first downs, 478 total yards, 7.7 yards per play, and four touchdowns on four trips to the red zone. This defense has a lot of issues that need to be addressed. So what needs the most attention? I think two things come to mind. The Bears still need an EDGE to complement Montez Sweat. Dayo Odeyingbo looked slightly better yesterday, but made mistakes and still lacked necessary impact. Austin Booker was remarkably absent during the game yesterday. Any optimism that he could be the game wrecker on the DL was put into question after his performance. So at a minimum, the Bears need a DE2 opposite Sweat to help generate pressure from the opposite side. Ideally, the Bears can secure an EDGE that can be a primary pass rusher and shift Sweat to DE2. A Kayvon Thibodeaux could be a more affordable option. Shifting focus to the defensive backfield, and what was previously viewed as a team strength looks like a defensive weakness after Week 1. Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson were both burned on several instances, leading to chunk plays by players like Jalen Coker, Darren Waller, and Tetairoa McMillan. While the DL needs to put pressure on QBs sooner, both Johnson and Stevenson appeared to have a difficult time keeping up in man coverage. Given the importance of Johnson in particular, this should be sounding alarms across the Bears organization. He hasn’t looked quite right since his groin and core injuries early in the 2025 season. While the addition of Kyler Gordon or a quick return of Coby Bryant could help cover the issues on the outside CBs, I am walking away deeply concerned with the issues at starting CB. If the Bears are going to take a swing, I am more inclined to do so on an impact CB. A guy like Joey Porter Jr. could push Jaylon Johnson to CB2 and give him better matchups. I think this type of addition could go a long way in improving the pass defense for the Bears. The Bears already have a ton of resources wrapped up in the defense, but given the initial returns on offense, Ryan Poles should pull out all of the stops to ensure that the defense can contribute to a legitimate championship run. Now it’s your turn! Do the Bears need to aggressively add to their defense? Sound off in the comments!
author: Mongo Peanut

title: Bengals vs. Buccaneers: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly
summary: The Bengals opened the 2026 season with a win, and for once, the defense had a lot to do with it. There were some familiar warts along the way, but Cincinnati made enough plays to hold off Tampa Bay, 33-27, at Paycor Stadium. Whew. A Week 1 game that actually ended with the Bengals on the happy side of things. Here are the best and worst from Cincinnati’s season-opening win. The Good […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) checks in with head coach Zac Taylor between plays in the second quarter of the NFL Week 1 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Bengals opened the 2026 season with a win, and for once, the defense had a lot to do with it. There were some familiar warts along the way, but Cincinnati made enough plays to hold off Tampa Bay, 33-27, at Paycor Stadium. Whew. A Week 1 game that actually ended with the Bengals on the happy side of things. Here are the best and worst from Cincinnati’s season-opening win. The Good The defense came to play Well, hello there. After everything we heard about Cincinnati’s rebuilt defense during the offseason, we finally got to see it against an actual NFL offense. And the unit immediately made its presence felt. The Bengals forced fumbles on three consecutive Tampa Bay possessions in the first half. Myles Murphy strip-sacked Baker Mayfield, and Demetrius Knight Jr. scooped it up and returned it 27 yards for a touchdown. Then Bryan Cook forced a fumble from Bucky Irving, with Boye Mafe recovering. A few plays later, Joe Burrow found Mike Gesicki for a touchdown. On the next Tampa possession, Barrett Carter forced another Mayfield fumble near the goal line, and Cook recovered it in the end zone. Three straight possessions. Three turnovers. Cincinnati eventually forced four fumbles and recovered all four, while also sacking Mayfield four times. The Bengals turned those takeaways into 24 points. That’s a pretty good way to start a new defensive era. Mike Gesicki was exactly what Cincinnati needed Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins weren’t exactly having their usual Sunday. So, naturally, Mike Gesicki decided to have a day. Gesicki caught five passes for 78 yards and a touchdown on seven targets, leading Cincinnati in receiving. He also came up big late in the first half, catching three passes for 52 yards on the drive that ended with an Evan McPherson field goal. The Bucs spent plenty of attention on Chase and Higgins, and Burrow simply went somewhere else with the football. That’s what makes this offense so interesting. If defenses want to take away Cincinnati’s two star receivers, there are going to be opportunities for guys like Gesicki to make them pay. Chase Brown and the run game This was not the old-school Bengals running the ball 40 times and winning 17-13. But it was a much more balanced attack. Cincinnati ran the ball 27 times and threw it 35 times, and Chase Brown finished with 16 carries for 56 yards and a touchdown. He also caught five passes for 23 yards. More importantly, the Bengals showed a willingness to use the run as something other than a change of pace. Brown’s five-yard touchdown run capped an 80-yard, 12-play drive in the second quarter and pushed Cincinnati’s lead to 21-3. If Dan Pitcher’s offense really is going to lean into a more balanced approach in 2026, Sunday was a pretty encouraging first look. Money Mac is back Evan McPherson had himself a day. Four field goals. Four makes. Twenty yards. Thirty-two yards. Fifty-five yards. Fifty-eight yards. Those last two are particularly important because Tampa Bay had started to make things uncomfortable. Cincinnati wasn’t consistently finishing drives with touchdowns, but McPherson kept adding points. He accounted for 12 of the Bengals’ 33 points and gave Cincinnati some breathing room when the offense wasn’t quite clicking. Oh, and the 58-yarder was just ridiculous. It’s nice having that in your back pocket again. The offensive line quietly did its job This probably won’t generate nearly as many headlines as a scoop-and-score or a 58-yard field goal, but it might be one of the more important things to come out of this game. Joe Burrow was sacked just once. He finished 25-of-35 for 254 yards, one touchdown and one interception, while completing passes to nine different receivers. There were still some issues, but Burrow generally had enough time to work through his reads. Considering how much of Cincinnati’s success ultimately depends on keeping No. 9 upright, that’s a pretty significant development. Sometimes the best thing an offensive line can do is make you forget it’s there. Sunday was one of those days. The Bad Joe Burrow’s pick-six There’s no way around this one. Burrow had a pretty solid afternoon overall, but his third-quarter interception was brutal. With Cincinnati leading 27-13, Burrow tried to hit Andrei Iosivas, and Tampa Bay linebacker Josiah Trotter stepped in front of the pass and took it 27 yards for a touchdown. Just like that, a 14-point game became a seven-point game. It wasn’t the kind of mistake that cost Cincinnati the game, but it absolutely gave Tampa Bay life when the Bucs needed it. Burrow finished with 254 yards and a touchdown, so this wasn’t some disaster of a performance. But that interception was a bad one, and he’ll know it. The good news? The Bengals responded. The defense still missed too many tackles Four forced fumbles and four sacks will get you a lot of attention. But this wasn’t a flawless defensive performance. Cincinnati missed tackles, and Tampa Bay was able to move the football despite the turnovers. The Bengals also committed multiple offsides penalties, which is the kind of self-inflicted stuff that can become a real problem against better teams. That’s the tradeoff with an aggressive defense. You want guys flying around trying to make plays. You also need them to know where the line is. Cincinnati found that line a few times Sunday—and stepped over it. Ja’Marr Chase was basically a decoy Two catches. Twelve yards. Four targets. That’s it for Ja’Marr Chase. Obviously, this isn’t going to happen every week. Tampa Bay made a concerted effort to take Chase away, and Burrow responded by distributing the ball elsewhere. That’s actually a positive development. Still, there’s a difference between taking Chase away and simply not getting him involved. The Bengals didn’t need Chase to win this game. But there will be Sundays when they absolutely will. The offense left some points out there Cincinnati scored 33 points, so complaining about the offense feels a little ridiculous. Still, there were stretches where the Bengals had opportunities to put Tampa Bay away and couldn’t quite do it. The Bengals went 2-for-5 in the red zone, according to the game statistics. That’s an area that could come back to bite them against a team that doesn’t hand them four turnovers. The offense did enough. But it didn’t exactly leave the Bucs’ defense picking up the pieces. The Ugly That pick-six made this way too interesting This is where things got uncomfortable. Cincinnati was up 27-13. Tampa Bay had struggled to protect the football. The Bengals’ defense was flying around. Then Burrow threw the pick-six. Suddenly it was 27-20. The Buccaneers had momentum, the crowd had gotten a little quieter, and everybody watching was thinking the same thing: Please don’t do this. Fortunately, McPherson answered with a 58-yard field goal, and the defense eventually forced its fourth turnover of the afternoon. But Cincinnati turned what could have been a comfortable fourth quarter into a game that required some actual late-game execution. Tampa Bay wouldn’t go away Credit to the Bucs. After falling behind 24-10 at halftime, Tampa Bay kept hanging around. The Buccaneers cut the lead to seven in the third quarter, and Baker Mayfield eventually ran for an eight-yard touchdown with 3:19 left to make it 33-27. That’s when Cincinnati finally got the kind of close-out drive it has been looking for. The Bengals possessed the ball for the final 3:19 and didn’t give Tampa Bay another opportunity. So, yes, it got ugly. But Cincinnati actually finished the job. And honestly, after some of the fourth-quarter endings Bengals fans have endured over the years, I’ll take an ugly close-out over another…

title: Bengals Week 1 awards from 33-27 win vs. Buccaneers
summary: The Bengals are 1-0. That’s a pretty good place to start. Cincinnati opened the 2026 season with a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and while there were certainly some things that need cleaning up, there were also plenty of individual performances worth recognizing. The new-look defense stole the show, Evan McPherson reminded everyone […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals center Ted Karras (64) celebrates with place kicker Evan McPherson (2) after McPherson made a field goal in the 4th quarter over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Bengals are 1-0. That’s a pretty good place to start. Cincinnati opened the 2026 season with a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and while there were certainly some things that need cleaning up, there were also plenty of individual performances worth recognizing. The new-look defense stole the show, Evan McPherson reminded everyone why they call him “Money Mac,” and a few guys who probably weren’t at the top of anyone’s bingo card made some big plays. So, without further ado, let’s get into this week’s award nominees. Most Valuable Player (MVP) Criteria: This award goes to the player whose performance had the greatest direct impact on securing the victory. Nominee 1: Demetrius Knight Jr. — Linebacker Stats / Moments: Knight Jr. opened Cincinnati’s scoring with a 27-yard fumble return touchdown after Myles Murphy forced a Baker Mayfield fumble. Why MVP-worthy: Talk about making an entrance. Knight’s defensive touchdown gave the Bengals their first points of the season and immediately gave the new-look defense some life. He wasn’t just in the right place at the right time, either. Knight was flying around all afternoon and looked very comfortable in his first regular-season game with a much larger role. When you’re trying to change the identity of a defense, plays like this are exactly what you’re looking for. Nominee 2: Evan McPherson — Kicker Stats / Moments: McPherson connected on all four of his field-goal attempts, including kicks from 55 and 58 yards. He finished with 12 points. Why MVP-worthy: When the offense couldn’t quite finish drives, McPherson did. The 58-yarder in the fourth quarter was especially important. Tampa Bay had just cut Cincinnati’s lead to seven, and the Bengals needed something to stop the momentum. Enter Money Mac. That kick pushed the lead back to 10 and gave the defense a little more breathing room. Four-for-four with two 50-plus yarders is a pretty strong way to start the year. Nominee 3: Bryan Cook — Safety Stats / Moments: Cook forced a fumble and recovered a Tampa Bay fumble, which was Baker Mayfield’s goal-line gaffe in the first half. Why MVP-worthy: Cook was simply around the football. His fumble recovery came after Mayfield coughed the ball up near the goal line, preventing Tampa Bay from potentially coming away with points. He also forced another Buccaneers fumble, helping Cincinnati maintain control of a game that ultimately became much closer than it looked at halftime. After spending the offseason talking about what Cook could bring to a revamped secondary, Bengals fans got a pretty good first taste. Nominee 4: Mike Gesicki — Tight End Stats / Moments: Gesicki caught five passes for 78 yards and a touchdown on seven targets, leading Cincinnati in receiving. Why MVP-worthy: When Tampa Bay made it difficult to get Ja’Marr Chase involved, Burrow went elsewhere. Gesicki was the primary beneficiary. His two-yard touchdown reception gave Cincinnati its first offensive touchdown of the season, and he consistently found ways to move the chains. You don’t necessarily need your biggest stars to dominate every week. Sometimes you need the guys underneath them to make the defense pay for all that attention. Gesicki did exactly that. Unsung Hero of the Week Criteria: Awarded to a player whose efforts were significant yet flew under the radar, often stepping up in a rotational role, making an impact that doesn’t necessarily show up in the box score, or taking advantage of an opportunity created by injuries. Nominee 1: Dexter Lawrence II — Defensive Tackle Why Unsung-worthy: The stat sheet doesn’t really tell the story here. Lawrence didn’t need a bunch of sacks or splash plays to make his presence felt. He consistently affected what Tampa Bay wanted to do up front and helped create opportunities for the players around him. Nuggets from #Bengals PFF grading data: -Dexter Lawrence with 11 true pass set rushes. His win rate was 36%. That's best in the NFL among all DI (min. 10 attempts). – CBs did a nice job tackling in run game, Jalen Davis and Dax Hill, both graded out 84+. Hill with 2 stops. -… — Paul Dehner Jr. (@pauldehnerjr) September 14, 2026 And that’s exactly why Cincinnati went and got him. The Bengals invested heavily in their defensive front this offseason, and Lawrence’s Week 1 performance was one of those games where the tape was more impressive than the box score. Not exactly a bad debut in stripes. Nominee 2: Barrett Carter — Linebacker Stats / Moments: Carter finished with a team-high eight tackles, recorded a half-sack, and forced a fumble at the goal line. Why Unsung-worthy: Knight Jr. gets the highlight-reel touchdown, but Carter was everywhere. The goal-line forced fumble was enormous. Tampa Bay was threatening to turn a Bengals defensive stop into points, and Carter simply took the football away. Eight tackles, a half-sack and a forced fumble is a pretty busy afternoon. And unlike the defensive touchdown, this is the kind of production that can get lost when one side of the ball generates four turnovers. Nominee 3: Boye Mafe — EDGE Stats / Moments: Mafe recovered a fumble after Bucky Irving lost the ball and was part of a defensive front that helped force four Tampa Bay turnovers. Why Unsung-worthy: Mafe wasn’t necessarily the guy getting all the headlines, but he was involved in the chaos up front. The Bengals wanted a more aggressive, deeper defensive line rotation in 2026, and Mafe’s ability to contribute in that rotation is going to matter. Recovering a fumble isn’t glamorous. It is, however, extremely useful. Nominee 4: Chase Brown — Running Back Stats / Moments: Brown carried the ball 16 times for 56 yards and a touchdown while adding five receptions for 23 yards. Why Unsung-worthy: Brown wasn’t spectacular statistically, but he was steady. His five-yard touchdown run extended Cincinnati’s lead to 21-3 in the second quarter, and he was involved throughout an offense that ran 27 times compared with 35 pass attempts. More importantly, the Bengals didn’t abandon the running game when things weren’t perfect. Brown is going to be a major part of that balance if Cincinnati sticks with this approach. Play of the Game Criteria: The single most impactful or memorable moment that significantly shifted the game in Cincinnati’s favor. Nominee 1: Demetrius Knight Jr.’s Scoop-and-Score Myles Murphy knocked the ball loose from Baker Mayfield, and Knight Jr. picked it up and raced 27 yards for the touchdown. It’s hard to beat a defensive touchdown for this award. It was Cincinnati’s first score of the season and the first big statement from a defense that has spent the offseason trying to change its reputation. Something poetic about Demetrius Knight Jr. being the first to score a touchdown for the Bengals this year. After getting a ton of hate last year & this offseason, nice to see him get his moment. If you believe in omens, this’d be a great one for his sophomore year… pic.twitter.com/QKY2PbonmF — Bengalscentre (@benga1scentre) September 14, 2026 Nominee 2: Bryan Cook’s Goal-Line Fumble Recovery Mayfield lost the football near the Cincinnati goal line, and Cook recovered it in the end zone. Tampa Bay was knocking on the door. Instead of seven points—or at minimum a field goal—the Bengals walked away with the football. That’s the kind of play that can completely change a game. Bryan Cook with a great debut for the Bengals. Flies all around the field, is physical, and made some huge splash plays with a forced fumble and a fumble recovery on two separate plays. pic.twitter.com/YUCHzyKULl — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 15, 2026 Nominee 3: Evan McPherson’s 58-Yard Field Goal With Tampa Bay having cut Cincinnati’s lead to 27-20, McPherson drilled…

title: AFC North Roundup: Ravens and Steelers start fast while Browns stumble
summary: The first week of the 2026 season offered an early reminder that nothing is likely to come easily for the Cincinnati Bengals in the AFC North. Baltimore and Pittsburgh both opened with victories, although they got there in very different ways. The Ravens overwhelmed Indianapolis behind Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry, while the Steelers leaned […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: T.J. Watt #90 of the Pittsburgh Steelers warms up prior to the game against the Green Bay Packers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The first week of the 2026 season offered an early reminder that nothing is likely to come easily for the Cincinnati Bengals in the AFC North. Baltimore and Pittsburgh both opened with victories, although they got there in very different ways. The Ravens overwhelmed Indianapolis behind Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry, while the Steelers leaned on a familiar formula as T.J. Watt helped rescue an uneven offensive performance. Cleveland was the lone division rival to stumble out of the gate, with turnovers, penalties and protection problems contributing to a difficult opening day. T.J. Watt still has plenty left in the tank Anyone expecting age to finally catch up with T.J. Watt may have to wait a little longer. Coming off a disappointing 2025 season by his lofty standards, the 32-year-old linebacker looked much more like the player who has spent the better part of a decade wrecking opposing offenses. Watt recorded two sacks and provided the biggest play of Pittsburgh’s 20-13 victory over Atlanta when he intercepted Cooper Rush and returned it 35 yards for a fourth-quarter touchdown. It was an impressive start for a player whose seven sacks last season represented one of the lowest totals of his career. Against Atlanta, however, there was little evidence that the four-time All-Pro has lost his ability to take over a football game. That was fortunate for Pittsburgh because its new-look offense was hardly dominant. Aaron Rodgers began what he says will be his final NFL season by passing for 221 yards and a touchdown. The Steelers struggled to run the ball effectively, and several dropped passes contributed to an inconsistent afternoon. Rodgers was at his best when Pittsburgh needed to put the game away, completing three passes on a final possession that consumed the remaining 4:16. Ravens offense comes out firing Baltimore’s opener wasn’t nearly as suspenseful. The Ravens piled up 506 yards of offense in a 41-23 victory over Indianapolis, with their two biggest stars doing most of the damage. Henry showed that turning 32 hasn’t made him much easier to tackle. He carried 24 times for 144 yards and three touchdowns. The performance also pushed him farther up the NFL’s career record lists, giving him 125 rushing touchdowns and 130 total scores. Jackson was equally impressive after a 2025 season that fell short of his usual standard. He completed 17 of 25 passes for 324 yards while adding 40 yards on seven rushing attempts. He accounted for touchdowns both passing and running. Perhaps the most encouraging sign for Baltimore was how quickly the offense took control. Jackson threw for 229 yards before halftime, and Zay Flowers accounted for 150 receiving yards on only five catches. The one concern coming out of the performance was Flowers’ hamstring, which kept him out of the second half, but he’s listed as day-to-day, so it doesn’t appear serious. Another downer was that Baltimore lost promising rookie wideout Ja’Kobi Lane to a wrist injury and is set to have surgery that will sideline him for a month. Rough beginning for Cleveland Things went considerably differently for the Browns. Deshaun Watson’s first start in nearly two years began with an interception on Cleveland’s opening possession and never really settled down. Jacksonville’s defense sacked Watson five times and kept him under pressure throughout the game. Cleveland compounded those problems with mistakes of its own. Rookie receiver KC Concepcion Jr. lost a fumble, the Browns were flagged 11 times for 75 yards, and the offense converted only one of eight third-down opportunities. Two possessions inside the Jacksonville 20 also ended without touchdowns. There were a couple of encouraging moments. Raheim Sanders broke a 74-yard kickoff return that helped produce a field goal, while Watson connected with Denzel Boston on a 46-yard touchdown late in the game. But Cleveland finished with only 272 total yards, and the late score did little to disguise an afternoon filled with problems.

title: Browns legend Joe Thomas: Team’s failures broke him one year, Manning’s wild request
summary: When Cleveland Browns Hall of Famer Joe Thomas spoke to DBN’s Barry Shuck a couple of years ago, he was open and honest about how difficult it was to play for a losing team. Thomas, like former Browns DE Myles Garrett, put on great performances on the field only to see their team lose over […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - NOVEMBER 27, 2016: Left tackle Joe Thomas #73 of the Cleveland Browns kneels during timeout in the second quarter of a game against the New York Giants on November 27, 2016 at FirstEnergy Stadium in Cleveland, Ohio. New York won 27-13. (Photo by: Nick Cammett/Diamond Images/Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images When Cleveland Browns Hall of Famer Joe Thomas spoke to DBN’s Barry Shuck a couple of years ago , he was open and honest about how difficult it was to play for a losing team. Thomas, like former Browns DE Myles Garrett , put on great performances on the field only to see their team lose over and over again. Thomas and Garrett are locked together as the best modern-day Cleveland players , who both rarely saw any chance of winning championships in the orange and brown. While Garrett was moved in a trade, Thomas continues to talk about the Browns, including comments on Baker Mayfield and, recently, Deshaun Watson . Most of the time, Thomas has presented a measured approach to talking about his career and football. This video, talking about how Cleveland’s struggles broke him after one game, was less measured and spoke to what many Browns fans have also felt, while not actually playing at an all-time great level: Joe Thomas says he cried after playing a perfect game in a 30 point loss to Tom Brady and realized he had spent 10 years fooling himself into believing the Browns were a Super Bowl team before each season “The way I entered every season was like, if I need to get the most out of… pic.twitter.com/i9ksUFXIby — dank (@cptdankkk) September 15, 2026 Later in the interview, Thomas talked about a phone call he received from QB Peyton Manning when the Denver Broncos were trying to trade for him . The Hall of Famer noted he was happy in Cleveland, even if he was broken by the team’s performance, so he would not demand a trade. Manning then had a much more extreme idea: Peyton Manning wanted Joe Thomas to take a 💩 on the GM’s desk so he would get traded 😂 pic.twitter.com/lhu7IlXe2E — Bussin' With The Boys (@BussinWTB) September 15, 2026 Putting the two videos together, you have to wonder if Thomas now regrets not asking for the trade when he could have joined a Super Bowl-caliber team. From a heartfelt, sad statement about how he felt after playing a “perfect” game but losing by 30 to a discussion about defecating on GM Ray Farmer’s desk, the Joe Thomas experience. summary: It is Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season, and there is no drama about the Cleveland Browns’ position in national power rankings: they are pretty much dead last. A few sites still have them at No. 30 or No. 31, but overall, the average dropped 0.8 spots to 31.4. Some sites have the likes […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 13: A Jacksonville Jaguars fan poses for a photo prior to the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Cleveland Browns at EverBank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season, and there is no drama about the Cleveland Browns’ position in national power rankings: they are pretty much dead last. A few sites still have them at No. 30 or No. 31, but overall, the average dropped 0.8 spots to 31.4. Some sites have the likes of the Dolphins, Titans, or Falcons in consideration of being worse than Cleveland. Here is a summary of how the Cleveland Browns are viewed across mainstream media outlets in NFL Power Rankings heading into Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season. CBS Sports – No. 31 (no change) How much longer can they go with Deshaun Watson? He wasn’t the only reason they lost to the Jaguars, but he wasn’t good either. ESPN – No. 32 (down 1 spot) Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Denzel Boston The second-round pick’s production — two receptions for 59 yards and a TD — came in garbage time, but Boston’s 46-yard touchdown catch on a deep post was the kind of play he made throughout training camp. He also had the most snaps (47) and routes run (26) of any Browns receiver in Week 1, a sign of the big role that the team has planned for him going forward. NFL.com – No. 32 (down 2 spots) Last year, Cleveland’s defense managed to keep the Browns competitive in a bunch of games. Week 1 informed us that a different story will play out in 2026. The offense was horrendous with Deshaun Watson under center. The Browns hurt themselves by committing 11 penalties, and their defense resembled little more than a sieve against Trevor Lawrence’s Jaguars. It’s looking like it’ll be a long season on the shore of Lake Erie. Sporting News – No. 32 (no change) The Browns’ quarterback situation is bad, but the state of the running game and defense is even worse to begin the Todd Monken era. They were no match for the Jaguars and may struggle to beat anyone for a while. Yahoo Sports – No. 30 (no change) The Browns’ defense is supposed to keep them in games, even with Jared Verse replacing Myles Garrett. That wasn’t the case in the opener as the Browns looked like they really missed Jim Schwartz as defensive coordinator. Trevor Lawrence had four touchdowns and Jacksonville had 31 points with 12:08 left in the third quarter. If Cleveland’s defense is bad, there’s no hope at a respectable season. Bleacher Report – No. 32 (down 2 spots) It is going to be another long season at the Factory of Sadness. Deshaun Watson’s stats weren’t bad in a blowout loss to the Jaguars, but his lone touchdown throw came in garbage time and for most of the game the Browns had no vertical passing attack. That let the NFL’s best run defense from a year ago tee off on running back Quinshon Judkins, who averaged less than three yards per carry. The even bigger disappointment was a Browns defense that ranked inside the top-five last year. Sure, Myles Garrett is gone. But the Jaguars did whatever they wanted offensively in Week 1, whether it was on the ground or through the air. It was an ugly performance all the way around. And the Browns are the NFL’s worst team. Again. USA Today – No. 31 (down 1 spot) Shedeur SZN (Week 3?) is surely almost here, Browns fans − particularly if Baker Mayfield finally exacts revenge on the franchise that dumped him in favor of Deshaun Watson four years ago. title: Cleveland’s defense could adjust some snap counts after first game
summary: The Cleveland Browns’ defense looked lost to open the season, and looked like a shadow of its former self from when Jim Schwartz was the defensive coordinator. There was hardly any pressure, the tackling was poor, and the playmaking was lacking. I know Myles Garrett is gone, but one player shouldn’t turn a defense to […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - SEPTEMBER 13: Mason Graham #94 of the Cleveland Browns reacts after a play during the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Cleveland Browns on September 13, 2026 at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cleveland Browns’ defense looked lost to open the season, and looked like a shadow of its former self from when Jim Schwartz was the defensive coordinator. There was hardly any pressure, the tackling was poor, and the playmaking was lacking. I know Myles Garrett is gone, but one player shouldn’t turn a defense to complete trash. Looking at the snap counts, there are a couple areas where some adjustments could be coming next week. Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on defense for the Cleveland Browns ’ Week 1 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Defensive Line Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats DL Jared Verse 37 65% 3 tackles, 1 assist (4 combined). 1 TFL. DL Isaiah McGuire 37 65% 2 assists (2 combined). DL Mason Graham 34 60% 3 tackles, 2 assists (5 combined). 1 sack, 2 TFL, 1 QH. DL Adin Huntington 29 51% 2 assists (2 combined). DL Mike Hall 29 51% No stats registered. DL Sam Williams 23 40% 1 tackle, 3 assists (4 combined). DL Maliek Collins 22 39% 1 QH. DL Derek Barnett 17 30% No stats registered. We expected a lot from Jared Verse , and we got complete mediocrity, at least for one week. Verse graded out to around a 57.2 by PFF and did not generate any pressures. I thought Mason Graham made one of the bigger impacts defensively. It’s nice to see that right out of the gate after he started a bit slow as a rookie. PFF graded him as a 63.0. One of the biggest surprises with snap counts was how much action Adin Huntington saw. Perhaps we will see that number go down as veteran Maliek Collins gets more acclimated to football again. For what it’s worth, Huntington, Collins, and Mike Hall all graded poorly by PFF. Linebacker Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats LB Carson Schwesinger 57 100% 3 tackles, 7 assists (10 combined). 1 TFL, 1 QH. LB Quincy Williams 55 96% 3 tackles, 1 assist (4 combined). LB Easton Mascarenas-Arnold 19 33% 2 assists (2 combined). LB Winston Reid 1 2% No stats registered. It was a pedestrian game for Carson Schwesinger , who was around a 52.5 with his PFF grade. Quincy Williams , the new linebacker to the group, received the worst grade on defense with a 29.7. Maybe this is one of the reasons why: In all the years of watching football film this is a first from a LB in coverage. Zero movement for the first 2s. That's a choice from Quincy Williams (#5) pic.twitter.com/ipKErUGBDn — Browns Film Breakdown (@BrownsFilmBDN) September 15, 2026 Tackling in general was an issue for Cleveland: The Browns defense had 17 missed tackles against the Jaguars, per @NextGenStats , which only trailed the Denver Broncos for the most in the NFL in Week 1. Cleveland's missed tackle rate (21.8%) was also the third highest. Todd Monken was asked about the tackling effort on Monday:… — Daniel Oyefusi (@DanielOyefusi) September 15, 2026 Cornerback Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats CB Tyson Campbell 57 100% 3 tackles, 4 assists (7 combined). CB Denzel Ward 57 100% 1 tackle, 4 assists (5 combined). 1 FF. CB Myles Harden 25 44% 1 tackle, 1 assist (2 combined). Denzel Ward was the Browns’ top-graded player defensively, grading out to a 90.5. At least one player remained consistent on this defense. Myles Harden seemed to be picked on a bit early. He was one of the Browns’ lowest-ranked defenders on the day. Safety Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats S Ronnie Hickman 57 100% 3 tackles, 5 assists (8 combined). S Grant Delpit 57 100% 1 tackle, 2 assists (3 combined). 1 pass defended. S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren 14 25% 1 tackle, 2 assists (3 combined). Last, but not least, one of the surprises in terms of snap counts came at safety, where rookie Emmanuel McNeil-Warren only played 14 snaps (25%). It’s not that I expect him to be an everydown player, but I was envisioning his role being between 40-60% of the snaps each week as a big part of the defense. For the reps he did receive, he graded out to a 69.2, which was the third-highest on defense. It’ll be interesting to see if the team works him more into defensive packages moving forward. Ronnie Hickman did not have a good day. It wasn’t a great day for Grant Delpit either, but he at least made a play on a couple passes.

title: Despite Week 1 loss, one group on the Browns offense improved
summary: The Cleveland Browns played a terrible game in Week 1, with a lot of blame going to QB Deshaun Watson on offense, and then the team’s defense in general. But were other areas responsible for the low output offensively too? There was one unit that actually played at a very high level, believe it or […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 13: Quinshon Judkins #10 of the Cleveland Browns runs the ball against the Jacksonville Jaguars during the first quarter of the game at EverBank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns played a terrible game in Week 1, with a lot of blame going to QB Deshaun Watson on offense, and then the team’s defense in general. But were other areas responsible for the low output offensively too? There was one unit that actually played at a very high level, believe it or not. Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on offense for the Cleveland Browns ’ Week 1 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Quarterback Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats QB Deshaun Watson 51 100% 16-of-22 (72.7%) for 205 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT. 6 carries, 38 yards (6.3 YPC), 1 fumble. We can’t just look at the stat line for Deshaun Watson and think he wasn’t a problem. With that said, there are two sides to this. Fans are fed up with Watson. We thought we were done with him after the owner’s comments last year, and yet here he is, starting again. How many empty scoring halves of offense under Watson have we been subjected to? And then when you listen to the clip below, they’re exactly right, what the hell are we doing here, Todd Monken ? We are coddling Watson with kid gloves. "Listen to that. It that not something you'd say to your QB in 6th grade? I'm serious. We're all gonna have to deal with it for the rest of the season. This is just an abomination." 🚨 @KenCarman to @SportsBoyTony on #Browns head coach Todd Monken's comments on Deshaun Watson's… pic.twitter.com/thcnHKHElX — 92.3 The Fan (@923TheFan) September 14, 2026 Now, with all of that in mind, sure, there were a few positives I saw from Watson. I thought his deep ball in garbage time was thrown well, and he had some nice scrambles. He is certainly not tentative about running after his two Achilles injuries. The problem is, this is what, year four of us seeing Watson with the Browns? We’re sick of trying to cherry pick a few highlights to hope he’ll be better. That’s stuff you’d want to point out with Shedeur Sanders as a youngster, not Watson at this point, who has proven he is too turnover prone and doesn’t put points on the board. Running Back Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats RB Quinshon Judkins 33 65% 12 carries, 33 yards (2.8 YPC). 2 catches, 17 yards (2 targets). RB Raheim Sanders 18 35% 1 carry, 1 yard (1.0 YPC). 3 catches, 25 yards (3 targets). FB Michael Burton 6 12% No stats registered. The Browns were blown out so early that it again made it difficult to rely on the running game. Also, this is a Jaguars front that thrived at stopping the run a year ago. Nonetheless, there was nothing really special about the way Quinshon Judkins ran in Week 1. His backup, Dylan Sampson , is out with an injury now. Fullback Michael Burton got six snaps in. Wide Receiver Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats WR Denzel Boston 47 92% 2 catches, 59 yards (4 targets), 1 TD. WR KC Concepcion 35 69% 4 catches, 43 yards (5 targets). 3 carries, 15 yards (5.0 YPC), 1 fumble. WR Jerry Jeudy 32 63% 2 catches, 26 yards (4 targets). WR Tylan Wallace 15 29% No stats registered. WR Isaiah Bond 7 14% No stats registered. Despite his fumble, I liked that KC Concepcion was utilized in a variety of ways like he was in the preseason. Based on touches, he was the most involved receiver by far. Denzel Boston caught two passes, including a deep ball for a touchdown. You can see the frame he has and how Browns quarterbacks will be confident in throwing the ball his direction, thinking it’ll either be a catch of a contested play, but not an interception. Concepcion and Boston received decent grades for Cleveland from PFF in the high 60s, making them the team’s second- and third-highest graded players offensively. It was surprising to see Tylan Wallace receive 29% of the snaps. I didn’t think he’d even be involved in the offense. He even out-snapped Isaiah Bond , who had seemed to have a solid camp for Cleveland. Tight End Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats TE Harold Fannin 42 82% 2 catches, 21 yards (3 targets). TE Blake Whiteheart 20 39% 1 catch, 14 yards (1 target). Harold Fannin wasn’t even looked at until late in the second half. Ridiculous. Blake Whiteheart caught the opening pass, but didn’t have anything else come his way. Cleveland only went with two tight ends getting reps. Offensive Line Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats OL Spencer Fano 51 100% OL Elgton Jenkins 51 100% OL Austin Barber 51 100% OL Tytus Howard 51 100% OL Zion Johnson 50 98% OL Zak Zinter 1 2% Austin Barber was the Browns’ highest-graded player, per PFF, receiving a grade of 82.6. You get the feeling that he’ll remain at right guard, even when Teven Jenkins returns. Overall, the new Browns’ offensive line blocked well. However, the penalties stacked up and were killers. PFF is attributing all 5 of the Jaguars’ sacks to Deshaun Watson , and 0 being on the offensive line. The offensive line and wide receiver play remain encouraging, if we’re looking for optimism moving forward. PFF credits all Browns offensive linemen with allowing ZERO sacks. Deshaun Watson was sacked 5 times, which means PFF is attributing all 5 sacks to the quarterback. pic.twitter.com/wMlENfI8qF — The Dawgs – A Cleveland Browns Podcast (@thedawgspodcast) September 15, 2026 ESPN agreed in their assessment of the Browns’ offensive line: Despite the Browns' struggles on offense in Week 1, Cleveland's offensive line graded out well in ESPN's blocking metrics: 🏈 T-3rd in pass block win rate 🏈 7th in run block win rate Both metrics measure how often offensive lines successfully sustain their blocks for at least… — Daniel Oyefusi (@DanielOyefusi) September 15, 2026

title: Browns Week 1: Cleveland’s identity is now in question
summary: The Cleveland Browns’ Week 1 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars revealed plenty about the team beyond what the final score showed. There were plenty of assumptions made about this team heading into the season. Many of those assumptions were validated in Week 1, while others told a different story about where this team is currently at. Many expected Cleveland’s defense to be the team’s […]
full_text: The Cleveland Browns’ Week 1 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars revealed plenty about the team beyond what the final score showed. There were plenty of assumptions made about this team heading into the season. Many of those assumptions were validated in Week 1, while others told a different story about where this team is currently at. Many expected Cleveland’s defense to be the team’s biggest strength and the key to keeping them competitive this season, but Week 1 showed that may not be the case. The defense allowed 24 points and 234 yards in the first half alone. They struggled to get any pressure on Trevor Lawrence . While the offense did little to help them, it was even more disappointing to see how the defense performed. The Jaguars won 13 games last season and have a strong offense, so this performance may not indicate what the defense will look like in the coming weeks. Still, the initial showing was far from promising. On the offensive side of the ball, there wasn’t much positivity going into the season about Deshaun Watson and the passing game. That feeling was clearly validated by what happened in this game. There was optimism that the offensive line would improve from last season with the addition of several new players, but the group continued to struggle in Week 1. Again, it is not truly indicative of what they will look like for the rest of the season. It was difficult to find many positives from the group, outside of a strong performance from Austin Barber , who was the highest-graded PFF rookie offensive lineman in Week 1. Hopefully Barber can inspire the rest of the offensive line as the team prepares for their Week 2 game matchup against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. For now, the Browns identity, which was assumed to be a good defense and solid rushing attack, is in question, added to all the questions about the quarterback position.
