title: Lions Week 2 preview: Breaking down Bills’ offensive, defensive schemes
summary: The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills will square off in a “Thursday Night Football” battle to kick off Week 2. The Bills went through a coaching change this offseason, and while an internal promotion of Joe Brady to head coach kept their offense intact, hiring Jim Leonhard as defensive coordinator has the Bills’ defense shifting […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Head Coach Joe Brady of the Buffalo Bills arrives at the stadium prior to the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills will square off in a “Thursday Night Football” battle to kick off Week 2. The Bills went through a coaching change this offseason, and while an internal promotion of Joe Brady to head coach kept their offense intact, hiring Jim Leonhard as defensive coordinator has the Bills’ defense shifting from a 4-2 to a 3-4 front. Let’s take a closer look at the Bills’ coaching staff, the scheme they run, and some scouting notes from last week’s game along with some previously viewed games in 2025. Bill s head coach: Joe Brady NFL coaching seasons: Entering ninth season in the NFL Offensive coordinator : Four; Bills 2024-25 and Panthers 2020-21 Passing game coordinator : LSU 2019 (National Championship – QB Joe Burrow) Influences: Sean Payton Coached under: Payton (Saints), McDermott (Bills), Matt Rhule (Panthers), Ed Orgeron (LSU) Playcaller : Yes Dan Campbell coached alongside Brady during the 2017-18 seasons in New Orleans, and has this to say about the start to Brady’s head coaching career: “I know Joe Brady very well. That’s a heck of a start there.” Offensive coordinato r: Pete Carmichael NFL coaching seasons : Entering 27th season in the NFL Offensive coordinator seasons : Entering 16th season Previous coaching positions : Senior offensive assistant, passing game coordinator, QB coach, WR coach, TE coach Influences: Sean Payton (20 seasons), Marty Schottenheimer, Pete Carmichael Sr. (Father) Coached under: Payton (Saints, Broncos), Schottenheimer (Chargers, Washington), Chris Palmer (Browns) Detroit staff connection: John Fox, Senior Assistant (with Lions in 2023) Offensive scheme Passing game : Pro-Spread Running scheme : Man, Inside-Zone Scouting notes : Efficient offense due to success in the run game and quick pass completions Spread philosophies at their core Heavy influences from Payton (Saints) and Bengals-style (how they use Joe Burrow) Week 1: 11 personnel 33% of snaps, 12 for 12%, 13 for 40% Note: Bills spent so much time in 13 in Week 1 because Texans stayed in nickel sets 60/40 pass-run split in Week 1 QB Josh Allen can throw to all levels of the field Tested Texans deep in Week 1 more than he’s done in the past Under center 65% of the time in Week 1 Play-action 41% of dropbacks in Week 1 Allen has 81 career rushing TDs (most among QBs in NFL history) North-South rushing attack runs right at the teeth of the defense Week 1 blocking percentages: Man roughly 40%, Inside-Zone 30% Dan Campbell on Bills’ offense: “Can’t say enough about this quarterback. He’s a catalyst for them. And it’s a good O-line. They’ve got weapons, and a good back.” “They have three tight ends. They have three real guys that have three different roles that they’re all three pretty good at. And (Jackson Hawes) 85 can block a little bit. We liked him coming out and he proved to be a pretty good blocker last year. So, he’s kind of their heavy-Y. And then Dalton (Kincaid), 86, he’s a mismatch in the pass game, man. He’s one of these big skill, get through the defense, one-on-one matchups. And then (Dawson) Knox does it all. He does everything. He’s the guy, he’s the jack of all trades and he makes it right. He’s kind of the glue that, ‘What do you need? I’m the release guy, I’m the blocker, I’m the hybrid H-back, I’m the split me out one-on-one.’ He does it all.” Defensive coordinator: Jim Leonhard NFL seasons as a player : 10 years at safety (Bills, Ravens, Jets, Broncos, Saints, Browns) NFL coaching seasons : 3 years in the NFL (8 in college) Defensive coordinator seasons : First-year Previous roles : DBs coach, passing game coordinator, assistant head coach (Broncos) Influences: Rex Ryan, Mike Pettine, and Vance Joseph for scheme; Sean Payton for coaching style Coached under: Payton (Broncos), Joseph (Broncos), Bret Bielema (Illinois), Paul Chryst (Wisconsin) Played for : Pettine (Browns, Bills, Jets), Ryan (Jets, Ravens), Payton (Saints), John Fox (Broncos), Jack Del Rio (Broncos), John Harbaugh (Ravens), Dick Jauron (Bills) Defensive scheme Base : 3-4 Base, attacking front Coverage : Zone-heavy Scouting notes (from Week 1): Defense modeled after the Broncos 3-4 attacking scheme Big defensive shift after previously playing in a 4-2 front; required new personnel Defensive philosophy switch will take time to adapt 5-man front in base (3 down DL, 2 pass-rushing LB) – roughly 40% of defensive snaps in Week 1 4-man front in subpackages (2 DL and 2 PR-LB) – roughly 60% Vs. 11 personnel: faced 42 snaps, 25 in nickel (36% of snaps) and 17 in dime (24%) Vs. 12, 13, and Jumbo: 30 snaps, 28 in Base defense (39%) Picks and Stunts are foundations of pass rush Pressure on 36% of passing snaps Blitz 26% of snaps Zone coverage around 80% — Cover-3 was highest at 31%, then Cover-6 (22%), Cover-4 (19%), Cover-2 (7%) Man 18% —mainly Cover-2 (10%) and Cover-1 (8%) Dan Campbell on Saints’ defense: “This defensive line is their catalyst over there. (DT) Ed Oliver and (EDGE Greg) Rousseau, man, really good player. Length, explosive. They’ve got (EDGE Bradley) Chubb on the other end. Big boy in the middle, man. That’s an active defense and it was a big win for them (in Week 1).”

title: Lions, Bills injury report: CB D.J. Reed added Tuesday
summary: The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills are prepping for a Thursday night Week 2 showdown, and with a short week ahead, they’re doing another set of walkthroughs. On Tuesday, the Lions ran another set of walkthroughs, meaning participation levels for these practices are only estimates based on what the coaching staff projects each player could […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: D.J. Reed #4 of the Detroit Lions walks off the field after an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills are prepping for a Thursday night Week 2 showdown, and with a short week ahead, they’re doing another set of walkthroughs. On Tuesday, the Lions ran another set of walkthroughs, meaning participation levels for these practices are only estimates based on what the coaching staff projects each player could have produced in a full practice. With that in mind, let’s take a look at Tuesday’s injury report and get you up to date with what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . Injured list updates RB Isiah Pacheco (MCL/Back) — injured reserve, expected to be out until December During his Monday press conference, Lions coach Dan Campbell noted that Pacheco’s back injury required surgery, and it was “going to be a while” before he would be able to get back on the field. NFL Insider Ian Rapoport reported soon after that Pacheco’s surgery was to address a nerve in his back and that his recovery time (roughly 12 weeks) could give him a chance to be back in December. Estimated no practice on Tuesday LG Christian Mahogany (hip) RT Blake Miller (knee) Campbell confirmed on Monday that Mahogany’s injury was not “something serious long-term, but it could be tough to get him ready for Thursday.” That’s Campbell’s way of saying we should probably expect to see Ben Bartch at left guard against the Bills. Campbell also addressed Miller’s absence, noting that his injury was less clear and they would need more information before making a decision on his status. Fortunately, Miller spoke to the media on Monday and expressed a bit more optimism about being able to play on Thursday. “I’m doing everything I humanly can to get my body feeling the best it can feel. Even with the progress just today that I’ve made, I’m happy, and I’m optimistic,” Miller said. Estimated limited practice C Juice Scruggs (knee) CB D.J. Reed (foot) — NEW INJURY Scruggs is estimated to have practiced both days this week, which, even if it’s limited, is a good sign that coaches believe he’ll have a chance to play Thursday. Reed was added to the injury report on Tuesday, suggesting he either injured himself during the walkthrough or was limited by discomfort. Unfortunately, Campbell isn’t scheduled to talk to the media again until after Thursday night’s game, so we will have to wait until Wednesday’s injury designations for an update on his status. Estimated full practice DB Christian Izien (groin) Another full practice is a good sign for Izien, and based on Campbell’s comments on Tuesday, he may be on track to make his Lions debut this week. “Last week, we were close but wanted to give him a few more days,” Campbell said of Izien’s potential return from injury. “He’s looked pretty good through the week, and we’ve continued to run him in preparation, hopefully, for this game. He took reps yesterday, so I would say he’s trending the right way—not totally there yet, but there’s a good chance.” Additionally, Izien told The Athletic’s Colton Pouncy he expects to play on Thursday , further supporting this possibility. title: Dan Campbell pours cold water on Detroit Lions Joey Porter Jr. trade rumors
summary: It’s no secret that a lot of people are connecting dots when it comes the Detroit Lions and Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. The 26-year-old defender is in the midst of a contract dispute with the Steelers, and sat out of Week 1 with a back injury. Per ESPN, the Steelers are open to […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 12: Joey Porter Jr. #24 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on from the field during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Houston Texans at Acrisure Stadium on January 12, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s no secret that a lot of people are connecting dots when it comes the Detroit Lions and Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. The 26-year-old defender is in the midst of a contract dispute with the Steelers, and sat out of Week 1 with a back injury. Per ESPN, the Steelers are open to hearing trade requests, and Porter is interested as well . Combine that with a thin Detroit Lions secondary—and over $38 million in cap space following a pair of contract restructures —and it’s easy to make a surface-level deduction that Detroit could be one of the team’s interested in courting Porter. Plenty of media outlets have made that connection. On Tuesday, though, Lions head coach Dan Campbell was asked if the significant amount of cap space— estimated to be second-most in the NFL —could be used on some sort of big acquisition now or before the trade deadline. “I don’t see that,” Campbell said. “I would say this, though: it gives us options, whether that be our own guys or—it just gives us flexibility here before the season starts because there’s a lot that can happen.” It’s worth noting that Campbell was not specifically asked about Porter—and he wouldn’t be able to talk about him directly, either, as it would be considered tampering. As for other potential uses of that cap space, the Lions have admitted publicly that they are interested in making both tight end Sam LaPorta and safety Brian Branch long-term players in this organization—both are eligible for contract extensions. Branch remains on the Physically Unable to Perform list after suffering an Achilles injury in December, while LaPorta is back in action after losing the last half of his 2025 season to a back injury. Detroit also likes to have a significant amount of freed cap space to manage their roster in case of injury. So, while things could always change, it doesn’t appear the Lions are currently interested in making a big roster move.

title: NFL Week 2 power rankings: Detroit Lions’ defensive concerns remain despite win
summary: The Detroit Lions opened the 2026 season with a 31-30 overtime win over the New Orleans Saints, and while a win is a win in the “ugly” month of the season, not all national writers were left impressed or optimistic. Let’s take a look at where the national media believe the Lions stand entering the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell watches a replay against New Orleans Saints during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions opened the 2026 season with a 31-30 overtime win over the New Orleans Saints, and while a win is a win in the “ugly” month of the season, not all national writers were left impressed or optimistic. Let’s take a look at where the national media believe the Lions stand entering the 2026 season in this week’s power rankings. The Athletic: 8 (Previous rank: 9) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : What we learned: A throwing motion negates a fumble The Lions were saved when an apparent Jared Goff fumble was ruled an incompletion thanks to a statute many had never heard of before. The Lions went on to survive a crazy second-half comeback by the Saints that exposed several significant flaws . But, hey, they’re still 1-0 entering a big Thursday night showdown. Yahoo Sports: 9 (Previous rank: 9) From Frank Schwab : The Lions almost blew a 21-0 lead. They held on when they forced an incompletion on a 2-point conversion in overtime. Detroit’s defense had played very well in building that lead, then let the Saints back in the game. Lions head coach Dan Campbell blamed the offense’s inefficiency for the lead slipping away. “I’m like, man, we’ve got to be more efficient on offense,” Campbell said. “We kind of spit and sputtered there and then they … had some tempo going.” The Lions face a very tough Week 2 game against the Bills, who will host their first regular-season game in their new stadium Thursday night. Sports Illustrated: 10 ( Previous rank: 8) From Connor Orr : A slightly more conservative Lions offense than we’re used to, with Jared Goff throwing at about half the average depth of target as Tyler Shough, but an efficient one nonetheless. I liked the Drew Petzing wrinkle of lining Penei Sewell back up on the right side and then rushing opposite to keep the Saints on their heels. The Lions’ secondary is going to be their cross to bear in 2026, but can the offense be so good it doesn’t matter? ESPN: 11 (Previous rank: 8) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : Non-QB newcomer debut: OC Drew Petzing Week 1 certainly wasn’t pretty, but Petzing’s offense looked like a well-oiled machine as it marched downfield for a 10-play, 70-yard drive in overtime that was capped by a 4-yard touchdown grab from WR Amon-Ra St. Brown. Petzing spent his past three seasons in Arizona, and in his Lions debut, he helped RB Jahmyr Gibbs record a career-high 34 touches. Quarterback Jared Goff thought Petzing “adjusted good” and “settled us down when we needed it and got us into the right plays. USA Today: 12 (Previous rank: 11) From Nate Davis : If you didn’t think missing starting safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch was a big deal, then you didn’t see Saints QB Tyler Shough raid this defense for 410 yards through the air Sunday. NFL.com: 13 (Previous rank: 15) From Nick Shook : The Lions played with a level of sloppiness typical of Week 1 but still managed to build a comfortable lead before watching it evaporate in the second half and scrambling to hang on for an overtime win. It’s not an ideal way to start the season, but credit Detroit for bouncing back from a dramatic collapse to record the victory. Sporting News: 13 (Previous rank: 15) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions were pushed into an overtime grind with the game Saints, bringing up lingering concerns about their defense outside of Aidan Hutchinson. But the high-priced trio of Jahmyr Gibbs, Jared Goff and Amon-Ra St. Brown saved the day, like they often will need to do. CBS Sports: 15 (Previous rank: 19) From Pete Prisco : They beat the Saints, but it was a lot tougher than expected. The secondary is going to be a problem until they get their starting safeties back. The Ringer: TBD (Previous rank: 16) From Diante Lee: Article not released at the time of publishing.

title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Can the Buffalo Bills finally win the AFC?
summary: For the first time this season, the Detroit Lions hit the road, heading to Orchard Park, New York, to face the Buffalo Bills. The Bills have a brand-new home in Highmark Stadium, and what a game to open it, primetime on “Thursday Night Football.“ Detroit is coming off an overtime thriller at home against the […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Terrel Bernard #8 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates fumble recovery during the fourth quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first time this season, the Detroit Lions hit the road, heading to Orchard Park, New York, to face the Buffalo Bills. The Bills have a brand-new home in Highmark Stadium, and what a game to open it, primetime on “Thursday Night Football.“ Detroit is coming off an overtime thriller at home against the New Orleans Saints, needing a stop on a two-point conversion to win. Buffalo defeated a tough team in the Houston Texans in a shootout on the road. Both teams are top Super Bowl contender in their conferences, and this game is a rare good game for a Thursday night. This could be a statement win for whoever comes out on top. If Detroit wins, they are moved up the chain as a threat in the NFC. If Buffalo wins, they’ll reinforce the belief around the league that they’re the team to beat in the AFC. Let’s dive in on the Bills and see why they’re the toughest team on the Lions’ schedule this season. Buffalo Bills 2025 Season 12-5 record (2nd in AFC East) 4th in points for, 12th in point allowed Overall DVOA: 8th (4th on offense, 20th on defense) 2025 was a slight step back for the Bills compared to 2024, as they lost to the Denver Broncos in overtime in the AFC Divisional Round. In 2024, they reached the AFC Championship Game, where they lost to the Kansas City Chiefs. The team, once again, failed to live up to the offseason hype, and their inability to reach the Super Bowl despite the talent on the roster cost their head coach, Sean McDermott, his job afterward. Quarterback Josh Allen was coming off his MVP season in 2024, and while his stats were similar to the year before, he was sacked the most times ever in his career: 40. Allen threw for 3,668 yards (11th in the league) with 25 touchdowns and 10 interceptions. His success on the ground continued, as he rushed for 579 yards and 14 touchdowns, averaging 5.2 yards per carry. Speaking of running the ball, Allen got a big help in running back James Cook, who led the NFL in rushing yards with 1,621, a career high. He also found the end zone 12 times and averaged 5.2 yards per carry. His ability to move the rock between the tackles helped take some of the weight off Allen’s shoulders, who had previously had to do all the heavy lifting. It also strengthened their read-option play calling, as teams accounted for Cook more than Allen. For the passing game, Allen struggled to have a dominant top receiver on the team, as Khalil Shakir led the team in catches (72) and yards (719), but only scored four touchdowns. The touchdown leader was tight end Dalton Kincaid, who got 39 catches for 571 yards and five touchdowns. Defensively, the Bills didn’t really stand out in anything particular. EDGE Joey Bosa was one of their top contributors, getting five sacks and leading the league in forced fumbles with five. EDGE Gregory Rousseau led the team in sacks with seven, and safety Cole Bishop led the team in interceptions with three and tackles (85). Buffalo had the 17th-ranked passing defense and 12th-ranked run defense per DVOA, so that side of the ball wasn’t their best, and they relied on their offense to win games. 2026 offseason Key additions: EDGE Bradley Chubb, CB Dee Alford, S Chauncey Gardner-Johnson, WR DJ Moore (trade) Key losses: G David Edwards, EDGE Joey Bosa, EDGE A.J. Epenesa, CB Cam Lewis, HC Sean McDermott 2026 NFL Draft picks Round 2: EDGE TJ Parker Round 2: CB Davison Igbinosun Round 4: OT Jude Bowry Round 4: WR Skyler Bell Round 4: LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr Round 5: S Jalon Kilgore Round 5: DT Zane Durant Round 7: CB Toriano Pride Jr. Round 7: P Tommy Doman Jr. Round 7: G Ar’Maj Reed-Adams Buffalo did more addition than subtraction, starting with the firing of McDermott. With McDermott gone, the Bills promoted offensive coordinator Joe Brady to head coach. On the defensive line, the Bills needed veteran help and upgrades, and they believe they got some. While losing Epenesa to free agency and Bosa to possible retirement, the Bills signed Chubb to a three-year deal worth $43.5 million. The secondary got some help as well, getting cornerback Dee Alford and former Lions safety Chauncey Gardner-Johnson. The Bills’ biggest loss was guard David Edwards, and losing two veterans on the defensive line forces them to shake things up there. Cornerback Cam Lewis was the biggest loss in the secondary for Buffalo. The Bills addressed most of their losses in the 2026 NFL Draft, taking EDGE TJ Parker and cornerback Davison Igbinosun in the second round. The Bills gave up one of their second-round picks for Chicago Bears wide receiver DJ Moore, giving Allen a boost in the passing game and a clear WR1 for the team. The rest of the draft was for depth purposes, snagging multiple offensive linemen and secondary players, while getting a new punter as well. Overall, the Bills roster doesn’t have as much turnover as other teams, with the biggest change at head coach. They believe they are close to winning a Super Bowl, so I get the few moves they made. 2026 season thus far (1-0) Week 1: Defeated Houston Texans, 36-31 Stats: 5th in points scored, 22nd in points allowed Overall DVOA: 4th (2nd on offense, 23rd on defense, 3rd on special teams) What a game to start the year for the Bills; going on the road and defeating the Texans isn’t easy. The Texans’ defense is tough, and the Bills needed to score on their final drive to win and put up 36 points. Allen had a solid game, throwing for 334 yards and two touchdowns, rushing for 23 yards on six carries and scoring two more times. Cook was limited most of the game, rushing for 57 yards, averaging 4.4 yards per carry, and had three catches for 12 yards. Allen didn’t take long to find success with his new weapon in Moore, as he finished with five catches for 100 yards and a touchdown. Kincaid finished as the leading receiver with five catches for 130 yards, and wide receiver Joshua Palmer found the end zone on his only catch for 34 yards. Defensively, the Bills had a rough day in slowing down the Texans offense, allowing quarterback C.J. Stroud to throw for 274 yards and two touchdowns. While Stroud played well, former Lions running back David Montgomery led the charge, rushing for 60 yards and two touchdowns while also catching three passes for 19 yards and a touchdown. If the Texans needed to score, they gave the ball to Montgomery. The Bills forced two fumbles and recovered both; one turned into a field goal early in the game, and the last came on the final drive, leading to the Bills kneeling it out. Rousseau finished with two sacks, and both fumbles were caused by him, making him the most impactful player on the defense on Sunday. If not for his big day, the Bills might have lost the game. Injury notes Key players ruled out : None Key players to monitor : DT T.J. Sanders (knee), RB Ty Johnson (hamstring) Injuries haven’t really affected the Bills much at the start of the year. Defensive tackle T.J. Sanders and running back Ty Johnson missed Week 1, but both could potentially play in Week 2 (both listed as limited on Monday). Johnson is dealing with a hamstring injury, but it appears the team held him out to get him ready for Week 2. Sanders is dealing with a knee injury after popping up on the injury report late last week, and Brady downplayed the severity of the injury, saying he missed last week as a precaution. Biggest strength: Quarterback Facing off against a former MVP in Allen, it’s hard not to see him as the team’s biggest strength. The offense runs through Allen overall, and without him, this team wouldn’t be the same. Allen isn’t your typical dual-threat quarterback; the man acts like a bulldozer while running with the football. Allen isn’t afraid of contact like most quarterbacks, and his agility is…
author: Brandon Knapp

title: Lions vs. Saints Song of the Game: ‘Paradise by the dashboard light’ by Meat Loaf
summary: The rush to judgment in the NFL after Week 1 is maddening. We enter the season fully aware that September football is ugly, and Week 1 lies. Yet the dizzying speed, emotion, and overall cacophony of the NFL’s return creates monsters of us all. FIRE THIS GUY! THAT QUARTERBACK SUCKS! I TOLD YOU THEY WERE […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions celebrates 31-30 win against the New Orleans Saints with Chuck Clark #36 after the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The rush to judgment in the NFL after Week 1 is maddening. We enter the season fully aware that September football is ugly, and Week 1 lies. Yet the dizzying speed, emotion, and overall cacophony of the NFL’s return creates monsters of us all. FIRE THIS GUY! THAT QUARTERBACK SUCKS! I TOLD YOU THEY WERE GOING TO BE TERRIBLE THIS YEAR! The Detroit Lions eked out a win over the New Orleans Saints, and no matter what your expectations for the team were in 2026, this game confirmed those greatest fears and/or highest expectations. The first half proves the Lions, when firing on all cylinders, are capable of blowing out anyone. Or the second half definitively shows Kelvin Sheppard is a fraud, the secondary stinks, and the Lions’ Super Bowl window is closed. Y’all, can we just sleep on it? Detroit Lions Week 1 Song of the Game: “Paradise By The Dashboard Light” by Meat Loaf Yes, “Song of the Game” is back due to popular demand me just wanting to do it again and bring some fun back to the site. If you weren’t around or don’t remember, Song of the Game is exactly what it sounds like: a song that attempts to capture the essence of the Lions’ game. We talk about it here, do it weekly, and then we have a crazy, disjointed playlist by the end of the season. If you want to relive previous Lions seasons, you can find the playlists we curated below: 2016 , 2017 , 2018 , 2019 , 2020 , 2021 , 2022 . And if you want to read previous versions of our Song of the Game columns, you can find those here . It’s only appropriate that the first song to kick off this playlist is one that matches the Lions’ season opener in length. Meat Loaf’s most iconic duet stretches nearly eight-and-a-half minutes, taking the listener through a journey of love, thrills, painful indecisiveness, and regret. Yeah, that sounds about right. Now, I’m going to admit right here that this song is overtly sexual, and it’s going to make for some awkward metaphors. So buckle up. This one isn’t for the faint of hearts. We’re glowing like the metal on the edge of a knife Glowing like the metal on the edge of a knife The Lions’ 2026 season got off to a somewhat strong start. After shaking off a three-and-out, the offense put together an impressive 13-play, 89-yard drive. Jahmyr Gibbs had gains of 11, 21, and 11 yards before eventually walking in untouched for the season’s first score. The rushing lanes were occasionally gaping, the blocking schemes were complicated, and the offensive line—despite losing Christian Mahogany halfway through the drive—was humming. Oh, baby, we were cookin’. After Meat Loaf and Ellen Foley spend the first 3:30 glam rocking to each other about the sex their characters are about to have, the song kicks in a funky beat and a faux radio call of a baseball game is laid over the track. It’s about as blatant a sex metaphor as you can get, as the not-so-convincing radio announcer describes a series of plays in which the runner crosses each base and nears home. He’s taking a pretty big lead out there Almost daring him to try and pick him off The Lions were inching closer and closer to a decisive Week 1 win. Derrick Barnes, interception. Gibbs, touchdown. Roger McCreary, sack fumble. Amon-Ra St. Brown, touchdown. Ford Field was feeling it, Lions fans were in awe of the team’s defense finally coming together with a marriage of pass rush and coverage. It was starting to feel like Detroit’s offseason plan was coming together perfectly. Stop right there Just before we find out whether this “base runner” is “safe at home,” Foley screams out to stop everything. The song comes to a screeching halt. Before the baseball player is ready to “consummate” his trip around the bases, she begs for long-term commitment and faith. And just like the Lions failed to seal the deal cleanly, Meat Loaf struggled to find an answer. I gotta know right now, before we go any further Do you love me? Will you love me forever? Baby, baby, let me sleep on it Well, let me sleep on it I’ll give you an answer in the morning As with every NFL fanbase after every game, the noise following the Lions’ 31-30 win has been loud and exaggerated. The doubters now have definitive proof the Lions are doomed. The endlessly faithful point to the first half as irrefutable evidence everything is going to be fine once things settle in. Me, I’m not so sure. I’m not ready to give an answer. There were promising developments in the run game, offensive line, and pass rush. But there were troubling, ominous signs in the secondary, defensive game plan, and offensive inconsistency. Everyone is in a rush to find out answers and come to undeniable conclusions. Why can’t anyone just admit: we still don’t know. We need more time. Let’s sleep on it. Meat Loaf’s marathon of a song ends in tragedy. The male character expresses grief, regret, and sorrow for those exciting days. He’s stuck in a relationship bonded by carnal pleasure instead of true love. He’s tormented by his past, hasty choices and just wants it all to end. Unlike the narrator, though, the Lions have a chance to quickly put the past behind them. Thursday is a new opportunity to recapture that glowing edge of a knife and find true success—not just fleeting sparks. You can follow along with this year’s playlist with this direct link to Spotify , or the embedded player below.

title: Film study: How Drew Petzing helped Detroit Lions’ recapture their run game vs. Saints
summary: If the Detroit Lions want to reestablish themselves as Super Bowl contenders, improving the run game has to be at the top of the priority list. Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints was a strong start. Throughout the season, I plan on writing these film studies to break down different elements of the game. […]
full_text: If the Detroit Lions want to reestablish themselves as Super Bowl contenders, improving the run game has to be at the top of the priority list. Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints was a strong start. Throughout the season, I plan on writing these film studies to break down different elements of the game. Each week will focus on something different or build on a previous film study. Some weeks will focus on the offense; others, the defense. It could be a single play in great detail, a critical series, or anything that catches my eye and that I think will be interesting to dig into. This week it’s the run game that will be put under the microscope. With that said, I want to make one thing clear: I do not have all of the answers . The approach to this series will be one where I am learning, studying the film, and growing my own knowledge of the Lions and the ever-evolving game of football. So if you have questions, disagree with something, or have constructive criticisms and corrections, please join the discussion in the comments section. Main takeaways After watching all of the Lions’ run plays from Week 1, there are three main takeaways I came away with: Occasional “key breaker” changeups A detailed approach in making similar schemes look different Isaac TeSlaa is a difference-maker “CRUNCH” key breaker My favorite run play of the game is in this first one featured below. This run scheme is known as a “CRUNCH” concept. Fundamentally, the concept involves cross-blocks with roots in trap and belly schemes. This concept, visually shown below, hinges on backside trap blocks (yellow) from the tight end as well as both the left and right guards. The run is designed to hit the strong-side C gap, between right tackle Blake Miller and tight end Brock Wright. Miller (green) kicks out the wide-9 edge defender, while Wright follows behind and traps the inside 3-technique defensive tackle. This cross-block concept continues down the line as center Juice Scruggs and left tackle Penei Sewell (orange) glide up to the second level. This run scheme creates two advantages worth highlighting. First, the cross-blocks between the right tackle and the tight end give each blocker an advantageous angle for his respective assignments, putting each player in a better position to succeed. Those angles create a natural wall in the C-gap alley, similar to classic belly and trap schemes. Second, linebackers are often given keys to follow pulling guards. This CRUNCH concept is designed to break those keys. On this play, both guards give pull to their left, while the intended run gap is to their right, creating a false read for the linebackers. When you watch the video clip of the play below, keep your eyes on linebackers No. 55 and No. 20. No. 55 immediately points in the direction of the pulling guards and hesitates, while number 20 is off to the races to fill in the direction of the pulling guards. Key breaker plays are a great changeup to have in any good scheme, both for the current game and for future opponents to be cognizant of while game planning. The next play shows a slightly similar action, but in a zone-blocking scheme. Watch right tackle Blake Miller similarly kick out the edge defender, while tight end Sam LaPorta slides inside with a lead fold block into the play-side zone scheme. A critical takeaway here is that the good coaches make the same schemes look different while making different schemes look the same. Drew Petzing gives a small taste of that with those blocking actions above. In the series of plays, it’s taken to another level. Heavy personnel shell game Throughout Dan Campbell’s tenure as the Lions’ head coach, the team has consistently used six offensive linemen personnel packages, previously featuring Dan Skipper. Now Skipper is wearing a headset, but the heavy personnel packages are here to stay. Petzing called heavy personnel five times in Week 1, each with a different twist. Now, I don’t know the exact verbiage for these plays, but for the sake of clarity in showing the differences in each variation, I’ll use some of my own terms to define elements. Play 1 – Heavy Left, Tackle Swap, Power Right The Lions’ first touchdown of the season grabbed plenty of attention as Petzing pulled out a wrinkle by swapping Penei Sewell back to the right side with Blake Miller to the left, while sixth offensive lineman Larry Borum checked in and was declared eligible. The Lions immediately ran right behind the All-Pro with a power concept. Note LaPorta’s strong combination block with Sewell, initiating the double-team before peeling off to block the second-level linebacker, allowing Gibbs to walk in untouched. Heavy Left: six offensive linemen, with the sixth lined up to the left. Tackle Swap: left and right tackles swap positions. Power Right: run concept. Play 2 – Heavy Right, DUO Right, “tag” Man On the second called play with heavy personnel, the Lions did not line up with any personnel deception. Sewell was in his normal left tackle position, with Miller and Borum to the right. This is where I will be honest: I am not entirely sure what the run concept initially called here was, but my suspicion here is that it was a DUO scheme with a “man” tag based on the defensive alignment. The Saints respond to the heavy personnel with two 2i-techniques in the A gaps. This throws a wrench in a traditional DUO concept. DUO typically presents with double-teams of the guard and center against the A-gap defender, with a second double team of the other guard and tackle against the opposite B-gap defender. With both A gaps occupied and neither B gap occupied, adjustments have to be made. Borum and Miller double the strong-side C-gap defender, while the “man” tag calls for each guard to take a man base block of the 2i-techniques. Center Scruggs immediately releases to the second-level linebacker. Heavy Right: six offensive linemen, with the sixth lined up to the right. DUO, “tag” Man: run concept. Play 3 – Heavy Left, Miller Extra, Inside Zone Right Next, a new variation of heavy emerges, with Blake Miller as the “extra” sixth offensive lineman and lining up outside of and next to left tackle Sewell. The Lions also ran this with an unbalanced alignment, putting two tight ends on the Heavy Left side. With all the attention of the tight ends and both starting tackles on the left side, Petzing calls an inside zone run concept to the weak side with Borum at right tackle. Heavy Left: six offensive linemen, with the sixth lined up to the left. Miller Extra: Blake Miller becomes the extra lineman. Inside Zone Right: run concept. Play 4 – Heavy Right, Sewell Extra, DUO Right, “tag” Man The fourth iteration of heavy is a blend of Plays 2 and 3. Heavy Right: six offensive linemen, with the sixth lined up to the right. Sewell Extra: Penei Sewell becomes the extra lineman. DUO, “tag” Man: run concept. Play 5 – Heavy Left, Tackle Swap, Power Right Same as Play 1, and almost another Gibbs touchdown. A few key notes here. On all five of the heavy personnel plays, Larry Borum was declared the eligible receiver, regardless of the various alignments. Given that the Lions varied how they aligned all three tackles, it is not hard to imagine how difficult this could be for a defense to track. Who is eligible? Where is the eligible receiver aligned? Where is the strength? It’s a game of Three-Card Monte, but with Sewell, Miller, and Borum. Isaac TeSlaa shoutout The last play of this film study is a quick shoutout to the wide receivers and their role in the run game, particularly Isaac TeSlaa. While TeSlaa was limited to zero receptions on a single target, he was still a difference-maker in the game. This outside zone toss sweep only works because TeSlaa down-blocks on edge defender Tyree Wilson. TeSlaa strains and maintains his block until Gibbs rounds the corner. Despite finishing the play on his tail, TeSlaa will earn the respect of his teammates and coaching staff for doing the dirty work.

(Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first time in the 2026 season — and one of the few times that this is scheduled to be the case — the Green Bay Packers will be buried in the midst of the early Sunday kickoff window in Week 2. Green Bay’s matchup with the New York Jets, to be aired on FOX, is far from a prime game for the network. The other two competing games — Eagles-Titans and Panthers-Falcons — will be limited in their broadcast areas as well. Here’s the country’s TV map for the early window on FOX, from 506sports.com, showing Packers-Jets in green: That’s Minnesota-Chicago in blue, getting most of the airplay, with Eagles-Titans in red and Carolina-Atlanta in yellow. Adding insult to injury for Packers fans this week is FOX’s choice of commentators for their game. title: Green Bay Packers News: Brandon Cisse makes a good first impression
summary: Nobody really wants to hear about bright spots after the way the Packers started the season, but there were a few in Week 1, and rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse was one of them. Yes, Justin Jefferson got the better of him on one noteworthy play, but Justin Jefferson has a way of doing that. He’s […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Brandon Cisse #2 and Kaleb Johnson #26 of the Green Bay Packers run onto the field prior to the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Nobody really wants to hear about bright spots after the way the Packers started the season, but there were a few in Week 1, and rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse was one of them. Yes, Justin Jefferson got the better of him on one noteworthy play, but Justin Jefferson has a way of doing that. He’s victimized better corners than Cisse well past the first game of their career. But outside of Jefferson’s score, Cisse was on target and on task, playing 49 snaps in his first game in the NFL, the most of any Packers defender that didn’t hit 100% in Week 1. The Packers’ defensive backfield has been the target of no small number of questions this offseason, but if this is what we can expect from Cisse, those questions should largely go away. He and Keisean Nixon will have their problems, I’m sure, but every competent snap helps every other defensive back do his job better. That’s the real takeaway from Cisse’s performance. Rising tides in the secondary tend to carry all boats, and every decent performer takes just that much pressure off of everyone else. If Cisse continues to grow and perform well, it’ll only help a Packers team that can use all the help it can get right now. title: Carrington Valentine got picked on in the red zone vs. the Vikings
summary: While the Green Bay Packers’ defense did well on Sunday — if you can believe it — as the unit ranks among the NFL’s highest in fewest yards per play allowed through Week 1’s action, one glaring issue on the defense did pop up at the end of the Packers’ loss to the Minnesota Vikings: […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images While the Green Bay Packers’ defense did well on Sunday — if you can believe it — as the unit ranks among the NFL’s highest in fewest yards per play allowed through Week 1’s action, one glaring issue on the defense did pop up at the end of the Packers’ loss to the Minnesota Vikings: cornerback Carrington Valentine’s play when the Vikings were on the warning stripe of scoring a touchdown. Valentine played for just 13 snaps as Brandon Cisse’s replacement at left cornerback, as the second-round rookie dropped out of the game due to a cramp. You’ll see it out there that Benjamin St-Juste played one snap of defense on Sunday, but he was only on the field for a kneel-down, not a real play against a live offense. It was Keisean Nixon and Cisse at outside cornerback, and when Cisse left, it was Valentine who subbed in for him. Unfortunately, Valentine had five pretty bad plays in those 13 reps, and they all came when Minnesota was over the 50-yard line. CV pic.twitter.com/ME47WYs76N — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 16, 2026 The first play was an explosive run; Valentine did little at the point of attack. This has been an issue for Valentine since he came into the NFL, and it was why the Packers actually rotated in Kamal Hadden and Nate Hobbs for Valentine on run looks before those two players were ultimately injured last season. If you need a reminder of Valentine’s ability to play strong on the perimeter, here’s another example: a screen-turned-touchdown from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Dallas Goedert in the Packers’ playoff loss from the 2024 season. The second play was a bootleg where Valentine had to follow Justin Jefferson across the field, and Jefferson was able to cut the distance to the goal in half without Valentine ever being a factor on the play. The third play is a pin-and-pull play where Valentine doesn’t set a hard edge until he’s basically out of bounds, making it more difficult for his teammates to be involved. Valentine doesn’t initiate contact with the running back until they hit the goal line, at which point it doesn’t even matter. The fourth play? Another run directly at Valentine. This one starts on the right hash, and Valentine doesn’t set an edge until he’s outside of the numbers, letting the Vikings cut the distance to the sticks in half. And the final play is that same boot action look again, as Minnesota found a call they liked, but this time Jefferson scores a touchdown because Valentine missed a tackle around the seven-yard line. All in all, it was a pretty poor showing for Valentine on Sunday. The worst place to play him is in the red zone, as the Vikings showed, but it’s where the defense spent a lot of time because of the failures of the offensive line . Personally, I don’t think it’s a bad idea to start spelling Valentine with St-Juste, if Valentine does get playing time, in obvious run looks or the red zone. St-Juste was clearly brought in as a CB4 and a special teams contributor, but with a 6’3”, 200-pound frame, I feel like he gives you a better chance on the perimeter than the 5’11”-and-change, 189-pound Valentine in those situations. Valentine is fine as a middle-of-the-field coverage player, but a goal-line threat he is not.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Packers Defense: Jonathan Gannon has a lot of answers
summary: While former Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley called defenses with pretty predictable structures, as he mostly called in plays out of a 4-3 base and a nickel defense, we were promised a more diverse set of answers under Jonathan Gannon, who runs a 3-4 base. While it wasn’t enough to stop the Minnesota […]
full_text: (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images While former Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley called defenses with pretty predictable structures, as he mostly called in plays out of a 4-3 base and a nickel defense, we were promised a more diverse set of answers under Jonathan Gannon, who runs a 3-4 base. While it wasn’t enough to stop the Minnesota Vikings from scoring 39 points ( Thanks, offensive line! ), we did get a look at what types of answers Gannon has on defense last Sunday. I want to break down these answers as two sets of families, because there are several defenses that have the same personnel groupings: the 3-4 family and the nickel family. 3-4 Family 3-4 — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:39:24.426Z The photo above is the Packers’ typical 3-4 defense, with two edge defenders on the field, three interior defensive linemen (think 300-pounders) and two off-ball linebackers in the box. I won’t explain this one too much, since you guys are probably well familiar with how this defense works. It’s been around for decades, and it’s what 3-4 teams generally call against two-receiver sets. 6-1 (Cooper dropdown) — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:44:04.424Z One change-up that Gannon has is adding a sixth player to the line of scrimmage, which, in the Packers’ case, is Will linebacker Edgerrin Cooper. This is Gannon’s answer to heavier formations where the offense is in an obvious running situation. The screenshot above is from a situation where the Vikings had two backs and a tight end on the field and only needed three yards to move the sticks. In this look, the weak-side edge defender (in this case it’s Dani Dennis-Sutton at the top of the screen) is “reduced” into a third defensive tackle role and Cooper drops down on the edge to replace him. In short, it’s a way for the Packers to clog up running lanes at the point of attack while not tipping off to the offense that they’re doing so, as they aren’t getting into a new personnel package — only the spacing is changing. Nickel Family Nickel — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:39:57.074Z The photo above is nothing special; it’s just your run-of-the-mill nickel defense. There are two edge defenders (3-4 outside linebackers or 4-3 defensive ends, depending on the scheme), two interior defensive linemen (again, think 300-pounders) and two off-ball linebackers. The spacing is similar to a 4-3 defense, with the major difference being that instead of a strong-side (Sam) linebacker, that player has been replaced by a nickelback (in this case, it’s safety Javon Bullard at the top of the screen). Penny (LVN kick inside) — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:46:32.316Z The Packers have different ways to get into different spacings out of this group, though. In the preseason, Gannon debuted his penny defense , which is essentially a 3-4 defense on the line of scrimmage with just one off-ball linebacker (generally, 3-4 defenses sub out the Will linebacker for the slot defender). Gannon had a couple of new wrinkles for the regular season, though. Because Green Bay’s Will (Cooper) is a player that the Packers want on the field full-time, they play him on the edge. So do the Packers sub out an edge rusher to get the nickelback on the field? No! Edge defender Lukas Van Ness (top of screen), who can hold his own on the interior, has been regularly kicking inside in these nickel subpackages, allowing Green Bay to sub out a 300-pound defensive tackle. That’s how the Packers were able to play penny out of nickel personnel in this game. For what it’s worth, Green Bay used a true slot defender against the Vikings, a different look from their preseason set — when they played split safeties and then Xavier McKinney 15 yards deep in the middle of the field over the split safeties. This formation is used when the Packers want to stop the run (with their spacing) against three-receiver sets, but still want to play coverage (with their personnel, by bringing a slot defender onto the field). Mint (LVN kicked inside) — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:39:40.707Z This is another nickel personnel subpackage that the Packers have. It’s similar to penny, in that Van Ness is kicking inside to a defensive tackle position, but instead of the team playing a five-down front with one off-ball linebacker, the team plays a five-down front with two off-ball linebackers. To make the math work out of nickel personnel, Bullard, the slot defender, actually plays the edge defender position opposite of the true edge rusher (Bullard is at the top of the screen here). The Packers are using this against two-receiver sets (which usually demand a 3-4 base defense) in obvious passing situations. For example, the screenshot above comes from a 2nd and 10 when the Vikings played two tight ends and a running back. The thinking is that a team in Minnesota’s situation would want to pass the ball, but is baiting the defense to get into their base defense to match their personnel. The Packers are comfortable enough with Van Ness inside (something he didn’t do at all in the preseason outside of rush packages) and Bullard on the edge to call opposing offenses’ bluffs. Other 3 LB package (new) on 3rd & XL — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:40:23.789Z This is the final package I want to talk about, and it was sort of a one-off. The Packers called this three-off-ball-linebacker set just one time, on a third and extra long against the Vikings. There’s only one interior defensive lineman on the field, the head-up nose tackle, while two inside linebackers are walked up over the guards and two edge defenders are outside of the tackles. This is Green Bay’s answer to screens and draws: Taking off a 300-pounder for an extra off-ball linebacker, who in this case is Isaiah McDuffie, to help run and chase on a tackle. — There are a lot of different defenses that Gannon called this weekend, and they all have their own specific usage. For the most part, the team matches offensive personnel with defensive personnel — meaning two-receiver sets are matched with a 3-4 base and three-receiver sets are matched with a nickel defense. Certain situations call for different options, though, which is why the Packers played it’s 6-1 against heavy personnel in run downs, penny against light offenses in run downs, mint against heavy offenses in pass downs and their three-linebacker set when a screen or draw was coming on an extra long down and distance. So far, the Packers lead the NFL in yards per play on defense (Thanks again, offensive line!), so it’s hard to make the case that the plan didn’t work in Week 1. We’ll keep an eye on Green Bay’s defense week-to-week and let you all know if anything is changing with their plan.

title: Packers sign former draft pick, visitor Eric Johnson II
summary: After releasing receiver Chris Hilton Jr., the Green Bay Packers had three open spots on their practice squad. The Packers will be filling at least one of those spots on the roster this week, as Sports Illustrated’s Bill Huber has reported that the team will sign defensive lineman Eric Johnson II. Johnson is an interesting name, […]
full_text: (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After releasing receiver Chris Hilton Jr. , the Green Bay Packers had three open spots on their practice squad. The Packers will be filling at least one of those spots on the roster this week, as Sports Illustrated ’s Bill Huber has reported that the team will sign defensive lineman Eric Johnson II . Johnson is an interesting name, as we highlighted him as a possibility for Green Bay after cutdowns, since he was a pre-draft visitor for the team in 2022, when the Indianapolis Colts selected him in the fifth round. At the cutdown deadline, there seemed to be little reason for the addition of Johnson, but clearly things changed when Nazir Stackhouse was claimed off waivers by the Tennessee Titans and Jaden Crumedy was signed off the Packers’ practice squad by the Houston Texans, leaving Green Bay with no bodies on the defensive line on the practice squad. Updated with bench correction. Eric Johnson II was drafted with pick 159 of round 5 in the 2022 draft class. He scored a 9.39 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 90 out of 1459 DT from 1987 to 2022. https://t.co/de2dJlN1US #RAS #Colts pic.twitter.com/eUYwWMaVRg — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 30, 2022 In his NFL career, Johnson has played 51 games in the regular season (40 for the Indianapolis Colts and 11 for the New England Patriots) and has recorded 700 defensive snaps and 132 special teams snaps (mostly on field goal block). This is Johnson’s fourth NFL team, as he was also a member of the Minnesota Vikings and Atlanta Falcons (the Packers’ Week 3 Thursday Night Football opponent) during training camp. Johnson is one of eight players who have worked out with the Packers this week so far. In total, the team brought in three interior defensive linemen, three wide receivers, a quarterback and an international edge defender for tryouts. I would not be surprised if the practice squad is filled with two other signings by Wednesday’s practice.

title: Adam Stenavich explains the Packers’ offensive line woes
summary: On Tuesday, the Green Bay Packers’ coordinators had an opportunity to speak to the media for the first time since the team’s opening-week loss to the Minnesota Vikings. Obviously, coming out of that game, where the Vikings scored 29-straight points but only had to post one drive of over 28 yards during that run because […]
full_text: (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Tuesday, the Green Bay Packers’ coordinators had an opportunity to speak to the media for the first time since the team’s opening-week loss to the Minnesota Vikings. Obviously, coming out of that game, where the Vikings scored 29-straight points but only had to post one drive of over 28 yards during that run because the offense was coughing up the ball on short fields, the center of the Packers universe right now currently revolves around the offensive line position. Early on in his press availability, offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich tried to calm the media storm around the position, stating, “I’m not gonna freak out or overreact or anything like that. This is the first game of a 17-game season.” That makes one of us. I’m very much freaking out! When Stenavich was asked about how the team could have avoided putting quarterback Jordan Love in such a bad position, he said that the majority of the issue on the line came from “miscommunication upfront. The backs and linemen not on the same page.” Hopefully the team pulls it together for the pass-rush plan this week, but they had multiple weeks to prepare for the Vikings, and they’re staring down a stretch where they’ll play two games in five days, as they have the Atlanta Falcons on Thursday Night Football right after they play the New York Jets on Sunday. The other big subject that fans had questions about was how former undrafted player Donovan Jennings earned the start at left guard once Aaron Banks (knee tendinitis) was ruled out, over draft picks like Jager Burton, Anthony Belton, John Williams and Travis Glover, who were either on the bench offensively or were healthy scratches during the game. Stenavich stated that “We felt like Donovan was doing a better job in practice.” Previously, head coach Matt LaFleur said that the team preferred Jennings, who has only gotten extended playing time in one NFL game — six snaps against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 17 last year — in his NFL career, because of his “time on task.” The team generally played Burton at left guard with the starting unit throughout training camp, until the last week of camp, when Burton was cross-trained more as a center (Burton played both positions in college) and Jennings was pushed into the left guard position. Stenavich also mentioned that the team isn’t ruling out transitioning Belton back to guard, the position he played during the 2025 regular season, to help the team. Belton has spent both of his NFL training camps at the tackle position, as the team has been short on bodies there, and could potentially move to guard full-time during both of his regular seasons. This begs the question: Did the staff not think they would struggle at guard for a second season and potentially need to develop their former second-rounder to play that position, rather than one he ultimately wasn’t needed for during the regular season? In other contradictory news, Stenavich stated that ideally the team would have liked tight end Tucker Kraft to run the sneak play on fourth-and-one, but that they didn’t want to use him in that scenario, as Kraft was coming off his ACL tear. LaFleur previously said that Kraft’s injury was not a factor in the decision. When the coaching staff can’t keep their stories straight, it’s hard to know what the truth is.

title: Packers Film Room: Setting up a slant
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ payoff here isn’t huge, but I always love seeing how a call is set up in real time. We’ve got three plays we’re going to look at real quick, with the first two plays informing the third. Play 1: 2nd & 9, 8:28 remaining in the 3rd quarter In their drubbing […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ payoff here isn’t huge, but I always love seeing how a call is set up in real time. We’ve got three plays we’re going to look at real quick, with the first two plays informing the third. Play 1: 2nd & 9, 8:28 remaining in the 3rd quarter In their drubbing of the Rams in Australia, the 49ers made liberal use of a specific type of motion in their offense. I’ve heard a lot of names for that type of motion being thrown around – “Banana” being my favorite – but I believe it’s called Dash motion, so that’s what we’ll use until I learn otherwise. It’s not too different from what we’ve been seeing in Green Bay (and around the league) for years, but it’s different enough to mention it. The blocker will go in motion before the snap, and it’s kind of a long, looping motion behind the line. Arcing behind the line, instead of more of a straight line. At the snap, he’ll start towards the line and block. It kind of looks like a mix between Orbit motion and a TE motion block. When using this motion, the 49ers had the blocker (Kyle Juszczyk) attack different parts of the line, keeping the Rams defense off balance. The Packers used this a handful of times against the Vikings, to middling results. It seems pretty clear that it was not originally in their playbook, but they had a package of plays armed with it for this game. I assume we’ll the use expanded in the coming weeks. When using Dash motion, the Packers basically did one thing: Mark Redman [86] was the Dash blocker (most of the time). He’d go in motion at the snap and kick out the EMOL (End Man On Line), while Jacob Monk [62] would pull from his RG position. The handoff would go to the RB, who would run behind this. They hit a nice run with it early, but, as I said earlier, the results were middling. As they used it a few more times, a trend emerged: the outside defender from the side Redman was originally aligned on would blitz. Play 2: 1st & 10, 7:23 remaining in the 3rd quarter A couple plays after the play we just looked at, the Packers showed the same thing. Redman as the outside TE in YY Wing on the right, going in Dash motion. Redman kicks out the EMOL, Monk pulls and Isaiah Rodgers [2] blitzes. Play 3: 2nd & 4, 1:24 remaining in the 3rd quarter On the next drive, the Packers try something a little different. They’re no longer in YY Wing and the Dash motion man is Josh Whyle [81], but they’re using Dash all the same. Instead of closed side of the field, Matthew Golden [0] is lined up wide outside of where Whyle was originally aligned. The Packers are seeing if the Vikings have an automatic boundary blitz called when Dash motion is called. If it is an auto blitz check, the Packers are running Golden on a slant behind it. Rodgers does a good job of hiding his intentions until the ball is snapped. As soon as it’s snapped, Rodgers makes a beeline for the backfield. Jordan Love [10] takes a glimpse over, sees Rodgers blitzing and fires a quick throw over to Golden. Eric Wilson [55] is buzzing over, but he can’t get to the ball and Golden is able to dip under the tackle to pick up a few more yards. I love it when a plan comes together. I even slowed down the throw so you can enjoy it that way if you prefer. Albums listened to: she’s green – swallowtail ; Tom Waits – Rain Dogs

(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Bad losses tend to put everything in the larger universe of Packers-related takes in free fall for a while, but at a certain point, it feels like even the most outlandish takes aren’t exaggerating anymore. Dating back to last year’s Broncos game, the Packers have collapsed again and again, week after week, and every time it happens, it feels like we reach a new critical mass of takes. I’ve heard from readers and listeners since Sunday suggesting all manner of causes for the Packers’ trouble, ranging from the implausible (the league told the refs to penalize the Packers as retribution for the hit on Kyler Murray) to the absurd (the Packers lost because Jordan Love has bad body language). But the weirder and more gut-wrenching ways in which the Packers lose, the harder it becomes to dismiss anything. Are the Packers just cosmically unlucky? I mean, even if you think Matt LaFleur is the worst coach in the world, you’d think things would break his way a couple of times in the span of what’s now a six-game losing streak. How many random drops or weird bounces or phantom flags can possibly go against one team in one stretch? All that to say, as exhausting as the wild and wacky and weird takes might be right now, it’s almost impossible to find your way out of the fever swamps, too. Much like the Packers, we’re going to have to ride this out to the bitter end. summary: Welcome back to Battle Red Blog’s NFL Power Rankings roundup! full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Nico Collins #12 of the Houston Texans celebrates after scoring a touchdown with Xavier Hutchinson #19 against the Buffalo Bills during the second quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to Battle Red Blog’s NFL Power Rankings roundup! Every year, I take the honor of leapfrogging from website to website, taking the pulse on the greater NFL punditry and their thoughts on the Houston Texans. Last week, I kicked off the 2026 Power Rankings with my own, personal power rankings, but now in Week 2, I’ll return to the standard format of gathering other analysts’ thoughts on the Texans from organizations such ass The Athletic, CBS Sports, and ESPN. Houston is fortunate not only to have one of the more successful programs in the NFL, but also some of the best coverage in the league, highlighted by ESPN’s DJ Bien-Aime, Sports Illustrated’s Conor Orr, and Yahoo! Sports’ Frank Schwab. All three have frequently appeared on the list below, and I’ll be looking forward to seeing their hot takes this season. Orr was one that I took note of being a bit more harsh on the Texans than other pundits, much to my chagrin. But, following his Sports Illustrated cover story of Will Anderson Jr., it appears Orr has now joined the Texans bandwagon! Hopefully, his seal approval is more of a blessing than a curse this season. Last year, I teed off the 2025 power rankings by attempting to set the table on what I thought to be the expectations on the Texans entering the 2025 season: While the Texans still had a very successful 2024 season by most standards, they ultimately still did not break through the glass ceiling of the divisional round, where every Texans team of the past has met their high watermark. Now, with the element of surprise in the rearview mirror, the Texans need to prove that they have learned from last year’s faults. They have to prove it to the fans and critics alike that they truly have Super Bowl talent. They have to prove to everyone that, finally, this year will be different – NFL Power Rankings Week 1: Where are the Texans? (2025) …well, last year ended up not being very different! A third divisional round loss in a row for this new era of Texans football has fans feeling some Deja vu, if not a sense of impending doom for the end of this season. Led by coach DeMeco Ryans and quarterback CJ Stroud, these Texans have enjoyed remarkable success since the 2023 season, carrying Houston to arguably its most dominant stretch in the franchise’s 25-year history. As for the 2025 season specifically, it may have gone down in flames, but if you put weight in analyst Aaron Schatz’s famous DVOA (Defense-Adjusted Value Over Average) metric, then you’d be pleased to hear that the 2025 Texans were the highest rated team in franchise history (Bryan Knowles, Aaron Schatz’s FTN Football Almanac 2026, p. 97). So, maybe the Texans did improve their playoff record in 2025, but they at least are making progress somewhere. That is a HELL of a throw from C.J. Stroud to Nico Collins. pic.twitter.com/azBOAHZCn6 — Jacob Barzilla (@JacobBarzilla) September 13, 2026 That leads us to this season, the big one. The one Texans fans the world over have been waiting for. 2025 was just an appetizer in comparison to the hype that this year’s Texans team has built. Not only did Houston firmly establish itself as a Super Bowl contender with their weekly destruction of opposing offenses all of last year, they also spent all of this offseason proving to the public that they are “all-in” on winning the championship this season. Texans general manager Nick Caserio spent heavily to keep their young core on defense happy, signed multiple starting-caliber offensive linemen in free agency, and then used two top-40 picks in the 2026 NFL Draft to further secure Houston’s biggest weak spots: defensive tackle (McDonald, 36th Overall) and interior o-line (Rutledge, 26th Overall.) This time last year, Houston was still proving itself to suspicious national analysts, but now, many of those same analysts are picking the Texans to be a Super Bowl team in 2026. The expectations quite literally couldn’t be higher, and, if they go another year fizzling out in the second round of the postseason, there could be mutiny. The same result three years in a row has created tension in the fanbase, and the controversy surrounding QB CJ Stroud only magnifies the tension. His and the Texans’ decision to “table” extension negotiations until after the season places a massive personal stressor onto Stroud to ball out this year, and will encourage fans to demand perfection from him in every game. The bottom line is: this Texans roster is possibly the best in franchise history, and Stroud has to prove he can pilot the ship before massive changes are made next offseason. The Super Bowl window is wide open, and it waits to shut for no one. Now, without further ado, let’s take a look at the Week 2 NFL Power Rankings following Houston’s 36-31 loss to the Buffalo Bills last Sunday: NFL.COM : 12. Houston had a chance to win the game in the final minute but saw it vanish in an all-too-familiar fashion, with a C.J. Stroud fumble . Overall, the Texans finished with 124 rushing yards on 32 carries, which helped create more passing lanes for quarterback C.J. Stroud en route to 287 passing yards. title: Texans vs. Bills Week 1 analysis: Turnover differential, final plays killed Houston’s chances
summary: The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 1: The Missed Turnovers: Last season, Houston ranked 3rd in forced turnovers. They left the game […]
full_text: (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 1: The Missed Turnovers : Last season, Houston ranked 3rd in forced turnovers. They left the game with zero. Yet, the stat sheet doesn’t always tell the tale. Houston missed at least three INTs and two fumble recoveries. Much has been said about Lassiter’s missed INT in the end zone. Jalen Pitre also had a golden opportunity to shut down a Bills’ drive with a near goal-line pick on a play that followed a Lassiter DPI giving the Bills the ball at the HOU 1. On a second quarter drive, Stingley somehow missed on a “ [KITTEN] it” throw from Josh Allen to Dalton Kincaid. Later that drive, if Blankenship was a quarter of a second earlier in his jump, Houston gets that INT. In the fourth quarter, after Houston had taken a 31-30 lead, on the first play of the drive, Allen fumbled the snap, but he managed to jump on it. Then there was the first play of the next drive after Houston went three-and-out (More later). Turnovers can be a fickle mistress from year to year. To start this season, she betrayed the Texans. The Final Plays : For most of the game, the offense carried Houston. After a first drive fumble, Stroud regained his composure, and the offense line did their part to keep the game moving. Yet, on the second to last drive for the Texans, problems returned. While hindered by a curious (at best) play call for a second down toss sweep to the right, when the team had most of its success running to the offensive left, the line could not offer the push needed to get at least one 1st down. On the final drive, they got Houston to the BUF 9. However, G Ed Ingram got badly beaten, forcing a 9-yard sack. At 20 seconds, Houston was forced to either get to the end zone from the 18 or get out of bounds. The next pass was an incompletion, leaving Houston with maybe two more shots. Unfortunately, the right side of the line failed again, as T Trent Brown got beaten, allowing the strip-sack fumble of Stroud. While one could argue the final two sacks were not on him, Stroud can’t shake the turnover narrative. In the post-game comments, all the right things got said. Yet will the outside noise become reality for the line and Stroud? The Critical Play: 4th Quarter, 3:13, BUF ball, 1st and 10 @ BUF 4; RB James Cook rushes for 12 yards to the BUF 16, Derek Stingley Forced Fumble, recovered by BUF at the BUF 19 This game did not lack for game-altering plays. Yet, this missed fumble recovery looms large. Consider the opening play of that final Bills’ drive. After Kroeger and the coverage units pinned the Bills at the 4, Buffalo went with a run play. Cook busted through the Texans defense to get out past the 16-yard line. Then comes Stingley, who knocks the ball out of Cook’s right arm with a well-timed punch. Should Houston recover there, they would have the ball inside the Bills’ 20. Worst case, the Bills use all of their TOs, Houston kicks the FG to go up 34-30, and the Bills, with only the possible 2-minute warning, have to go to the end zone with no timeouts. Possibly the Bills still get the TD, but the percentages would favor Houston a bit more, and perhaps with the momentum of forcing a turnover and punt in the previous two possessions, that might have been enough. FUN WITH NUMBERS: 8/76: Average number of penalties/average penalty yards for Texans in season-openers under Ryans: The first game of the season tends to be a bit sloppy, and the refs got plenty of arm exercises in this one. 7 flags for a whooping 106 yards for the Texans, 10 penalties for 85 yards against the Bills. For Houston, 61 of those yards came on two back-breaking flags (46-yard DPI on Lassiter setting up a Bills TD and a 15-yard Roughing the Passer on Mario Edwards keeping another Bills drive alive). In the three season-opening losses, the Texans average 9 flags for 91 yards. At this point, it is a feature of the Ryans regime that flags will be an issue to start off the season. GAME BALLS: RB David Montgomery : 20 carries for 60 yards and 3 receptions for 19 yards might not seem like much, but throw in 2 rushing TDs, along with a receiving TD, and he showed that Houston might have the back they need. It also allowed Woody Marks to be that change-up back, a role that will suit him better (9 rushes for 42 yards). It wasn’t enough in this game, but especially later in the season, getting nearly 30 total rushes at nearly 4 yards a clip with the RBs will be a good thing. P Kai Kroeger and the Houston Punt Coverage Units: Kroeger had 4 punts, averaging 52.0 yards/kick and landing two inside the 5. The coverage units limited the Bills to two returns for 10 total yards. Those two punts had the perfect height/spin to allow the coverage units to get down the field and pin the Bills deep in their territory. In theory, a great set up for that Texans’ defense. In reality…not so much. TE Dalton Kincaid: Yes, an opposing player is on the list. Then again, he fried any Texans’ defender he came against, from All-Pro Stingley to Blakenship. Coming back after being injured the past two seasons, against what may still be among the best secondaries in the league, and leaving with 5 receptions for 130 yards, including two 35+ yard receptions…yeah, give him credit for that one. SHOULD BE FORCED TO WRITE A DOCTORAL DISSERATION ON HOUSTON’S COVERAGE SCHEMES WHILE LISTENING TO MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY, TED CRUZ AND CAL MCNAIR ATTEMPT TO SING OPERA-STYLE “THE EYES OF TEXAS” S Reed Blankenship: That gamble on the INT backfired spectacularly, as DJ Moore got one of the easiest TD’s he’ll ever have. He didn’t exactly the best day in coverage against the Bills receivers, including getting torched by TE Dalton Kincaid on the final drive. His stats (7 total tackles (4 solo)) are the definition of empty. Arguably, the entire secondary could reside here, but Blankenship leads the pack. DC Matt Burke: The Most Interesting Defensive Coordinator in the World…did not have a good game at all. Sure, Josh Allen can make many a good defense look mortal, but Burke did not seem to have the right answers for slowing down the Bills’ offense. Perhaps most damning, he did not think to have a spy on Allen on a play that resulted in a 21-yard TD run when no defender touched the QB known for rushing. The second half went a bit better, but even those adjustments weren’t enough. Burke usually calls great defense since he took over the defensive play-calling. Not this day. NFL/TV Network Executives: The game of the weekend, and it was relegated to Sunday early afternoon? Sure, there are lots of factors to consider with primetime and marquee matchup times. It got national attention at its timeslot, but this seemed like a real marquee matchup, and one that did live up to the hype that a national/stand-alone game should promise. The Ohio State 4th Quarter Game Plan: Think Houston had a bad 4th Quarter? They didn’t have the worst one in the state of Texas this past weekend. That distinction must go to the Buckeyes of Ohio State. Up 23-3 in the 4th, they proceeded to get out scored 21-0 to end the game. If you are a Longhorn fan (or really can’t stand Ohio State), congratulations, you may continue your crowing. If not, well, I don’t think the insufferability of the previously mentioned groups will go away anytime soon. For the 3rd time in 4 seasons under DeMeco Ryans, the Texans start 0-1. Every time they started 0-1, they at least started 0-2. They will look to avoid that fate when they host the Cincinnati Bengals back at Reliant Stadium for 12:00 CDT kickoff.
