title: Week 1 Observations: A Thrilling Win (with Red Flags)
summary: For the second straight season, the Minnesota Vikings realized there are no longer four preseason games and woke up in the 4th quarter to deliver a satisfying (if frustrating) Week 1 victory. It was also historic: the Vikings were the first team in NFL history to be down by 12+ points with under 20 minutes […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - SEPTEMBER 13: Minnesota Vikings linebacker Dallas Turner (15) celebrates his strip sack of Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) during the fourth quarter of a NFL game between the Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers on September 13, 2026, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis MN. (Photo by Nick Wosika/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For the second straight season, the Minnesota Vikings realized there are no longer four preseason games and woke up in the 4th quarter to deliver a satisfying (if frustrating) Week 1 victory. It was also historic : the Vikings were the first team in NFL history to be down by 12+ points with under 20 minutes left in regulation and still win by 17+ points. Let’s hope what follows is a much more successful run through December. THE GOOD The team’s resolve. After witnessing their starting quarterback go down with a scary head injury minutes into the game, and then being bombarded with blitzes on offense and big plays on defense throughout the first half, it could have been easy to mentally check out of this one and regroup for Week 2. They didn’t do that. While the occasional mind-numbingly tedious no-show game still happens in the KOC era (think the Chargers game last year), it seems less frequent than in the Mike Zimmer era. The frustratingly slow starts still happen, but there seems to be more fight, leading to better outcomes. KOC does have the largest comeback in NFL history under his belt, after all. Justin Jefferson, Dallas Turner, Jalen Redmond, and Myles Price. About the only ones who realized the game had started. A special shoutout to Jefferson. I can’t tell you how fortunate we are to have him as our superstar and team leader. He was already comfortably in my Top 10 of favorite Vikings players ever, but after last season’s selfless role as a decoy amid the quarterback chaos, he’s quickly climbing the list. We have to get him a Super Bowl championship. 4th quarter Brian Flores. The most surprising aspect of the Vikings’ underwhelming first three quarters was the defense’s inconsistency (more on that below). That changed in the 4th quarter, when the Vikings’ defense looked like the elite, dominant unit that closed out the 2025 season. In the blink of an eye, the trap door opened beneath Jordan Love’s feet, and he collapsed into an abyss of nightmares that would make Freddy Krueger blush. Carson Wentz, QB2. Wentz won me over last year with his toughness, so I was thrilled to see him return in 2026. He missed a couple of easy throws but was strong overall and exactly what you want from your backup. He went 12 of 19 for 133 yards and three TDs, which was good for a 123.5 quarterback rating (58.8 QBR). THE SO-SO The offensive line. While the statistics looked better afterward than they did in real time, this was anything but a stellar start for the unit. Against a pass rush missing Parsons — and that will never be confused with the mid-80s Chicago Bears —the Packers generated a 40% pressure rate, along with six QB hits and three sacks. While Darrisaw and Jackson held up well in pass protection, the right side of the line did less well, with Brandel, Fries, and O’Neill giving up six combined pressures, per Pro Football Focus. This will need to improve to handle some of the NFL’s more elite pass-rushing units. 1st through 3rd quarter Brian Flores. It was curious why Flores didn’t plan better for the returning Tucker Kraft and Jonnu Smith. Both averaged over 20 yards per reception. It also seemed there was a late recognition of coverage issues before Christian Watson’s 81-yard touchdown reception. I’d chalk that up to some Week 1 hiccups that are easy to fix. But even without that play, Jordan Love still would have exceeded 300 passing yards. Ditto the adjustments to generate pressure that would get home earlier. Despite blitzing on a ridiculous 78% of pass attempts, per Next Gen Stats, the Vikings’ first sack didn’t come until the final play of the 3rd quarter. Flores not systematically breaking down protection schemes more quickly was weird to see. Again, long-term, these are about 1 out of 10 in terms of concern. Love was still only 9-of-19 in the first half (but those 9 completions went for 199 yards). It’ll be addressed. But it did happen, so we need to note it. THE BAD Opening day KOC. For the third time in his five seasons, the Vikings came out flat as a pancake in Week 1. Jonathan Gannon held the Vikings to just 239 total yards despite game-planning all week for Kyler Murray. If a knucklehead like me noted that Gannon might try to channel his inner Buddy Ryan in Micah Parsons’ absence, I’m fairly certain KOC should have expected that, too. THE TBD Kyler Murray, QB1. In his brief appearance before the injury, Murray didn’t calm the nerves. The opening interception was very bad. The protection did him no favors, but the limited sample size we’ve seen hasn’t lent itself to overwhelming confidence about how the rest of the season will go. We shall see. Again, I think Murray will have a strong season, but right now I’m basing it on vibes. Hopefully we get more clarity in Week 3. Get well, Kyler. CONCLUSION A win is a win, and that’s all that matters. But taking off the purple-colored glasses for a moment, several red flags must be acknowledged. The Vikings’ comeback was aided by both Matt LaFleur’s bad decisions and several Packers penalties in critical, high-leverage situations, giving Wentz and the offense multiple second chances. A couple of them were questionable. The Packers also benefited from a non-call on a hit to Wentz’s head and a helmet tackle on Jefferson. I believe this social media post was on point: The fans of the team responsible for the creation of the Aaron Rodgers Rule (courtesy of a completely legal hit by Anthony Barr) is once again mad about the enforcement of the Aaron Rodgers Rule. https://t.co/P8SqjEzkwJ — The Daily Norseman (@DailyNorseman) September 14, 2026 For three quarters, the Vikings were outplayed at home by a team missing its best players on offense and defense. A performance like this at Lambeau in Week 10 would mean we aren’t leaving with another victory. The quarterback question is still up in the air. Is Murray the answer? What if he isn’t? If so, what’s Wentz’s ceiling? Maybe we haven’t seen the last of J.J. McCarthy starting for the Minnesota Vikings. We waited all summer for Week 1 to deliver some clarity, and we got nothing. The highs of this victory mirror those of Week 1 last year. We promptly went out at home on Sunday Night Football and laid an egg in Week 2 against a thoroughly mediocre Atlanta Falcons team. This time, we face the defending NFC North champion Chicago Bears on the road. Oh, and they just dropped 59 points on the Carolina Panthers. This will not be easy.

title: Vikings Crush Packers: Flores’ Blitz, Wentz’s Relief, and the Murray Question
summary: The Minnesota Vikings demolished the Green Bay Packers in Week 1 — but lost Kyler Murray to a concussion on the 11th play. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano break down the film, the blitz, and what’s next. Tyler Forness opened with a bold comparison: “If you remember Enron in 2001, Vikings just did the reverse, […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Carson Wentz #11 of the Minnesota Vikings looks to pass against the Green Bay Packers in the second quarter of a game at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings demolished the Green Bay Packers in Week 1 — but lost Kyler Murray to a concussion on the 11th play. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano break down the film, the blitz, and what’s next. Tyler Forness opened with a bold comparison: “If you remember Enron in 2001, Vikings just did the reverse, where they started out in the dumps and they were riding high on the stock market.” After Murray’s concussion — he was fencing on the field, a telltale sign — Carson Wentz entered and steadied the offense. “Wentz wasn’t the reason for the turnaround,” Forness clarified. “But he was the reason why the ship didn’t sink.” The defense, meanwhile, was suffocating. Brian Flores blitzed Jordan Love relentlessly — and it worked. “Every single one of Jordan Love’s passing yards came against the blitz,” Forness noted. “He was 0 for 5 with a clean pocket.” Dave Stefano compared Flores’ approach to boxing: “B-Flo is almost being a prize fighter… body blows will wear you down quicker… and then comes the knockout punch.” Key Points: Kyler Murray’s concussion : Murray showed fencing signs and entered the protocol. He was symptom-free and in meetings Monday, but Forness cautioned: “Concussions are weird, and they hit everybody differently.” Carson Wentz is the likely starter Sunday at Chicago. Carson Wentz’s relief effort : Wentz delivered what Forness called “one of the best throws I’ll probably see all year” — a two-point missile to Justin Jefferson. His arm talent kept the Vikings afloat when everything could have capsized. Dallas Turner’s breakout : Seven of 10 pressures were quick (under 2.5 seconds), with a 27.2% pressure rate per PFF. “Lo and behold, it only took him one game,” Forness said, answering critics who said Turner only produced cleanup pressures. Flores’ blitz-heavy dominance : Flores sent five-plus rushers almost exclusively. Jordan Love had no answers — 0 for 5 when not blitzed — and the pressure compounded as the game wore on. Defensive line depth paying off : Jalen Redmond, Levi Drake Rodriguez, and Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins — Kwesi Adofo-Mensah’s 2024 cutdown-day bet — delivered key plays at roughly $2.4 million combined. “Kwesi deserves his flowers for that move,” Forness said. Big Citrus stops Love : Caleb Banks (Big Citrus) stuffed Jordan Love on a pivotal 4th down — with no tush push. “You run at the rookie,” Banks said. Forness added: “The dumb part was not having anybody to help push him.” Will Fries struggles : The guard whiffed on multiple blocks, including the blown assignment that triggered Murray’s interception. “He’s got a lot to prove,” Forness warned, noting a near-$20 million cap hit. Theo Jackson’s bad angles : Jackson took poor pursuit angles repeatedly. “Theo Jackson shouldn’t be playing. He shouldn’t be on the field.” J.J. McCarthy’s status : No beat reporter asked about McCarthy at the presser, which Forness said “tells us everything we need to know about where J.J. McCarthy is currently in this organization.” Looking ahead : The Vikings travel to Soldier Field to face Caleb Williams and the Bears. Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: The Real Forno Show is your go-to Minnesota Vikings podcast for film breakdown, honest analysis, and unfiltered takes. Tyler Forness watches the tape so you don’t have to, and Dave Stefano brings the fan’s perspective. From Vikings 1st & SKOL on the Bleav Network — subscribe, ring the bell, and never miss an episode. Fan with Us!!! Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . What do you think? Will Flores’ blitz-heavy approach hold up against Caleb Williams at Soldier Field, or will the Bears’ offense expose the cracks? Drop your thoughts below — and tune in Thursday for the full preview.

title: Patriots vs. Steelers preview for NFL Week 2
summary: With a disappointing 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in the NFL opener last Wednesday, the New England Patriots got their 2026 season off on the wrong foot. The goal now is to avoid an 0-2 start against a Pittsburgh Steelers team that started its own season with a victory. What can be expected from […]
full_text: With a disappointing 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in the NFL opener last Wednesday, the New England Patriots got their 2026 season off on the wrong foot. The goal now is to avoid an 0-2 start against a Pittsburgh Steelers team that started its own season with a victory. What can be expected from the Steelers, though? Let’s take a closer look at them ahead of Sunday’s matchup. Steelers key stats The Steelers opened the 2026 season with a victory but in a competitive AFC North are currently still only ranked third. Obviously, a lot will change over the coming weeks both with this and other rankings. Record: 1-0 (3rd AFC North/8th AFC) Scoring differential: +7 (11th) Turnover differential: +1 (t-8th) Offense: 20.0 points/game (t-22nd), 264.0 yards/game (25th), 1 giveaway (t-8th), -0.251 EPA/play (30th), -0.251 EPA/dropback (27th), -0.252 EPA/run (27th) Defense: 13.0 points/game (t-6th), 238.0 yards/game (3rd), 2 takeaways (t-5th), -0.358 EPA/play (2nd), -0.638 EPA/dropback (1st), -0.113 EPA/run (13th) What the Steelers’ season opener against the Falcons shows us, though, is that the defense was ready to play. The unit dominated an Atlanta team starting its third-string quarterback and scored the decisive points when T.J. Watt returned an interception 35 yards for a fourth-quarter touchdown. Pittsburgh’s own offense, on the other hand, had a rough go itself despite ultimately doing enough to secure a W. Steelers 2026 season Even though it was not a particular display of power, the Steelers opened their first season under head coach Mike McCarthy with a win. However, it remains to be seen just how representative that performance against the Falcons actually was. Week 1: 20-13 win vs. Atlanta Falcons (1-0) The Patriots, despite their own issues in Week 1, project to be a much tougher opponent for Pittsburgh. Steelers active roster Roster up-to-date as of Sept. 16, 8 a.m. ET | *denotes nominal starter Quarterback (4): Aaron Rodgers (8), Mason Rudolph (2), Will Howard (18), Drew Allar (16) Running back (3): Jaylen Warren (30), Rico Dowdle (13), Eli Heidenreich (29 | KR) Fullback (1): Riley Nowakowski (37) Wide receiver (6): DK Metcalf (4), Michael Pittman Jr. (11), Roman Wilson (14), Germie Bernard (17), Ben Skowronek (15), Kaden Wetjen (10 | PR) Tight end (3): Pat Freiermuth (88), Darnell Washington (80), Robert Tonyan (85) Offensive tackle (3): Troy Fautanu (76 | LT), Dylan Cook (60 | RT), Max Iheanachor (71) Interior offensive line (6): Mason McCormick (66 | LG), Zach Frazier (544 | C), Spencer Anderson (74 | RG), Ryan McCollum (62), Brock Hoffman (67), Gennings Dunker (73) Interior defensive line (7): Keeanu Benton* (95), Cameron Heyward* (97), Derrick Harmon (99), Yahya Black (94), Sebastian Joseph-Day (69), Gabriel Rubio (96), Kevin Jobity Jr. (92) Defensive edge (4): T.J. Watt* (90), Alex Highsmith* (56), Nick Herbig* (51), Jack Sawyer (33) Linebacker (4): Patrick Queen* (6), Payton Wilson* (41), Cole Holcomb (55), Carson Bruener (44) Cornerback (5): Joey Porter Jr. (24), Jamel Dean* (35), Asante Samuel Jr.* (22), Daylen Everette (23), Brandin Echols (26) Safety (4): Jalen Ramsey* (5), Jaquan Brisker* (3), Rayshawn Jenkins (20), Robert Spears-Jennings (28) Specialists (3): Chris Boswell (9 | K), Cameron Johnston (19 | P/H), Christian Kuntz (46 | LS) If the game against Atlanta is any indication, the Steelers offense once again revolves around Aaron Rodgers. The future Hall of Famer dropped back to pass 42 times in the season opener and went 40-for-24 with 221 yards, a touchdown and two sacks. He did distribute the ball well, but his 5.5 yards per attempt shows that he found most of his success in the short and intermediate areas; he went 0-for-6 on passes of more than 20 yards. This, in turn, was bad news for No. 1 wide receiver DK Metcalf. Averaging a depth of target of 19.0 yards, he caught only four of nine targets for 40 total yards. The success might have been inconsistent, but the target share itself shows that Metcalf remains Rodgers’ favorite target — a group that also includes Roman Wilson, tight end Pat Freiermuth and running back Jaylen Warren. The three were targets 17 times between them. Overall, Pittsburgh’s passing game had its ups and downs last week —something that was also true for the rushing attack. The Steelers offense was okay but not particularly impressive either, even though it did enough to secure a win against a struggling Falcons team. The Patrick Graham-led defense, on the other hand, performed at a high level. The standout performer was, once again, the aforementioned T.J. Watt. Not only did he register the aforementioned pick-six, he also had a pair of sacks and an additional tackle for loss. Fellow edge A.J. Highsmith notched two sacks as well, while Nick Herbig had a pair of quarterback pressures without taking down Atlanta QB Cooper Rush. The team’s secondary held up well, even without Joey Porter Jr: the fourth-year cornerback sat out the season opener, officially due to a back injury. However, his ongoing contract dispute with the Steelers and the trade rumors surrounding him are impossible to be ignored either. His status will be one of the big stories to watch over the coming days leading up to the game. In Porter’s place, Asante Samuel Jr. got the start at outside cornerback. With Pittsburgh playing predominately zone defense versus Atlanta, he and the rest of the starting secondary — a group typically also including Jamel Dean, Jalen Ramsey and Jaquan Brisker — limited the Falcons to 143 passing yards; Brisker also caught an interception. In the kicking game, the Steelers showed some weakness: Atlanta averaged 11.0 yards on its three punt returns, and 30.8 yards on four kickoff runbacks. Kicker Chris Boswell also went just 2-of-3 on his field goal tries, even though his miss came from 56 yards out. Steelers reserves Practice squad (17): RB Travis Homer (21), RB Lew Nichols III (31), WR Max Hurleman (84), WR Brandon Johnson (89), WR Brandon Smith (89), TE Lake McRee (81), OL Steven Jones (79), OL Doug Nester (72), DT Kyler Baugh (65), DT Esezi Otomewo (93), ED Bradyn Swinson (57), LB Julius Welschof (45 | exempt), LB Jacoby Windmon (53), CB Sebastian Castro (49), CB Doneiko Slaughter (40), CB Car’lin Vigers (42), S Bishop Fitzgerald (38) IR (3): OT Jack Driscoll (68), DT Logan Lee (91), S DeShon Elliott (25) PUP (1): CB Donte Kent (34) The Steelers’ reserve lists features a familiar name: ex-Patriots fifth-round draft pick Bradyn Swinson joined the club’s practice squad after getting cut by the Patriots. Also worth pointing out here is nominal starting safety DeShon Elliott, who is starting the year on injured reserve because of a hamstring issue. Steelers coaching staff Head coach: Mike McCarthy Coordinators: Brian Angelichio (OC), Patrick Graham (DC), Danny Crossman (ST) After 19 seasons with the Steelers, former head coach Mike Tomlin announced his resignation in January. Eleven days later, Mike McCarthy was announced as his successor — reuniting him with his former Packers quarterback Aaron Rodgers. The change up top also led to a major shakeup further down the ranks. Brian Angelichio, Patrick Graham and Danny Crossman were all hired as coordinators, replacing Arthur Smith, Teryl Austin and Danny Smith, respectively. Also part of the group is Robert Kugler, the former Patriots assistant offensive line coach who was hired by McCarthy as Pittsburgh’s new tight ends coach this offseason.

title: Drake Maye ready to bounce back against the Steelers in Week 2
summary: Drake Maye had a forgettable regular season opener, tossing three interceptions in his final three possessions to seal a 13-10 New England Patriots loss to the Seattle Seahawks. However, there is no time to dwell on those mistakes: Week 2 against the Pittsburgh Steelers awaits. And for Maye, it will be an opportunity to bounce […]
full_text: Drake Maye had a forgettable regular season opener, tossing three interceptions in his final three possessions to seal a 13-10 New England Patriots loss to the Seattle Seahawks. However, there is no time to dwell on those mistakes: Week 2 against the Pittsburgh Steelers awaits. And for Maye, it will be an opportunity to bounce back against a team that qualified for the playoffs in 2025. So, how is he planning on doing that? By bringing the proper mindset to the preparation. “We’re on to Pittsburgh. We have another week and another chance in this league. That’s dealing with the ups and downs in this league. That’s part of playing in the National Football League,” Maye said during an appearance on WEEI earlier this week. “It’s just part of being an athlete at a professional level. My brothers and my dad played sports in college and have done things, and you have teammates — that’s what we have teammates for and coaches. They’ve experienced it. And at this capacity it’s just different when you’re playing this position at quarterback. Your mistakes and what you do with the football is at a more drastic level because your decisions change the outcomes of games. Just realizing that and also realizing that you got to go back out there and and have a next-play mentality.” Maye started the Patriots’ season opener fairly well, executing the take-what-the-opponent-gives-you game plan and helping his team head into the fourth quarter up 10-3. However, things fell apart from that point on. By his own admission, the third-year quarterback “lost patience” and ended up costing his game a possible victory and 1-0 start to the season. Against Pittsburgh, a similar outcome would put the reigning AFC champions under quite a bit of pressure already at this early stage in the season. Maye, however, is not letting that outlook impact his work leading up to Week 2. “He’s a guy who has a lot of confidence,” said left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker, who himself had a challenging first game . “We pat him on the back. We got him. We’re always riding for him, but he’s the type of guy who doesn’t really need that. He’s able to fix things on his own and come ready to work the next week.” “He’s been great,” added tight end Hunter Henry. “He sometimes takes too much of the burden. I think we all can be better. We all have to look at ourselves in the mirror. Obviously, we can’t turn the ball over, and he knows that. But, maybe if we finish a little longer, we run better routes, we block a little better, protect a little better, some of those things don’t come into play. We all have to be better. It’s not on just one guy. This is a complete team sport and that’s the beauty of football. Excited to go out there and compete with him again this weekend.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Examining the roster ties between Patriots, Steelers ahead of Week 2
summary: Some former New England Patriots and former Pittsburgh Steelers will meet again at Gillette Stadium. Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, four players in the fold this September have been members of both clubs during their NFL careers. With stays ranging from days to years, here’s a glance through those ties ahead […]
full_text: Sep 21, 2025; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; New England Patriots linebacker Robert Spillane (14) returns an interception during the third quarter at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brian Fluharty-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Some former New England Patriots and former Pittsburgh Steelers will meet again at Gillette Stadium. Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, four players in the fold this September have been members of both clubs during their NFL careers. With stays ranging from days to years, here’s a glance through those ties ahead of Sunday’s 1 p.m. ET home opener. PITTSBURGH Brandon Smith, wide receiver — The Patriots signed Smith to the practice squad last December. The 27-year-old wide receiver’s stay ended with his release ahead of the AFC divisional round in January. A futures contract with the Steelers arrived 48 hours later, and he was retained on Pittsburgh’s practice squad at its formation following the NFL’s 53-man roster deadline in August. Undrafted out of Iowa in 2021, Smith made previous stops with the Dallas Cowboys, DC Defenders, Arizona Cardinals and New York Jets. He has made three appearances as a standard elevation. Bradyn Swinson, outside linebacker — As the NFL’s cutdown deadline closed in, the Patriots waived a member of the 2025 draft class. Swinson subsequently went through the wire unclaimed en route to joining the Steelers’ initial practice squad. Taken in the fifth round at No. 146 overall last year, the 24-year-old former transfer from Oregon to LSU began his rookie campaign on the practice squad. He earned a promotion to the 53-man roster in November and went on to appear in four matchups, including the AFC Championship Game, handling 27 snaps on defense, 31 snaps on special teams and one solo tackle. Christian Kuntz, long snapper — Once a linebacker prospect by way of Duquesne, Kuntz entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2017 and became an August addition in Foxborough. He was waived following that year’s preseason finale as the roster reduced from 90. Kuntz proceeded to log stints with Denver Broncos, Jacksonville Jaguars and Dallas Renegades on the way to converting to long snapper. The 32-year-old has since had a hand in Pittsburgh’s operation for 86 games dating back to his 2021 debut. Kuntz has made 11 tackles on special teams during his AFC North tenure. NEW ENGLAND Robert Spillane, linebacker — Now a back-to-back Patriots captain, Spillane has appeared in 100 games, including 64 starts, since breaking into the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2018. Originally signed by the Tennessee Titans after serving as a rookie minicamp tryout, the Western Michigan product went on to spend four years in Pittsburgh while cutting his teeth on special teams and as a sub-package linebacker. He moved on to the Las Vegas Raiders in 2023 and Foxborough in 2025. Spillane’s run has spanned 602 tackles and 9.5 sacks, plus two forced fumbles, two fumble recoveries, eight interceptions and one touchdown return. A pick and a team-high 15 tackles were in the cards last September when the Steelers visited Gillette Stadium.

full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - JULY 24: Elliott Davison #35 of the New Orleans Saints lines up for a drill during a training camp practice at the Ochsner Sports Performance Center on July 24, 2025 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick E. Hingle/Getty Images) | Getty Images After 24 hours as a free agent, Elliott Davison has circled back to Gillette Stadium. The New England Patriots re-signed the safety to the practice squad on Tuesday. To make room, the organization announced the release of tight end Shane Zylstra from the 17-man group. Davison, 24, initially joined the practice squad as the calendar turned to September. Entering the second week of the regular season, the 6-foot, 200-pound safety landed among a series of transactions . He now returns for a second stint. Undrafted out of UTSA in 2025, Davison spent the entirety of last campaign on the practice squad of the New Orleans Saints and re-upped with a futures contract in January. The Roadrunners product went on to play 141 snaps between defense and special teams during his second NFL preseason, notching one start, before being waived at the league’s 53-man roster deadline in August. Zylstra, 29, brought New England’s practice squad to capacity with his arrival earlier in the month. The 6-foot-3, 245-pound tight end stands as a veteran of 35 games, including six starts, and was released with an injury waiver. He has caught 18 passes for 136 yards and four touchdowns over the course of 582 snaps on offense and 393 snaps on special teams. Entering the NFL as an undrafted free agent out of Minnesota State in 2020, Zylstra spent his rookie training camp with the Minnesota Vikings. The former Division II All-American proceeded to spend five years with the Detroit Lions between the practice squad, active roster and injured reserve. A stop with the Buffalo Bills followed during the 2026 offseason. The practice squad in Foxborough also currently includes running back Lan Larison, wide receivers Kyle Dixon, Cameron Dorner and Chandler Brayboy, offensive linemen Lorenz Metz, Jake Kubas and Jacob Rizy, defensive tackles Jeremiah Pharms Jr. and Eric Gregory, edge rushers Jose Ramirez and Xavier Holmes, linebackers K.J. Britt and Riley Wilson, defensive backs Kindle Vildor and Mike Brown, as well as punter Mitch Wishnowsky. In additional off-day movement, the club had offensive tackle Da’Metrius Weatherspoon and linebacker T.J. Maguranyanga in for workouts, per the transaction wire. The Pittsburgh Steelers visit Gillette Stadium next Sunday. The home opener is set for 1 p.m. ET.

But, hey, at least he wasn’t hit nearly as much in the opener as he was in Super Bowl 60 . 10th – Ralph Vacchiano (FOX Sports): Three interceptions by Drake Maye, an injury that will cost WR A.J. Brown a month, and they couldn’t beat a Seahawks team led by Drew Lock. Unfortunately, their schedule won’t get any easier . 11th – Conor Orr (SI): Drake Maye is primed for a silence-all-doubters game this week after throwing one of the most ill-advised situational balls of the last few regular seasons. Of course, the way opening week played out, New England is tasked with both an emotional exorcism this week against a bad Steelers team and a schematic streamlining. Luckily, it doesn’t look like Pittsburgh is posing much of a threat . 11th – Frank Schwab (Yahoo! Sports): The overreaction directed at Drake Maye proves that the hate of the Patriots hasn’t died just because Bill Belichick and Tom Brady are long gone. Maye didn’t play well in the opener and didn’t have a good postseason either. He played elite defenses in almost every game though. Maye is going to be good. He’s just not able to overcome a middling supporting cast — A.J. Brown was out for the second half and TreVeyon Henderson was inactive in the opener — against great defenses as a third-year player. He’s not nearly as bad as you’ll read on social media . 13th – Mike Florio (ProFootballTalk): Fortunately, blowing it twice in the same game counts as only one loss . 18th – Eric Edholm (NFL): Drake Maye’s three interceptions clearly contributed to New England’s meltdown in Seattle, but the quarterback wasn’t the lone culprit in the 13-10 defeat. title: Contract details for Christian Gonzalez extension with Patriots
summary: Leading up to their season opener in Seattle, the New England Patriots managed to put an end to one of the dominant stories of their summer. The team and Christian Gonzalez reached an agreement on a four-year, $135 million contract extension that makes him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history. “I’m extremely blessed and thankful,” […]
full_text: Leading up to their season opener in Seattle, the New England Patriots managed to put an end to one of the dominant stories of their summer. The team and Christian Gonzalez reached an agreement on a four-year, $135 million contract extension that makes him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history. “I’m extremely blessed and thankful,” Gonzalez said in his first public statements after putting pen to paper. “I love this team. I love Boston. I love the city. This is where I want to be, and I’m happy to be here. I’m glad we got it done.” The story of the pact is more nuanced than the raw numbers would suggest, however. To fully understand it, one also needs to understand its structure as well. CB Christian Gonzalez: Contract details Base value: $135,000,000 Maximum value: TBD Guarantees: $53,928,482 Base salary (2026): $2,259,482 Base salary (2027): $16,119,000 Workout bonus (2027): $300,000 Roster bonus (2026): $550,000 Roster bonus (2027): $1,700,000 Signing bonus: $33,000,000 2026 (age 24): Base salary: $2,259,482 Signing bonus (2023): $1,995,976 Signing bonus (2026): $6,600,000 Roster bonus: $550,000 Salary cap hit: $11,405,458 2027 (age 25): Base salary: $16,119,000 Signing bonus (2026): $6,600,000 Workout bonus: $300,000 Roster bonus: $1,700,000 Salary cap hit: $24,719,000 2028 (age 26): Base salary: $16,000,000 Signing bonus (2026): $6,600,000 Workout bonus: $300,000 Roster bonus: $1,700,000 Salary cap hit: $24,600,000 2029 (age 27): Base salary: $23,000,000 Signing bonus (2026): $6,600,000 Workout bonus: $300,000 Roster bonus: $1,700,000 Salary cap hit: $31,600,000 2030 (age 28): Base salary: $24,650,000 Signing bonus (2026): $6,600,000 Workout bonus: $300,000 Roster bonus: $1,700,000 Salary cap hit: $33,250,000 2031 (age 29): Base salary: $30,350,000 Workout bonus: $300,000 Roster bonus: $1,700,000 Salary cap hit: $32,350,000 While the full volume of Gonzalez’s contract extension does indeed make him the highest-paid cornerback in the league at an average value of $33.75 million, the devil is in the details. And those details show that his full guarantees at signing are only ranked second on that list: his $53.93 million do not come close to Devon Witherspoon’s $59.01 million. That said, Gonzalez does have a chance to add significantly to those guarantees if only he remains on the Patriots’ roster for the next two years. After all, his base salary, workout bonus and roster bonus for the 2028 and 2029 seasons are all automatically moving to “full guarantee” status if he only is with the team on the fifth day of the league year in 2027 and 2028, respectively. If so, he would add an extra $43 million to those $53.93 million above without any extra effort. Add a $5.07 million injury protection for the 2030 season and you get total guarantees of $102 million — besting Witherspoon’s $101 million. Those are not the only differences between Gonzalez’s deal and the previous record holder. As opposed to the Seahawks, the Patriots decided against including both option bonuses and void years in their CB1 deal — standard business for New England dating back to the Bill Belichick days (which is no surprise given that salary cap manager Richard Miller has been with the organization for over three decades now). For the Patriots and Gonzalez, the contract seemingly presents a solid middle ground. The player gets to reset the market according to his qualities, while the club has some built-in safety nets should injury or performance prevent a proper return on the investment. Most importantly, though, both were able to put a satisfying end to a saga that went on since the spring.

full_text: A loss is never great, but around the NFL, teams still had worse performances than what the New Orleans Saints put up against the Detroit Lions. NFL.com – 21 (+1) “I’ll spend the quiet moments of the next few days wondering how Week 1 might have played out had the Saints woken up before the third quarter of Sunday’s loss to the Lions. But the “what if” game is a favorite of fools, and we’re not court jesters. In the end, the Saints were one two-point conversion in overtime away from pulling off an upset that would’ve defined their season and proven to everyone they might be the surprise of the NFL this year.” Bleacher Report – 22 (-2) “The New Orleans Saints showed resilience by coming back from a 21-0 third-quarter deficit against the Detroit Lions. At the same time, Kellen Moore’s squad came up short in overtime and failed to finish. Moore and his staff have done a tremendous job making the Saints a competitive squad. This time a year ago, many viewed New Orleans as having the league’s least talented roster. By the end of the 2025 campaign, the Saints were pushing for a potential postseason appearance. Thus, expectations rose. New Orleans showed it could hang with the Lions despite playing poorly early in the contest. The ability to grind out a tough win when facing adversity is the next step the Saints must take. — Sobleski t ” CBS Sports – 23 (+1) “The Saints have to be thrilled with what they saw from Tyler Shough in the opener against the Lions. He threw for 400 and rallied after throwing picks. That’s a good sign.” PFN – 22 “It was admirable for the New Orleans Saints to march into Detroit and take a team like the Lions into overtime. Though the Saints were able to get a touchdown in overtime to match the one the Lions had previously, a failed two-point conversion to win the game saw the Saints pick up the narrow loss to start the new year.“ Sports Illustrated – 20 “I’ll say this about Tyler Shough, who I questioned a lot this offseason in terms of how much better he could get after a complete offseason: tough as nails down 21 points in the third quarter against a good team. title: Our offense vs. their defense: Baltimore Ravens
summary: After one week of NFL football being back, the New Orleans Saints currently sit with a record of 0-1 following their 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Devaughn Vele #14 of the New Orleans Saints scores a touchdown against the Detroit Lions during the third quarter of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After one week of NFL football being back, the New Orleans Saints currently sit with a record of 0-1 following their 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. Attention will now shift to another road matchup, this time versus the Baltimore Ravens, who are coming off of a 41-23 win over the Indianapolis Colts. The Saints will enter week two as the fourth-ranked offense in the league after gaining 469 total yards. They accumulated 378 passing yards (1st in the league) and 91 rushing yards (22nd in the league) during last Sunday’s slate. QB Tyler Shough leads both New Orleans and the NFL with 410 yards through the air even after throwing two interceptions and being sacked five times. Former Jacksonville Jaguar RB Travis Etienne Jr. led the Saints with 46 rushing yards, averaging just over five per carry. WR Chris Olave is also league-leading after his career-high 182 receiving yards on ten receptions even though he was kept out of the endzone by Detroit. Size in the passing game led to majority of the Saints’ scoring after WR Devaughn Vele and TEs Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant hauled in touchdowns. RB Kendre Miller punched in the other New Orleans TD on the ground. Meanwhile, the Baltimore defense is currently ranked sixth overall in the league after giving up just 251 yards of offense in week one. The Ravens allowed 149 yards through the air (5th in the league) and 102 yards rushing (13th in the league) in their first outing. Ravens LB Roquan Smith had a team-leading 11 tackles versus the Colts and secured an interception. CB Marlon Humphrey came up with the only other turnover for Baltimore after forcing and recovering a fumble. Safety Malaki Starks and LB Tavius Robinson earned sacks last weekend for the Ravens and combined for 17 total yards tackled for a loss. Baltimore’s defense held the Colts to just 16 points through three quarters before giving up a garbage time score. The Raven defense can play hardnosed, competitive football long into the game meaning New Orleans will not be able to rely on too many late heroics and scoring spurts if they want any shot of getting their record up to .500 and avoiding an 0-2 start.

title: A look back at the history between the Saints and Ravens
summary: The New Orleans Saints will hit the road in Week 2 to take on the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium this Sunday. These two teams first met on September 29, 1996, in the Louisiana Superdome, with Baltimore coming away with a 17-10 victory. Since then, they have played one another just eight times, with […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 07: Kyle Hamilton #14 of the Baltimore Ravens makes the tackle against the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome on November 7, 2022 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will hit the road in Week 2 to take on the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium this Sunday. These two teams first met on September 29, 1996, in the Louisiana Superdome, with Baltimore coming away with a 17-10 victory. Since then, they have played one another just eight times, with the Ravens holding a 6-2 advantage in the all-time series. The last time they faced one another, Baltimore defeated New Orleans 27-13 in the Caesars Superdome on November 7, 2022. The Ravens controlled much of the game, with Lamar Jackson and Baltimore’s rushing attack proving difficult for the Saints to contain. New Orleans did not earn its first victory over Baltimore until 2018, when the Saints escaped M&T Bank Stadium with a thrilling 24-23 win that ended when then Ravens kicker Justin Tucker missed an extra point with 24 seconds remaining. The Saints enter Sunday’s matchup looking to bounce back after a heartbreaking 31-30 overtime loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 1. New Orleans fell behind 21-0 before mounting an impressive comeback, eventually forcing overtime and having multiple opportunities to get the upset. Despite three turnovers, quarterback Tyler Shough threw for 410 yards and three touchdowns, while Chris Olave finished with 10 receptions for 182 yards. The performance offered plenty of reasons for optimism despite the loss, especially after the Saints showed the resilience to battle back from a three-touchdown deficit on the road. Baltimore enters the matchup 1-0 after opening its season with a 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. The Ravens piled up 506 yards of total offense, led by Lamar Jackson’s 324 passing yards and Derrick Henry’s 144 rushing yards and three touchdowns. For the Saints, Sunday’s matchup represents another difficult early-season road test and an opportunity to build on the fight they showed in Detroit. Baltimore has historically had the upper hand in this series, but New Orleans will look to change that while earning its first victory of the 2026 season. title: Saints vs. Lions: Game MVP
summary: The Saints went on the road and had to fight to force overtime against the Detroit Lions. As everyone knows, the Saints left Ford Field with a loss after a failed two-point conversion in overtime. The Saints were down 21-0 in the third quarter, and at first, things were not looking good. But even through […]
full_text: The Saints went on the road and had to fight to force overtime against the Detroit Lions. As everyone knows, the Saints left Ford Field with a loss after a failed two-point conversion in overtime. The Saints were down 21-0 in the third quarter, and at first, things were not looking good. But even through all of this mess, one player showed up Sunday for the entire game, and that was Chris Olave. Olave entered the season with a lot of people questioning whether he was worth the extension he received during the offseason. Whether it was because of health concerns or the lack of contested catches on the field, people were trying to find ways to justify their opinions on why the Saints should not have signed him to the deal he received. Well, on Sunday, his play quieted a lot of those doubters. Olave had 13 targets, 10 receptions, and 182 yards. Seven of his 10 receptions resulted in first downs. He averaged 18.2 yards per reception, and his average depth of target was 18.4 yards. Olave finished as the Saints’ highest-graded offensive player on PFF with a grade of 82.6. As of now, Olave is the league leader in receiving yards and receptions. Olave fought through cramping and was able to play over 50 snaps in Sunday’s game. Hopefully, Olave can stay on this path and truly establish himself as one of the best receivers in the league. Who would you say was the MVP of the game, and do you think Olave can stay on an elite pace all season? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Saints’ slow starts could become a problem if they continue
summary: The New Orleans Saints showed exactly why there is plenty to be excited about moving forward after Sunday’s 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. Unfortunately, they also showed a potential issue that could become much harder to overcome if it continues. For the 12th time under Kellen Moore, the Saints failed to score in the […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-SEPTEMBER 13: Head coach Kellen Moore of the New Orleans Saints reacts to a call during the second half of an NFL football game between the New Orleans Saints and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 13, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints showed exactly why there is plenty to be excited about moving forward after Sunday’s 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. Unfortunately, they also showed a potential issue that could become much harder to overcome if it continues. For the 12th time under Kellen Moore, the Saints failed to score in the opening quarter, and this time, the slow start helped put them in a massive hole. Erasing a 21-point deficit is definitely encouraging and shows the kind of resilience that you’d like to see from a young Saints team. But the fact that New Orleans needed to play from behind in the first place is something worth watching as the season progresses. The Saints cannot expect to repeatedly dig themselves out of holes and remain competitive throughout the season. Once New Orleans settled in, the production was there. And the starters not playing in the preseason has a lot to do with why it took so long to find a rhythm. But if this becomes a recurring trend, it could change the entire trajectory of the season. Sunday’s loss should not erase the optimism surrounding this team. If anything, the comeback showed how much fight this team has. But if New Orleans wants to take the next step this season, getting out of the gates faster has to become a priority. With the Baltimore Ravens up next, the Saints may not have the luxury of falling behind early and still having enough time to mount another comeback. Do you think it’s an overreaction to believe the Saints’ slow starts will become a problem, or was Sunday simply a case of early-season rust?

title: Week 1 Film Review: Highlights from the All 22
summary: After experiencing the Saints vs. Lions, I could not wait until the game film was uploaded to be able to see the ins and outs of the team so that true evaluations on the performance could be made. As I went to bed Sunday night, I had no idea what was in store for me […]
full_text: Saints Spot Concept on 2-Point Play After experiencing the Saints vs. Lions, I could not wait until the game film was uploaded to be able to see the ins and outs of the team so that true evaluations on the performance could be made. As I went to bed Sunday night, I had no idea what was in store for me — 7 hours of nightmare in the form of Mike Pereira slowly moving his hand back and forth while patronizingly explaining the definition of a forward pass. Takeaways from the Film Vernon Broughton has Arrived Though he plays a position that hardly shows up in the stat book and can go overlooked by the naked eye during the live broadcast, Vernon Broughton had a very good showing in his first regular-season action since Week 2 of last year. This was most noticeable when he lined up against Penei Sewell (one of the top linemen in the league), where Broughton was able to win multiple reps against the three-time first-team All-Pro. Although the sample size is small, if the Texas product can continue this trajectory, he will be viewed as a Trey Hendrickson-level steal by the Saints in the third round of last year’s draft. Stutsman vs Werner Both linebackers logged quality plays opposite Kaden Ellis this Sunday as they were faced with a tough challenge vs. the Lions. After watching the film, it was clear that each has their own strengths, but it seems like Stutsman is making the case to compete for the starting role throughout the year. Werner played like a savvy veteran and used his instincts to make multiple plays, including a nice TFL on Jahmyr Gibbs and an exceptional pass breakup down the middle of the field. Stutsman, on the other hand, was out of place on some plays but was able to recover due to his superior athletic ability. This is a great sign for the Saints, as the competition between the two seems to have them both playing good football against a very talented Lions offense. 2-Point Play The refs’ worst mistake in the game was missing the pass interference call in the end zone on Bryce Lance for the game-winning 2-point conversion. When watching the play live, I knew people would wonder how Olave wasn’t targeted, and I’m happy to weigh in. The Saints ran a modified version of the “Spot” concept (shown above), which is a great play call in this area. The read is simple, and after the initial motion by Olave to the interior of the 3-receiver bunch, Tyler Shough knew he was getting man coverage. The throw vs. man on this concept is THE CORNER ROUTE (the flat by Olave is intended to pull the flat defender away from the corner route, which it did). He found it slightly late, as the timing was thrown off by a good jam at the line — credit the Lions’ defense here. What was absurd to me is that the Lions defender had at least one hand covering Lance’s face while making contact with his body the entire time the ball was in the air. Am I blaming the refs for a loss? No. I am wondering how NFL officiating can have a review overturn an obvious fumble (which changed the outcome) while the refs are clearly afraid to “decide the game” by changing the outcome with a flag. End of the Day While the Saints had a sluggish start to the game, especially Tyler Shough, it was undeniable that they displayed a level of fight and belief in their quarterback that hasn’t graced the Black and Gold sideline since Drew Brees was captaining the offense. The film review gave me belief that this is a very talented roster with a smart coaching staff that will have plenty of success throughout the year.

title: Chris Olave looks ready to take another step after monster season opener
summary: New Orleans Saints wide receiver Chris Olave entered the 2026 season with plenty of expectations after earning second-team All-Pro honors last season. After Sunday’s season opener against the Detroit Lions, it is difficult to imagine the Saints asking for much more from their star wideout. Olave was one of the biggest reasons New Orleans was […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints drops a pass during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images New Orleans Saints wide receiver Chris Olave entered the 2026 season with plenty of expectations after earning second-team All-Pro honors last season. After Sunday’s season opener against the Detroit Lions, it is difficult to imagine the Saints asking for much more from their star wideout. Olave was one of the biggest reasons New Orleans was able to erase the 21-point deficit and nearly complete the incredible comeback, finishing with a career-high 182 receiving yards on 10 receptions. He was targeted 13 times and consistently gave Tyler Shough a reliable option as the Saints’ offense finally found its rhythm down the stretch. For a Saints offense that struggled to get anything going early, Olave eventually became the spark it desperately needed. The chemistry between him and Shough was especially encouraging, but it wasn’t surprising given what we’ve seen from the two this offseason. Shough finished with a career-high 410 passing yards, and a large part of that production came from his willingness to continue looking Olave’s way when the Saints needed a big play. The two connected for several significant gains throughout the afternoon, including a 47-yard completion that helped New Orleans continue its comeback attempt. Olave’s performance was also impressive considering the circumstances. The Saints were shut out in the first half and eventually fell behind 21-0 before their offense finally came alive. Rather than disappearing when the game became difficult, Olave became increasingly important as New Orleans mounted its comeback. The next step will be seeing whether Olave can stay healthy enough to turn this into a consistent season-long trend. If Sunday was any indication, Olave could be in for a massive season. Now, he will look to carry his momentum into Week 2’s matchup with the Baltimore Ravens.

title: NY Giants’ FB Patrick Ricard is the offense’s ‘secret sauce’
summary: The New York Giants talked … and talked … and talked as the season approached about being a physical football team. Even as the Giants were building the foundation of their offense, “we know it will be physical” was the answer you would get when asking what it might look like. We saw the physicality […]
full_text: Patrick Ricard | Getty Images The New York Giants talked … and talked … and talked as the season approached about being a physical football team. Even as the Giants were building the foundation of their offense, “we know it will be physical” was the answer you would get when asking what it might look like. We saw the physicality the Giants want to bring to the table during Sunday’s 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys, with Dallas COO Stephen Jones even admitting “ they outphysicaled us .” The poster child for that physicality, and for the kind of football team head coach John Harbaugh wants the Giants to be, is 300-pound fullback Patrick Ricard . After nine seasons as a member of the Baltimore Ravens with Harbaugh, Ricard followed the coach to the Giants in free agency. Sunday, Ricard played 37 offensive snaps as the Giants ran 37 times for 165 yards (4.5 yards per attempt) and held the ball for 36:40. If you haven’t done the math, 37 snaps per game for 17 games would come out to 629 snaps. Ricard played a career-high 698 snaps for the Ravens in 2022, the only time he surpassed 600 snaps. He played only 274 snaps last season. “The jobs and the roles that he’s being asked to play are built into our offense,” Harbaugh said. “Not everybody has those, but a lot of people do. “There’s a lot of things that Pat can do that nobody else can do. Nobody in the world can do some of the things that Pat Ricard can do. And that’s good for us. That’s unique for us. So, it helps us be who we are. It builds into our team persona, our team identity. And we love that. We love that about him as a player.” Ricard’s job boils down to hitting guys on the other team. Hard. Clearing holes for running backs or keeping pass rushers off quarterback Jaxson Dart. He is forever trying to remind defenders why he has the nickname “Pancake Pat.” “Nobody in the world can do some of the things that Pat Ricard can do.” — John Harbaugh “Whatever the coaches ask for me to do to help his team win, I’m going to do,” Ricard said. “I mean, look, I was an undrafted defensive lineman. I played D-line, I played offense, I played both sides of the ball. I played special teams. Line me up in the backfield, on the line, in the slot, have me do this, that. Whatever it is, I’m going to try my best.” One thing Ricard’s job rarely includes is touching the ball. In 133 career regular-season games, Ricard has 11 carries and 49 pass receptions. He doesn’t care. He knows what he is good at. “I played defense for most of my life, so for me to play on offense, I (couldn’t) care less if I ever get the ball,” Ricard said. “For me, it’s all about, I want to impose my will on defenses, and I have the most fun when I’m pancaking people and I’m springing big blocks for my guys to have success, getting lots of points, getting a lot of first downs, winning.” “If the ball comes my way, cool. If not, then I’m not going to be getting in (Matt) Nagy’s face like, ‘I need the ball,’ or getting mad at Jaxson for not giving me the ball. It’s fine by me because these guys that are on my team, they’re playmakers, dynamic, and I feel like they would be better with the ball in their hands and me blocking for them. So, that’s what I’m cool with.” ‘Secret sauce’ Ricard played both ways for the Ravens in his first three NFL seasons, totalling 225 snaps as a defensive tackle. He has been a full-time fullback since 2020. “Early on, I didn’t play offense in college, so for me it was like they had to almost limit what I could do my first maybe couple years just because I was still learning the position and learning offense in general,” Ricard said. “But I feel like now it’s like I’ve been in – I’ve had (senior offensive assistant) Greg Roman as my run game coordinator, offense coordinator, and now being back in his scheme, it’s like there’s so much to build off of to where they can plug and piece me in any spots.” Ricard really has one job. Block people, and do it with authority. At this point in his career, he can do it from just about every spot or angle imaginable. Sunday, he was in a true fullback alignment 15 times, was an inline tight end seven times, in the slot 11 times and aligned as a wide receiver four times. “Motion me, shift me, to where – I’ve done it all to the point where I can execute it at a really high level to where I feel like that’s like what G-Ro (Greg Roman) said about me is like I’m like the spaghetti sauce on the offense,” Ricard said. “I’m like the secret sauce to where you put me in different spots to get the advantage, and I’m usually a mismatch of who I’m blocking because I’m usually bigger than them, to where I think it’s really an advantage for the offense. “And it’s a lot of fun. It’s a lot of fun to be in this offense, to be moved around a lot in motion and shift and be in different spots. It’s almost like Where’s Waldo on Sundays, and it can be a lot for a defense to defend.” The Giants’ way The smashmouth style that Harbaugh has brought back to the Giants is reminiscent of the Giants’ championship teams of the Super Bowl era. Those teams generally dominated the line of scrimmage. They were gritty, not pretty. They had physical defenses. They had physical run games. And, by the way, they featured fullbacks. The Bill Parcells teams had Maurice Carthon. The Tom Coughlin teams had Madison Hedgecock and Henry Hynoski. When I posted the ‘ Kudos and Wet Willies ’ after Sunday’s victory over the Dallas Cowboys, I did not included Ricard in the ‘Kudos’. BBV commenters let me know about the oversight. Ricard has been feeling the love from Giants fans. “I definitely felt it when I signed here and I’ve been around,” Ricard said. “But after this game, my social media has been flooding with just so much support from Giants fans just telling me how much they love how I play, MVP of the game, all this stuff. And I think it’s more of just how excited they are to have a fullback and the way I play. “I’m all for it, I love it. I’m (going to) continue to play hard and do whatever I can to help the Giants keep getting wins.” Pat Ricard has been impressed with the dedication of his Giants teammates and the organization as a whole: "NYC is right across the river, and guys would rather be in the locker room hanging out two hours after the game" pic.twitter.com/1HZtYXo5i7 — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 15, 2026 ‘Hungry and humble’ New head coaches always bring a handful of their favorite players from prior coaching stops to help ease the transition and build a culture. Ricard is, of course, one of several ex-Ravens now wearing a Giants uniform. Ricard has been impressed by his new teammates from the start. “I just see how hungry and how humble everybody is here,” Ricard said. “They just – they want – there’s so many guys here that want to prove themselves. They want to win, and you just see it with how they work, how they prepare, and how much they love each other. “I remember when I first got here for OTAs, just seeing how much the guys are cheering each other on in our running workouts and being there for one another and hanging out in the locker room two hours after we were done for the day. And I’m thinking, I’m like, ‘Wow, New York City is right across the river, right there, and guys would rather be in the locker room hanging out two hours after.’ So, I feel like that was just things I noticed right away, and I think it’s so important for a team to want to win and want to be crazed, loving one another and working hard.” Hungry and humble is actually a great way to describe Ricard. Hungry to deliver pain to opposing defenses and win football games, and humble about how good he has been at his job for a decade now.

Harbaugh is rebuilding a broken culture. Coaching turnover and eight losing seasons over the last decade turned a proud franchise into a perennial bottom-dweller in the NFC East. And it might just lead the Giants back to the promised land. 2026 NFL season, Week 1: What We Learned from Sunday’s games | NFL.com What a way to kick off the Harbaugh era. Jaxson Dart was back, so too were Malik Nabers and Cam Skattebo, each of them making contributions to knock off the rival Cowboys in head coach John Harbaugh’s Gotham debut. Facing a franchise that popularized the triplets term, the Giants’ young franchise trio of Dart, Nabers and Skattebo proved to be the offensive catalyst. This was the start Harbaugh and the franchise needed and wanted. Their young guns were firing against a hated adversary. This wasn’t a pretty game. Too many penalties, too many fumbles, some drops. But for Harbaugh and New York, it was a beautiful result for the franchise’s new dawn. Why Malik Nabers’ mom wasn’t at Giants game for WR’s return: ‘He had to do this by himself’ | The Athletic “This game, Malik had to do this by himself,” Tonya told The Athletic on Monday. “He needed to go out there with no pressure from anybody and just perform… It worked out perfectly because if I had been there, I wouldn’t have been able to hide my emotion or my fear. He would have been able to sense that I was nervous or my anxiety was high, and I think I would have made him uneasy. So God’s timing is the best timing. And so this journey he needed to take by himself.” “We knew that it was his moment,” Tonya said. “For him to go out there, for him to decide that, ‘I’m ready,’ it took for him to trust this entire process. Trust the surgeon. Trust the surgery. Trust his workout and his recovery. He had to trust this entire journey for him to step out on that field and know that he was ready to play.” Presence and perspective for Malik Nabers in rousing NY Giants return | The Record Jaxson Dart took the last of three kneel-downs in victory formation, officially closing out Sunday night’s 28-20 triumph over the Dallas Cowboys, and he immediately knew where he was going with the football. Should Giants trade for Joey Porter Jr. with newfound cap space? | New York Post The ink barely dried on safety Jevon Holland’s restructured contract Monday before fan-driven speculation began that the Giants could use their additional $5.8 million in salary-cap savings to trade for Joey Porter Jr. The irony is that the Giants once were “splitting hairs” while trying to place cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Porter on the draft board as late first-round picks in 2023, league sources told The Post. title: Survey: What surprised you in the Giants’ win over Dallas?
summary: Most New York Giants fans picked their team to win against the Dallas Cowboys, but few outside of the Giants’ fandom actually expected the G-Men to come away with the victory. In fact, I suspect that most Giants’ fans hoped for a win, but were prepared for a hard-fought loss. Few were really expecting the […]
full_text: New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart runs with the ball against the Dallas Cowboys. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Most New York Giants fans picked their team to win against the Dallas Cowboys, but few outside of the Giants’ fandom actually expected the G-Men to come away with the victory. In fact, I suspect that most Giants’ fans hoped for a win, but were prepared for a hard-fought loss. Few were really expecting the Giants to come out and simply out-play the Cowboys from whistle to whistle. And so that brings us to this week’s question: What surprised you the most in the Giants’ win over the Cowboys? A) Jaxson Dart’s precision as a passer? He was downright surgical in picking apart Christian Parker’s defense, playing on time and in rhythm. Dart was fun as a rookie, but he needed to do a lot of work on playing within the structure of the offense. Against Dallas, Dart had great footwork, was seeing the defense well, marrying his eyes and feet to the tempo of the route concepts, and delivering the ball with great placement. His improved footwork also elevated his arm as he was routinely driving the ball outside the numbers as well as layering it with great touch. B) How well the Nagy-Callahan-Roman offense worked? John Harbaugh’s decision to hire these three men was looked at with derision and confusion from the media at large as well as the Giants’ own fanbase. We had no clue what the offense would look like, or how well it could function. We didn’t know if the three would reinforce each other’s weaknesses or if it would blow up in the Giants’ faces. As it turns out, the play-calling was generally excellent and the Giants used a variety of looks, alignments, and play designs that let them do what they wanted against the Cowboys. C) The run defense holding Dallas to 69 yards rushing. Most fans — and much of the media — were somewhere between “anxious” and “panicking” over the state of the Giants’ run defense after the preseason. It was widely predicted that the Giants would get runover by Dallas’ offense and that they’d be gashed on the ground. Instead, the Giants’ new-look defense held up against the Cowboys’ rushing attack and limited them to just 69 yards on the ground and held Javonte Williams to 3.4 yards per carry. D) Holding CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens to 72 total yards. Like the run defense, many fans and writers were worried (to say the least) about the Giants’ secondary. This was about as tough a test as you could imagine (short of Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins) to start the season for two new starting corners in a new defensive scheme. There were predictions that both would eclipse 100 yards receiving, but instead they fell short combined. The Giants weren’t able to take them out of the game completely, but they contained Lamb and Perkins and prevented Dak Prescott from generating the explosive plays upon which the Dallas offense thrives. Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Giants fans and fans across the country. What was the best surprise from Week 1? Are you feeling confident in the Giants? Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys:

title: Former NY Giants WR Sterling Shepard signs with Jets’ practice squad
summary: Former New York Giants wide receiver Sterling Shepard is returning to The Big Apple and is signing with the New York Jets practice squad, per a report from Mike Garafolo. Shepard joins the Jets as reinforcements with rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. considered “week to week” after suffering an ankle injury. The Giants drafted […]
full_text: Former New York Giants wide receiver Sterling Shepard | Getty Images Former New York Giants wide receiver Sterling Shepard is returning to The Big Apple and is signing with the New York Jets practice squad, per a report from Mike Garafolo . Shepard joins the Jets as reinforcements with rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. considered “week to week” after suffering an ankle injury. The Giants drafted Shepard out of Oklahoma in the second round of the 2016 NFL Draft with the 40th overall pick. He was immediately productive upon being drafted, catching 65 passes for 683 yards and 8 touchdowns as a rookie. He formed a dynamic duo with Odell Beckham Jr. and provided both toughness and reliability for over the middle for Eli Manning in the twilight of his career. Shepard’s best season as a Giant came in Eli’s last full season as a starter, when he started all 16 games, racking up a career-high 872 yards on 66 catches. Unfortunately, Shepard struggled with injury after that year. Over the next several years he would suffer multiple concussions, several hamstring injuries, a ruptured Achilles, and a torn ACL. Shepard joined the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2024 and played in 24 games for the Buccaneers between 2024 and 2025. He was briefly with the Houston Texans this summer, but was released in their final cuts.

title: Rams’ QB Matthew Stafford: NY Giants are a ‘dangerous’ team
summary: The New York Giants got the NFL’s attention with their well-deserved 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday. Matthew Stafford, quarterback of the Los Angeles Rams — who face the Giants on Monday Night Football in Week 2 — was among those who noticed what the Giants did to the Cowboys. On “Let’s Go”, […]
full_text: Matthew Stafford | Getty Images The New York Giants got the NFL’s attention with their well-deserved 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday. Matthew Stafford, quarterback of the Los Angeles Rams — who face the Giants on Monday Night Football in Week 2 — was among those who noticed what the Giants did to the Cowboys. On “Let’s Go”, a SiriusXM NFL Radio show he co-hosts with Jim Gray, Stafford called the Giants a “dangerous” team. “I watched the game,” Stafford said of Giants-Cowboys. “My brother-in-law [Chad Hall] is the receiver coach for the Giants, so I’m always pulling for him and pulling for those guys, except for this week when we play them coming up. But I saw a young team with a bunch of talent. “When you look at the defensive side of the ball, a bunch of pass rushers, I thought they did a really nice job in the pass game against the Dallas Cowboys who have as much talent as anybody in the pass game. I think Dak’s played at a high level for a long time now and with CeeDee [Lamb] and Pick [George Pickens] and all those guys, they’re really talented on the outside. So for them to get that win, 28-20, was a big start for their season.” Stafford noted the timing of the game. “Obviously, the young quarterback, Jaxson Dart, I thought played really well, played within himself, made some plays with his feet,” Stafford said. “They’re a dangerous team. I think every team in the NFL, it’s what people out there forget, year in and year out going through training camps and watching preseason, think they can pick who’s gonna win every game. And that’s why we play them. You put the ball down, you go play the games. And I thought the Giants did a heck of a job the other night. I thought it was cool on the weekend of September 11th, 25 years later, for the Giants in New York City to get a win, felt right and felt great to have the NFL have something like that happen and those guys play well.” The Rams, of course, are 0-1 after losing to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia. “It was tough. Obviously had a long journey and didn’t play the way that we wanted to play,” Stafford said. “There were some swing plays in that game where obviously the score was what it was at the end of the game and we thought we had some chances to make it a little bit closer. But didn’t happen. Always difficult to start the season that way, but learned from it, got an extra couple days of rest on the way back and coming into a Monday Night game. So [we’ll] figure out what we can do better, how we can go out there and execute at a higher clip and give ourselves a better chance to win a game.” The Rams are currently 7.5-point favorites, per FanDuel Sportsbook .
