full_text: The Daily Slop – 15 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Jayden Daniels vs Eagles Yes, Daniels had some struggles and looked off at times, but when the game came down to the wire, the 2024 Jayden Daniels kicked in and showed he’s still there, which is promising for the season ahead. Evaluating the performance is tricky because there were some bad plays, some unfortunate plays and a fair few really nice throws mixed in there as well. So let’s dive into it and see what we can take away. The first thing that stood out with Daniels, especially early on in the game, was that he just seemed a little off. Given that he’s not played a competitive game since late last season, that’s somewhat understandable, but he was slightly off with some throws which caused some incomplete passes. That isn’t the only reason the Commanders offense struggled though. While Daniels was a little off, he was also a little unlucky at times. It’s also fair to say that the Eagles defense is one of the best in the NFL, especially in coverage. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio has been one of the best defensive minds in football for over 20 years and his defensive structures have spread around the NFL for their ability to limit explosive plays and force opposing offenses to put together long and tough to sustain drives. The Commanders did dial up a few shots to try and attack down the field, but the Eagles had them covered pretty well. [H]e also mixed in some really nice throws, especially over the middle of the field. This turned into a bit of a trend for Daniels in this game. Much of his success came from him throwing over the middle on these types of concepts. Jayden Daniels had some rust to knock off early, but as soon as the 4th quarter hit, we saw the return of 2024 Daniels. Plenty of corrections to make, but plenty of promise to take out of this one too. Full breakdown: https://t.co/eAqHv4RAWY pic.twitter.com/HRXgXUtFhp — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) September 14, 2026 Commanders Roundtable Commanders uncertain about the status of at least 4 players ahead of Dallas game Head coach Dan Quinn noted that he will get a better picture on the game status on all the four injured players — linebackers Frankie Luvu and Jordan Magee, tight end Chig Okonkwo and safety Tyler Owens — on Wednesday as the team prepares for week two in the meantime. Linebacker Frankie Luvu was the first player to go down after he suffered a groin injury and was ruled questionable at halftime. In his first game as a Commander, tight end Chig Okonkwo was ruled as questionable in the final minute of the third quarter due to a hamstring injury. Linebacker Jordan Magee, who battled a chest injury during training camp, suffered a hamstring injury and was ruled questionable to return prior to the game’s final two warning. Safety Tyler Owens was ruled questionable to return due to an ankle injury that suffered in punt return coverage in the second-to-last play of the third quarter. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Commanders vs Eagles: 4 stats that tell the tale of the loss 26.8: the Eagles converted six of their 14 third down attempts, which may not be entirely concerning at face value, but how some of the conversions materialized is what hurts most. 26.8 represents the average yards gained across the Eagles’ six conversions, which hurts after the Commanders’ defense largely lived up to expectations in the first game under coordinator Daronte Jones. The first back breaker came in the opening seconds of the second quarter after QB Jalen Hurts connected with TE Dallas Goedert for a 17-yard touchdown on 3rd-and-goal. Facing a 3rd-and-2 near midfield, RB Saquon Barkley picked up 42 yards before WR Dontayvion Wicks proved no match for CB Mike Sainristil on a nine yard touchdown that put Philadelphia ahead, 14-3, midway through the second quarter. In the closing minutes of the third quarter, Hurts found DeVonta Smith for a 31 yard gain that eventually set up Jake Elliott with a 35 yard field goal that kept it a one possession game. Yet the last two were maybe the biggest blows for Washington’s defense in the final defensive series, first a 22-yard rush by Hurts on 3rd-and-18 before connecting with Goedert three players later for a 43-yard touchdown when the Eagles only needed six yards. There was a lot to like from game one, yet the secondary left a lot to be desired in week one with Mike Sainristil opening year three with an, at best, shaky performance. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Last Man Standig Dan Quinn rarely calls out players; Mike Sainristil’s mistakes crossed the line The Commanders had plenty to like in their opener, but missed opportunities — including an “unacceptable” lapse from the third-year corner — helped turn a winnable game into a division loss The public callout isn’t part of the Dan Quinn coaching playbook. At least not normally. Tonally, you would have been hard-pressed to sense Quinn’s frustration with cornerback Mike Sainristil based on his Monday media availability. The moments when this coach sounds like the angry version of himself from some movie or television universe typically surface publicly only in celebratory or motivational settings. Quinn saying the third-year cornerback’s focus on a second-quarter nine-yard touchdown pass during Sunday’s 24-22 road loss to the Philadelphia Eagles was “not acceptable” therefore spoke loudly on its own. The red-zone challenge came immediately after running back Saquon Barkley broke free for a 42-yard run over right guard to Washington’s 12. Two plays later, despite the urgent setting, Sainristil’s casualness felt more like a Sunday stroll. That’s certainly how Quinn interpreted his movements. For more from Ben Standig, click here Commanders.com 5 takeaways from Washington’s Week 1 loss to Philadelphia The rookies made plays If you were looking for positive signs from the Commanders’ rookie class, there were plenty of them against the Eagles. We’ll start with No. 7 overall pick Sonny Styles, who got more snaps than most of the Commanders’ impact players in the preseason but was still relatively limited. Head coach Dan Quinn said the Commanders were excited to “unleash” him, and the rookie’s athletic skill set shone through on several occasions. He bowled over Barkley on his way to the first sack of his career, showcasing his physicality and prowess as a blitzer. He also recorded two tackles for a loss on Barkley, one of which led to an Eagles punt three plays later. On offense, Antonio Williams was the Commanders’ top receiving threat. He caught all four of his targets for 64 yards, and each of them came at critical moments. His first catch set the Commanders up at the Eagles’ 1-yard line, and his second resulted in a 33-yard gain on third-and-14. His final catch of the night was a one-yard touchdown that gave Washington the chance to tie the score. The Commanders chose quality over quantity with this year’s draft class, and so far, it looks like that philosophy was the right one. title: NFL Week 2 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips
summary: What's the latest for three teams dealing with QB injuries? What are we hearing on the Rams and Chargers after bad losses? And which Week 1 debuts stood out?
full_text:
The 2026 NFL season is officially rolling. As we head into Week 2, insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 Week 1 saw the Seahawks, Vikings and Falcons all forced to turn to backup quarterbacks -- and in Atlanta's case, it was a third-stringer. Where do those franchises sit at QB entering Week 2? Jeremy and Dan also asked around about a tough opening week for the two Los Angeles teams. Is there concern yet for the Rams and Chargers? Plus, they debated debuts for coaches and rookies then offered up their best fantasy tips based on what they're hearing.

 It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 2.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 QB situations | Rams, Chargers concerns 
 Coaching debuts | Rookie debuts 
 Fantasy football takes  | Notes and more buzz 

 
 

 What's the latest on the quarterback situation for the Vikings, Seahawks and Falcons? 
 Graziano: Things seem straightforward for Minnesota. Based on what I've been able to gather, my sense is that Kyler Murray will start if he clears concussion protocol in time, and Carson Wentz is likely to start if Murray isn't clear in time. That sounds like a negative toward J.J. McCarthy , since it was him and not Wentz who competed with Murray for the starting job in camp. But this is more about the Vikings believing Wentz's veteran experience puts them in better position with limited preparation time when a QB gets hurt in-game (as happened Sunday) and/or there's uncertainty about who's going to start throughout the week.

 

 McCarthy was the emergency third QB on Sunday, so the team knew there was a chance they might have to play him. I could see a scenario in which Wentz starts this week with McCarthy as the backup, assuming Murray can't go.

 Fowler: That's certainly plausible. Murray took a nasty hit, and teams tend to be overly cautious when a player has assumed the fencing position, for good reason. But how players work through the five stages of the protocol often varies, so it's tough to know Murray's timeline at this point. Wentz is set up for success in Week 2 . He got hot last week  versus Green Bay , and Chicago just allowed 361 passing yards to Bryce Young .

 In Seattle, it's clear Sam Darnold will miss this week and possibly Week 3. But the Seahawks have refrained from putting him on short-term injured reserve, which is a good sign. The team seems confident that  Drew Lock is plug and play until Darnold returns.

 Graziano: Yeah, Seattle believes Lock can handle it, so he's the guy there for the foreseeable future. I'm personally interested to see whether they put in anything specific for Jalen Milroe in terms of plays or packages that take advantage of his running ability and maybe give their offense a little bit extra juice. Why not, if Milroe is going to be active anyway as the second quarterback?

 What about Atlanta? Kevin Stefanski probably thought he left the QB mess behind in Cleveland, but he has a situation on his hands, no?

 Fowler: Stefanski has seen it all at quarterback, but at least his signal-callers in Cleveland mostly stayed out of the training room. Tua Tagovailoa 's body seems to be betraying him at an inopportune time. The Falcons' best option remains third-year man Michael Penix Jr. , but he's not yet ready for live game action. Penix wants to be fully confident before stepping onto the field following left ACL surgery in November. And my understanding is the Falcons are leaving the comfort level part of his recovery up to him.

 Tagovailoa's injury, an oblique strain , can linger, which puts his Week 2 status up in the air. So,  Cooper Rush starting another week wouldn't be shocking. What helps Tagovailoa's case is his accuracy, which Stefanski highly values. If Tagovailoa's body doesn't totally break down in the short term and he can return before Penix is ready, perhaps Tagovailoa can provide a spark.

 Graziano: Penix is coming off his third ACL reconstruction , which is a lot of ACL reconstructions. I believe it takes a lot of mental work to convince yourself it's OK to go back out there and play. If Penix needs more time, I'm sure the Falcons will give it to him, though I believe we will see him on the field at some point this season. The Falcons are going to want to know whether he is a real long-term option moving forward.

 

 My sense is Tagovailoa was the favorite to start at the beginning of camp even when Penix was healthy but that Tagovailoa didn't perform the way the team had hoped he would. That has turned things into a confusing mess.

 Fowler: That two-week stretch, from the second preseason game rolling into the joint practice with the Colts, was rough for Tagovailoa. The schedule provides another wrinkle. Atlanta will play on Thursday night in Week 3, so even if Penix is close, that might not be the best week to reacclimate him.

 

 
 How high is the panic level in the Rams' building? What about for the Chargers? 
 Fowler: Well, the Rams' top-ranked offense scored seven points , and the league's best pass rusher is out at least a month . But other than that, everything's fine! I don't, however, sense heavy panic from the Rams, who seemed to approach the Australia trip with the excitement of a teenager asked to take out the trash. 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris knows the Rams' offense well, so San Francisco's ability to stymie Matthew Stafford shouldn't be a total shock.

 The Myles Garrett situation is more alarming. The Rams thought they could manage his knee injury with rest all camp and preseason, and it got exposed in Week 1. It leaves some uneasiness that they perhaps should have had this injury surgically repaired a tad sooner. But the Rams have plenty of defensive talent to offset the Garrett loss.

 Graziano: Garrett missed basically an entire month's worth of training camp with the knee problem, so those of us on the outside should have considered that a possible warning sign, at the very least. Aaron Donald being able to play Monday night would help, but the issues that came up in Australia went beyond Garrett's health. The Rams' expensive new cornerback tandem looked miscast in the defensive game plan, and they couldn't get the passing game clicking.

 The Rams are certainly not going to panic because of one game, even if it was an embarrassing loss to a division rival. But they are (and should be) taking the problems that were on display against the 49ers seriously. The operation needs to be sharper on both sides of the ball. One possible benefit of the Rams' controversial Australian travel plan is that they likely didn't need to get reacclimated upon their return home, since their body clocks theoretically never reset in the first place. We'll see if they come out looking sharper in Week 2 against the Giants.

 

 Fowler: The Chargers' panic meter will rise if they lose to the Raiders this week . Arizona was deemed terrible in the preseason, but the Cardinals are more respectable than that, particularly on offense. So, the Chargers' defense gets a mulligan after seeing the Cards in the opener. It's a veteran group that should improve.

 The bigger concern is how the Bolts' offense looked after wide receiver Ladd McConkey left the game with a rib injury. McConkey and Justin Herbert showed easy chemistry in that first half. They need McConkey, who is listed as day-to-day , to work his way back or concerns about the offensive attack will mushroom. I'm expecting a better running game from Los Angeles in Week 2 as it tries to find some continuity with the offensive line.

 Graziano: McConkey is a great player, but the game plan falling apart completely once he exited makes it seem as if it was flimsy to begin with. Where are the smart, creative run plays Mike McDaniel was calling last season in Miami? Wasn't running back Omarion Hampton supposed to explode in this scheme? Wasn't the…

title: 2026 NFL Power Rankings: How all 32 teams stack up for Week 2
summary: How do all 32 NFL teams stack up ahead of Week 2? Plus, we picked out the top newcomers from each roster.
full_text:
The opening week of the 2026 NFL season is now complete after the Chiefs defeated the Broncos 31-10 on "Monday Night Football." We saw a lot of scoring, as 49.4 points per game tied 2012 for the most in Week 1 since the AFL/NFL merger in 1970, per ESPN Research. But that still led to some close finishes, including an overtime win by the Lions over the Saints and the Bills' dramatic five-point victory over the Texans.

 How do these teams fit in our updated Power Rankings ahead of Week 2? To form the list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another, ranking them from No. 1 to 32.

 In addition to our 1-32 ranking, NFL Nation reporters named a non-QB newcomer -- defined as a rookie, offseason acquisition or coaching hire -- who shined in Week 1. From Texans running back David Montgomery scoring three touchdowns to third-round defensive tackle Domonique Orange 's big stop for the Vikings, we picked 32 players and coaches who impressed in their debuts. (And again, no quarterbacks allowed.)

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. Buffalo Bills (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Texans 36-31 
 Preseason ranking : 3 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR DJ Moore 

 Moore's five catches for 100 yards were somewhat aided when Houston safety Reed Blankenship went for an interception and missed badly, giving Moore an easy path to a 43-yard touchdown. However, Moore also did a lot of things that didn't end up in his standard receiving totals. He drew a 46-yard pass interference penalty and later an illegal contact flag. He also slapped away what appeared to be a very likely interception for Houston safety  Calen Bullock . It was everything the Bills could have asked for when they traded for Moore  in March. -- Aaron Schatz 

 

 
 

 

 2. Seattle Seahawks (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Patriots 13-10 
 Preseason ranking: 2 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: S Rodney Thomas II 

 Rookie running back Jadarian Price had a solid debut, but Thomas gets the nod for helping Seattle's defense hold New England to 10 points. Starting for an injured Ty Okada , Thomas had a pass breakup that resulted in an interception and an open-field tackle on consecutive drives. The plays got Seattle the ball back for drives that ended with a field goal and the tying touchdown. Thomas, a former starter with the Colts, signed a one-year, $1.4 million deal with the Seahawks and began on the practice squad. -- Brady Henderson 

 

 
 

 3. Baltimore Ravens (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Colts 41-23 
 Preseason ranking: 8 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle

 In his first game as Baltimore's offensive playcaller, Doyle kept the Colts on their heels by putting quarterback Lamar Jackson under center and using play-action. The result? For the first time in the Ravens' 31-year history, they had a 300-yard passer (Jackson), a 150-yard receiver ( Zay Flowers ) and a 100-yard rusher ( Derrick Henry ) in the same game. There will be plenty of opportunities for Doyle's unit to put up more points. Over the next seven games, Baltimore faces five teams -- the Saints, Cowboys, Browns, Bengals and Bills -- who allowed 27-plus points in Week 1. "Man, first NFL game, [he] came out of the gates on fire," Ravens head coach Jesse Minter said of Doyle. -- Jamison Hensley 

 

 
 

 4. Los Angeles Rams (0-1) 
 Week 1 result: Lost to the 49ers 27-7 
 Preseason ranking: 1 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: CB Trent McDuffie 

 The Rams traded four draft picks for the All-Pro cornerback in March as part of their effort to rehaul their CB room. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, McDuffie allowed only two receptions for 22 yards on four targets in Week 1, including two passes defensed. One of the passes defensed came in the first quarter, when McDuffie broke up a pass intended for Niners tight end George Kittle . McDuffie intercepted the ball but was just out of bounds. -- Sarah Barshop 

 

 
 

 5. San Francisco 49ers (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Rams 27-7 
 Preseason ranking: 9 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Mike Evans 

 Defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa was also impactful in his Niners debut, but it's hard to argue with Evans' production. He finished with six receptions for 49 yards and a touchdown, and each of those catches somehow went for either a first down or a score. That gave him the most receiving first downs by any player in a team debut since the Rams' Puka Nacua had six in 2023. Evans signed a three-year deal with the 49ers in free agency.  -- Nick Wagoner 

 

 
 

 6. Philadelphia Eagles (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Commanders 24-22 
 Preseason ranking: 5 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Dontayvion Wicks 

 Wicks had two catches for 73 yards and a touchdown against the Commanders. His 64-yard catch-and-run in the first half marked the longest reception of his career, providing a much-needed spark to the Eagles' new-look offense. Wicks, acquired via trade from the Packers in April, has assumed the role of WR2 behind DeVonta Smith . QB  Jalen Hurts and Wicks built a rapport over the spring and summer, and it translated to Week 1. -- Tim McManus 

 

 
 

 7. Chicago Bears (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Panthers 59-37 
 Preseason ranking: 12 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Kalif Raymond 

 The veteran wideout led the Bears with eight catches on nine targets for 84 yards. Five of his receptions came on third down, demonstrating the trust quarterback Caleb Williams quickly built with Raymond after  he signed  a one-year deal in March. Perhaps the moment most emblematic of his buy-in for what coach Ben Johnson asks of his offensive players is the block Raymond had during running back Kyle Monangai 's 61-yard touchdown in the third quarter. -- Courtney Cronin 

 

 

 
 

 8. Kansas City Chiefs (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Broncos 31-10 
 Preseason ranking: 13 

 Non-QB newcomer debut:  RB Kenneth Walker III 

 For one game at least, Walker was everything the Chiefs could've hoped for, bringing more explosive highlights to their rushing attack. Walker produced a career-high 173 rushing yards, with his best moment being a breakaway 60-yard touchdown on fourth-and-inches early in the third quarter. His best trait against the Broncos was his elusiveness, as he forced 14 missed tackles, the most by any Chiefs player in a game since 2018. Walker caught a short touchdown pass, too. -- Nate Taylor 

 

 
 

 9. Denver Broncos (0-1) 
 Week 1 result: Lost to the Chiefs 31-10 
 Preseason ranking: 4 

 Non-QB newcomer debut:  RB Jonah Coleman 

 You know it was a bad opener -- and the three-touchdown loss to the Chiefs was brutal -- when Coleman's 27-yard kickoff return made him the best non-quarterback newcomer. It was that kind of night for a team that returned more players from last season than any other in the league. Jaylen Waddle had one catch for 2 yards, safety Tycen Anderson had one tackle and Coleman was the only rookie in uniform for the game.  -- Jeff Legwold 

 

 
 

 10. New England Patriots (0-1) 
 Week 1 result: Lost to the Seahawks 13-10 
 Preseason ranking: 6 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: Edge rusher  Dre'Mont Jones 

 Signed to a three-year, $36.5 million deal in free agency, the eight-year veteran totaled four QB hits, one sack and two tackles. He was generally a solid presence setting the edge in the running game, as well. The Patriots targeted Jones over retaining K'Lavon Chaisson , who led the team with 7.5 sacks last season. Runner-up choice: sixth-round rookie linebacker Namdi Obiazor (TCU), who led the team with three special teams tackles, including one on the opening kickoff. -- Mike Reiss 

 

 
 

 11. Houston Texans (0-1) 
 Week 1 result: Lost to the Bills 36-31 
 Preseason ranking: 10 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: RB David Montgomery 

 Montgomery, who…

title: Super Bowl LXI odds: Rams' odds lengthen slightly, 49ers enter top 5
summary: Every NFL team's win total, as well as odds to win their division, the conference and Super Bowl LXI.
full_text:
One week of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, and while many fans, pundits and bettors are ready to overreact, bookmakers aren't overhauling their Super Bowl futures odds just yet.

 After losing their season opener to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia, the Los Angeles Rams remain the favorites for the title, though at a longer +650 than the +500 they came into the season with. The Niners made one of the biggest odds jumps of the week with their win, going from 19-1 to 14-1 for the Super Bowl.

 

 Another big positive mover was the Chicago Bears , who went from 24-1 before the campaign to 21-1 after a statement win over the Carolina Panthers . The Baltimore Ravens (10-1 to +900), Buffalo Bills (10-1 to +950), Seattle Seahawks (12-1 to 11-1) and Kansas City Chiefs (16-1 to 14-1) also made moderate moves following Week 1 wins.

 There were also a few major fallers on the odds board. The Los Angeles Chargers lengthened from 17-1 to 20-1 after a humbling loss to the Arizona Cardinals (300-1), and the New England Patriots moved from 18-1 to 21-1 after falling to Seattle on opening night.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings Sportsbook   and subject to change.

title: Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 2
summary: Will the Titans score any points against the Eagles? Can Ben Johnson solve Brian Flores' Vikings defense? Get ready for Week 2 with seven takes.
full_text:
Who's ready to put their thinking caps on? Big-time offensive scoring was the story in Week 1 of the NFL season, but Week 2 is now right around the corner. What will it bring?

 Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from last week to this week with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions -- those come later in the week. They aren't concrete takeaways off the past week of NFL action, either -- those are fired off on Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain things. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games for us to really find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

 This week, I'm starting off with my expectations for the schemer heavyweight fight of the century, my theories on the real skeleton key for the Bills' offense and my worry that the first shutout of the season will come this Sunday.

 Here are seven things I think for Week 2.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Ben Johnson is Brian Flores' kryptonite 
 Texans' offense will win games 
 Bengals defense is showing promise 
 Kincaid is the Bills' secret sauce 
 Titans will not score in Week 2 
 Lions have an Achilles' heel on defense 
 Lawrence is league MVP this week 
 Five extra inklings 

 

 
 

 I think ... Ben Johnson is Brian Flores' kryptonite 
 Two heinous crimes were committed Sunday by two of football nerddom's favorite coaches.

 Let's start with Johnson. The Bears scored 59 points against the Panthers, which is like if you scored 50 points, and then decided to score nine more points. Both running backs  D'Andre Swift  and Kyle Monangai  reached 100 yards and scored two touchdowns, and quarterback Caleb Williams added another two scores on scrambles of his own. And for those tracking Williams' accuracy metrics: 72.4% completion percentage with an off-target rate of only 13.8%.

 Everything worked for the Bears' offense, which barely left first gear against the Panthers. The Bears will face far stiffer competition in Week 2 against the Vikings and Flores, who rendered an unbelievable performance against the Packers in Week 1.

 The Vikings blitzed Jordan Love on 73.8% of his dropbacks Sunday -- the highest rate at which any quarterback has been blitzed since the 2023 season. The Packers were in a difficult position entering the game; starting left guard Aaron Banks was hurt, and the camp campaign to build up Anthony Belton at the starting right guard spot was abandoned late in the process. The Packers fielded 2024 fifth-round pick Jacob Monk at right guard and 2024 undrafted free agent  Donovan Jennings at left guard. It was Jennings' first career start and Monk's second.

 In an effort to insulate the young guards, the Packers kept more players in to block than basically any offense over the past few seasons. Love had three or fewer receivers in the route concept on an astonishing 15 dropbacks. Only three quarterbacks have had more such dropbacks over the past five seasons.

 Flores has little interest in occupying those routes with multiple defenders -- he'd rather throw bodies against the wall of your pass protection and find a weak point. Like water against a dam, it didn't really matter how many players the Packers kept in to protect -- if there was a weak point (which there often was), Flores had a rusher in that spot. His distinctive approach to early-down blitzing breaks the rules. It forces opposing offenses to play a different sport than the one for which they're prepared against other opponents.

 But Johnson knows Flores well. He called offense against him as the coordinator of the Lions -- twice in 2023, twice in 2024 -- then picked up another two games in 2025 as the head coach of the Bears. Across six matchups, Johnson's team is 5-1 -- the only loss was last season's opener and Williams' first start in Johnson's offense. Over those six games, Johnson's offense doesn't look like a 59-point monster ... but it's clearly better than the average offense against the marauding Vikings coordinator.

 

 So what does Johnson do that other teams can't replicate? A few things stick out. The first is communication. Flores' defense requires as much pre-snap coordination between 11 players as any in football -- that's why Harrison Smith is back and so valuable. He can be the coach on the field, changing the playcall after the defense sees the formation.

 Johnson rises to meet Flores. His offense is as communication-heavy as any in the league, and his group is empowered to make adjustments based on what it sees. Flores wants to get opposing offenses stuck in a bad protection look or run call; Johnson's groups are elite at getting out of such sticky wickets. Williams' pre-snap command, which has reportedly taken big strides through Year 1 and into Year 2 with Johnson, will be tested here.

 To challenge Flores' reliance on communication, Johnson will randomly snap the football quickly -- no motion, no checking. Immediate snaps. The Bears had 19 quick snaps against the Vikings in Week 11 -- snaps in which less than two seconds elapse between the line getting set and the ball being snapped. It was the most they had in any game last season, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Second most? The 17 such snaps in Week 1 ... also against Flores.

 

 The second thing that sticks out is formational. The Lions loved condensed sets under Johnson, and the Bears have continued that approach. Condensed sets are typically a bad idea against blitz-heavy teams. When you spread out the field, it's easier to identify suspicious defensive alignment that reveals who's blitzing from where. Against Flores and the Vikings, there's no point in trying to riddle things out -- the blitzes are too frequent and too varied. You'll think you're right, you'll actually be wrong, and then you'll be dead in the water.

 So Johnson turns into the skid. He gets as condensed as possible against Flores. In 2025, no offense had more condensed formations in any game than the Bears in Week 11 against the Vikings, with an average formational width of only 17.7 yards. Teeny tiny formations allow Johnson to throw the ball on out-breakers into a ton of space, to stress the Vikings' cornerbacks who are typically insulated by trap coverages and quick throws. It also allows Johnson to meet Flores' duplicity and disguise with the beautiful simplicity of the running game. With lighter players such as  Joshua Metellus and Dallas Turner on the edge against double-teams from extra tight ends and condensed wide receivers, the Bears can grind out physical yardage and set up the play-action pass.

 

 Does Flores have an answer to this approach? Yes ... but not on the chalkboard. The Vikings' first three picks in the 2026 draft were trench picks: defensive tackle Caleb Banks in the first round, on/off-ball linebacker hybrid Jake Golday in the second round and another defensive tackle in the third round in space-gobbler Domonique Orange . Any defense that plays in a division with the Bears needs to be serious about its run defense -- doubly true for Flores, who will never get to third-and-long against Chicago unless he has some run-stuffing hog mollies up front to slow down Swift and Monangai.

 

 Johnson won Assistant Coach of the Year in 2024. Second place in voting was Flores. When Flores was a young defensive assistant cutting his teeth in New England, Johnson was doing the same in Miami on offense -- twice a year, they saw each other. These two have circled their matchups like heavyweight fighters for years now, and on Sunday, we get another 90-minute dance in the ring. Bring your popcorn.

 

 

 I think ... the Texans' offense will win some games this year 
 The Texans' defense was a machine last season, and it entered 2026 with all of the Super Bowl hype. Houston just needed an offense that could do enough to win those games in which the defense struggled.

 Sunday was one such game. The Texans…

title: Dave Canales: Panthers need to 'play way better football'
summary: After watching film, the coach said Carolina needed to play smarter and Derrick Brown reminded everyone that it's just one game.
full_text:
Carolina Panthers coach Dave Canales said Sunday after the team's 59-37 loss to the Chicago Bears that he needed to watch film before pointing fingers at the problems from the historic defensive downturn. After watching the tape Monday, Canales said the team could have played smarter, noting penalties, poor technique and other mental gaffes.

 "We played hard," Canales said. "We played with great effort. The guys were together. All those things are true. Playing smart, that's where we fell short. And it was about executing our plan. It was about timely and costly penalties. Certainly, the turnovers ... against a really good team. That's not something that you can do to play the championship football that we need to play."

 The Bears' offense produced 552 net yards -- Chicago's third-most yardage earned in the Super Bowl era -- with 291 collected on the ground. The 59 points were the most allowed in Panthers' franchise history. The six rushing touchdowns produced by Chicago -- the most in a season opener since 1922, according to ESPN Research -- were shared by three players, including quarterback Caleb Williams , who also threw for 269 yards and two touchdowns for a 124.1 traditional passer rating.

 "We knew how they were going to attack us," Panthers linebacker Bobby Okereke said. "We practiced a lot of their concepts, and we got a lot of their concepts on game day. And we executed a good bit, but just the run game bit us in the ass today and we gotta be a lot better there."

 

 And yet, Canales' main takeaways after watching the film focused on turnovers and penalties.

 The Panthers' offense and special teams coughed up the ball twice on lost fumbles. Quarterback Bryce Young threw an interception on a pass to wideout Jalen Coker to end the first half, and the offense was stopped while failing to convert on a fourth-down play at the end of the third quarter. But even taking away the 17 points the Bears scored off those mishaps, Chicago still had a five-point advantage over Carolina because of what the defense allowed on the other side.

 The penalties, though, were inarguably a crux for the Panthers' letdown. Carolina was flagged 11 times for 84 yards, but it was more about the timing of infractions that lost ground. Team captain Derrick Brown was uncharacteristically charged twice -- once for roughing the passer and once for offside -- with the first penalty leading to a touchdown and the second negating an interception by fellow lineman Bobby Brown III  and leading to another Bears score.

 "S--- like that can't happen," Derrick Brown said after the game.

 Week 1 was the latest in a long line of defensive meltdowns for the Panthers under coordinator Ejiro Evero, who was hired by Carolina in February 2023 under coach Frank Reich. But it was also the biggest one to date, topping a brutal back-to-back stretch to end the 2024 season, when the defense gave up 551 yards to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 17 and 537 yards in the season finale against the Atlanta Falcons .

 "I like our system," Canales said Monday. "I like our scheme. I've seen this scheme work at a high level, and I've seen us work in this scheme at a high level."

 "It sucks, but it's one f---ing game," Derrick Brown said Sunday. "We've got a whole season."

 

 In 52 regular-season games as the Panthers' defensive coordinator, Evero's unit has given up the highest allowed scoring average in the league at 26.7 points per game, following Sunday's 59-point offering to the Bears. During that span, his group also ranks 26th in the league with a 345.9 yards allowed average per game.

 The unit also ranks second worst in the league during Evero's tenure in defensive EPA (expected points added) with a minus-250.9 points mark, according to ESPN Research. The defense is also allowing the highest Total QBR in the league (58.3) during that stretch.

 Following Sunday's loss, the Panthers rank last in points (minus-8.92) and yardage (minus-56) margin averages per game during the Evero era. But it is also worth noting that the offenses, largely anchored by Reich and Canales, have been among the bottom-third of the league throughout Evero's tenure.

 "I feel like we could just be better as a whole," outside linebacker Princely Umanmielen said about the defense's performance Sunday. "I feel like we could have been more disciplined as a whole unit and just as a whole team in general."

 

 During his second season at the helm, Evero's defense was the worst in the league against the run, allowing 179.8 yards per game. The unit also finished last in total yards average, giving up 404.5 yards per game. But last season, the unit improved across the board, ranking 20th in run defense (123.3 rushing yards per game) and 16th overall (327.2 total yards per game).

 The Panthers added safety Tre'von Moehrig , outside linebacker Patrick Jones II and defensive linemen Bobby Brown III and Tershawn Wharton in free agency during the 2025 offseason. They also selected outside linebackers Umanmielen and  Nic Scourton  and safety Lathan Ransom in the 2025 draft.

 This year Carolina continued to beef up its defense, paying a fortune for outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips and inside linebacker Devin Lloyd . They drafted defensive tackle Lee Hunter , cornerback  Will Lee III, safety Zakee Wheatley and linebacker Jackson Kuwatch as well. Plus, they signed veteran linebacker Bobby Okereke on Aug. 31.

 The Panthers didn't have Wharton, Jones and Scourton due to injury and Wheatley was a healthy scratch in Week 1. So, while the investment in the defense over the past two years wasn't in full force, the rest of the accumulated talent did little to stop the onslaught of Williams and D'Andre Swift .

 "Players and coaches alike gotta be better," DT Bobby Brown III said after going through Monday's meetings. "Players didn't execute all the time. Coach [Evero] already told us he didn't get us in the best calls all the time. But when we did have the call right and we felt like we [were] in good positions, everybody didn't show up and make the plays that needed to be made."

 Canales maintained Monday that the unit has the right talent to turn things around.

 "And that was one of the things I did share with the team today, I said, 'Look, I wouldn't have been able to sleep if I felt like we didn't have the pieces that we need right in this room.'" Canales said. "And a true statement to those guys. But we need to collectively come together and play way better football than that."

title: 'No block, no rock' is not just a mantra for Bears' offense
summary: When even the "little guys" are getting a hat on a hat, it's that much easier to post 59 points and over 500 yards.
full_text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. --  Chicago Bears  receiver  Jahdae Walker threw his right shoulder into Will Lee III , sending the Panthers cornerback to the turf and creating the opening for receiver Kalif Raymond to work his way shy of the first-down marker.

 It was late in Chicago's 59-37 win over Carolina, and the force of his block left Walker winded. Even in the thick of the Bears' offensive explosion, all the dirty work that Walker put in on 33 of his 34 offensive snaps was not lost on coach Ben Johnson.

 Five plays later, Johnson sent in a playcall that rewarded the second-year wide receiver. Walker caught a 1-yard touchdown and became the fifth different Bears player to score in the season opener.

 Walker, the former undrafted free agent, knew long before he made the team in 2025 that any role he'd earn on offense is dependent on him embracing the selfless, physical aspects of playing receiver that don't show up in a box score. But what's required of Walker isn't limited to players further down the depth chart. There's a rallying cry inside the offensive meeting rooms that everyone from star tight end Colston Loveland , who did not record a catch in Week 1 but has always been a willing blocker (27 run blocking snaps at Carolina), to rookie receiver Zavion Thomas must buy into.

 "Oh shoot, [Johnson] just says, 'no block, no rock' and that just gets us going because we all want the ball," Walker said. "So that's pretty much all we be thinking about. It's just you got to buy into it or you're going to get left."

 "No block, no rock" is a philosophy Johnson picked up during his days as a position coach with the Miami Dolphins . It's a common football expression that has been hammered into offensive players since Johnson became the Bears' head coach last year, making clear that if skill players want their touches, they have to be willing physical contributors.

 That requirement is most necessary in the run game. Chicago's 291 rushing yards led to six touchdowns, the most rushing touchdowns in a season opener since the 1922 Canton Bulldogs. The Bears had not compiled that many rushing yards in a game since they ran for 302 against the Denver Broncos in a 27-0 win in 1984.

 

 D'Andre Swift  (124 yards, 3 TDs) and Kyle Monangai (100 yards, TD) made franchise history by becoming the first Bears duo to each rush for 100 yards in a season opener. Quarterback Caleb Williams contributed to the run game with 65 yards, which resulted in his first career game with multiple rushing touchdowns (2).

 Of all 70 plays the Bears ran in Carolina, Johnson said Monangai's 61-yard touchdown run was his favorite. It wasn't just the offense's ability to score quickly one play after the Panthers turned the ball over on downs, nor was it Monangai keeping his balance in a track race to get away from defenders.

 Blocks by Raymond and tight end Cole Kmet allowed Monangai to get to the second level. As Walker ran in stride with his running back teammate, the block he had on Panthers outside linebacker Princely Umanmielen sprung Monangai loose. As stoic as he appeared on the sideline, Johnson says he was rife with excitement at all the things that took place for that to be the result.

 "We had a lot of our little guys going down and making big plays for us on the running game that ended up being some big runs for us," Johnson said. The Bears have amassed over 500 yards in a game twice under Johnson, including Week 1 at Carolina and a 47-42 win over the Cincinnati Bengals in November 2025. In the previous 25 seasons, a span that includes 413 games, there were two instances where the offense put up 500-plus yards.

 Just like in Carolina, the run game was a huge factor in that Cincinnati win with 283 rushing yards. Swift's breakout performance in the season opener coming off signing a three-year, $33.75 million contract extension is why Johnson said he's "vital" to everything the Bears do on offense.

 It also highlights the need from at least nine others on offense to make those plays happen routinely.

 As the 2026 Bears build their identity over the first quarter of the season, one thing is already established. To reach or top the 127 explosive plays (10-yard rush or 20-yard completion) they had last regular season will require the efforts of everyone, not just the players who wind up with the ball in their hands.

 "No block, no rock" is a mindset that will get its next test on Sunday against the  Minnesota Vikings  (1 p.m. ET, Fox) at Soldier Field.

title: Cashing in: Bengals rookie Howell impacts pass rush
summary: Howell believes the SEC made him ready for moments such as Sunday, when he had four QB pressures in the Bengals' win.
full_text:
CINCINNATI -- Just before he officially made his NFL debut, Cashius Howell was playing video games with his friends when he thought about something that sounds absurd when said out loud.

 Before he emerged as one of the best Cincinnati Bengals rookies in recent memory, he was a young defensive end transitioning from playing in the MAC at Bowling Green to being in the SEC with Texas A&M.

 And in hindsight, that was tougher than getting acclimated in the NFL.

 "Not like the NFL is easy or anything -- this is the best people in the world -- but I feel like it was more of a struggle trying to get from the MAC to the SEC than it was the SEC to the NFL, if that makes sense."

 It really shouldn't. But the last few months, including Sunday's win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers , shows why it does. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Howell matched defensive end Boye Mafe with a team-high four quarterback pressures.

 While defensive coordinator Al Golden playfully scoffed at the various analytics used to measure players, there was no disputing Howell's immediate impact.

 "He showed up [on Sunday]," Golden told reporters on Monday.

 Five months after the Bengals drafted him, it still seems incredulous to some at Paycor Stadium that Cincinnati was able to take the reigning SEC Defensive Player of the Year.

 Golden recalled that entering the draft, as many as 10 Bengals personnel out of a ballpark of maybe 12 people gave Howell a first-round draft grade. But after the first 32 picks went off the board, Howell was still available.

 The next day, he went to the Bengals with the 41st overall pick. And since then, the transition has been virtually flawless.

 Bengals right tackle Amarius Mims , considered one of the team's top ascending talents, said Howell is one of the best rookies he's lined up against in his three years in the league.

 As good as he looked against the Bengals in offseason workouts and training camp, the real eye-opener came in the joint practice against the Chicago Bears . Howell held his own against Chicago's Darnell Wright , who ranked fourth in the NFL last season in pass block win rate as a tackle (ESPN/Next Gen Stats).

 That was enough to not only warrant a closer look but validate the same feeling that Golden and others felt during draft weekend.

 "I don't know he fell to us in the second round," Mims said on Monday. "I don't know how that was possible. But I'm very glad he's on our team. He's going to be a great, great addition for us."

 Bengals defensive end Shemar Stewart was teammates with Howell at A&M in 2024, one year before Stewart declared for the NFL and the Bengals drafted him in the first round. And he doesn't seem to recall Howell having any learning curve when he arrived in College Station.

 "I just remember him dogging people out, doing people in," Stewart said with a big laugh. "That's the first thing that comes to mind when it comes to Cash."

 In his final year at A&M, he was second in the SEC with 11.5 total sacks. And in his first true NFL action, Howell made an early impact.

 In the first quarter, he shed Tampa Bay tight end Cade Otton before forcing right guard Cody Mauch into a holding penalty. The pressure helped Cincinnati's  Kris Jenkins Jr . secure the sack.

 

 Howell officially didn't register any stats while playing on 44% of the team's defensive snaps. But his output showed how a defensive lineman can affect the game without ending up in the stat book.

 While Howell has had a pleasant start, Stewart knows things will get tougher for his fellow Aggie as the season continues.

 "It's a long year," Stewart said. "It's not like college. It's definitely a lot harder on your body. You're going to be mentally and physically tired because rookies just have a lot more things to do on your plate."

 Howell is well aware of that. He said playing in the SEC, a conference filled with pro prospects, has allowed him to adjust to the NFL game speed while meticulous offseason work prepared him for the physical rigors of the league.

 And despite all the praise and early returns, Howell is fixated on keeping a short-term outlook instead of focusing on the potential of a promising rookie season.

 "I thank God in advance for whatever he has in store for me," Howell said. "Whatever that may be, I'm prepared for it. But I feel like it will be good."

title: Cowboys' TD record: I caught a TD pass from Dak Prescott
summary: Prescott needs four TDs to pass Tony Romo in the record book, so we sought the best moments from those who are helping him make history.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- Sometime soon, perhaps as soon as Sunday against the Washington Commanders , Dak Prescott will set another Dallas Cowboys record: most touchdown passes in team history.

 He has 245, leaving him three shy of the 248 Tony Romo threw from 2006 to 2016.

 "I might remember every single one of them," Prescott said.

 His first?

 "Slant to Dez in the fourth quarter against Chicago," Prescott said.

 True. Prescott's first touchdown pass was a 17-yarder to receiver  Dez Bryant in the third game of his rookie season after being selected in Round 4 of the 2016 draft. The Cowboys beat the Chicago Bears , giving Prescott his first career victory at AT&T Stadium.

 His favorite?

 "I don't think I have a true favorite, one that stands out," Prescott said. "Any of them that have been a game winner or some big-time, fourth-quarter touchdowns, those are the ones that stick out in my mind."

 Needing four touchdown passes against the Commanders in the Cowboys' home opener at AT&T Stadium on Sunday ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Fox ) might seem daunting, but Prescott has already reached that mark four times against Washington, the last coming in a 38-10 win in Week 18 of the 2023 season.

 Prescott has thrown touchdowns to 39 different players, including nine current teammates. CeeDee Lamb has the most with 35. Eleven have caught one.

 Instead of Prescott's favorite touchdown passes, ESPN asked nine current and former teammates to describe their favorite scoring receptions from the quarterback, including Lamb and right tackle Terence Steele , whose only career catch is a TD from Prescott.

 

 

 CeeDee Lamb, WR 

 Situation: Week 17, 2023, vs.  Detroit Lions , first quarter, third-and-13 from Cowboys' 8 

 Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes  should have sacked Prescott, but somehow he escaped at the goal line, drifted to his right and let go of a deep ball toward Lamb. Before he caught the pass, cornerback Kindle Vildor fell. Lamb caught the ball at midfield and was able to jog into the end zone for a 92-yard score.

 "Dak did a great job of beating the blitz. I did a good job of expanding on the scramble drill," Lamb said. "We preach extending drives and extending plays and that was a big part of that. That was one of the longest plays of my career. For sure, my most favorite."

 

 It was the longest completion of Prescott's career, the longest catch of Lamb's and the second-longest completion in team history. It was also Lamb's 111th catch of the season, which tied him for Michael Irvin 's team record for most in a season, which he later broke.

 Has he ever run that far without being chased?

 "Nah, I don't think I'll ever get that close to it again. Great time," Lamb said. "I enjoyed it. As you could tell, I trotted in the end zone. It was fire."

 

 

 Jason Witten , TE 
 Situation: Week 8, 2016 vs. the Philadelphia Eagles , overtime, second-and-goal from Eagles' 5 

 The Cowboys trailed 23-13 early in the fourth quarter, but Prescott forced overtime with a touchdown pass to Dez Bryant with 3:04 to play. In overtime, the Cowboys never gave the Eagles a chance to win it.

 Pressured on the play, Prescott went into scramble mode, first cheating up toward the line of scrimmage as some Eagles defenders converged and then sliding to his left. As chaos ensued, Witten just stopped in the end zone, leading to a wide open throw and a 29-23 win.

 

 "I was running away from the guy and I just kind of stepped back and so it kind of went against the grain if you will and stepped back instead of keeping on scrambling and mirroring him," Witten said. "He immediately saw it and immediately threw it. It was almost like he saw it at the same time I saw it -- and didn't even flinch ... it was at a critical time but that's my favorite one just because it was the Eagles and it was fairly early on in our time together.

 "For him to have seen that and anticipate what I was doing at the same time, because if he's a half second late, I don't know if we complete it. Mike Jenkins was the guy covering me. He was a crafty veteran guy and I just kind of did that move and Dak saw it at the same time."

 It was Prescott's first touchdown pass to Witten on a night when Witten set the Cowboys' record for most career starts and tied linebacker  Lee Roy Jordan 's team mark for most consecutive starts.

 

 Terence Steele, OT 
 Situation: Week 16, 2021 vs. Washington Commanders, third-and-goal from Commanders' 1 

 Steele was in his second year but wise enough to know if he dropped a pass in practice, offensive coordinator Kellen Moore would be unlikely to call the play in a game.

 "It'll sway the coach to not run it, but every time we ran it in practice, I caught it," Steele said, "so I think that gave him a lot of confidence to call it."

 It helped the Cowboys were already leading 28-7 in the second quarter against the Commanders, but when Steele heard Prescott say, "Red Raider report," a nod to Steele's Texas Tech days, the play was on.

 

 Steele started at left tackle that day but moved to jumbo tight end next to right tackle La'el Collins and dutifully told the referee he was reporting as an eligible receiver.

 "I'm supposed to slowly lose [his block] and let him beat me up the field and then I get in the end zone," Steele said. "And Dak throws me a perfect ball. Right between the hands."

 Steele spiked the ball so ferociously that it ended up in one of the field suites. Ezekiel Elliott was able to track the ball and make sure Steele had it.

 "I got it framed," Steele said. "They got it all painted up for me. It sits in my office right now."

 Steele became the first Cowboys offensive lineman since the 1970 merger to catch a touchdown. Prescott finished with four touchdown passes in a 56-14 win.

 

 

 George Pickens, WR 

 Situation: Week 16, 2025 vs.  Los Angeles Chargers , second-and-2 from Chargers' 38 

 Pickens  caught nine touchdown passes from Prescott in his first season with the Cowboys.

 His first choice for the favorite was a 34-yard catch-and-run on a slant at the Carolina Panthers  in Week 6.

 "Just running away from all the guys," he said.

 But then he remembered the go ball from Prescott against the Chargers.

 

 Using an outside release against Chargers cornerback Cam Hart , Pickens gained separation with a little stop-and-go. But then he noticed Prescott's pass was a little deeper than he thought.

 "Just definitely looking at the ball and changing my speed on how I should catch that ball," Pickens said. "It was a led ball, so I kind of knew, pick up the speed, but if it was a high ball or a ball that's kind of going to sit over his head, I would've made it fine."

 It wasn't the first time he and Prescott connected on that type of pass.

 "Definitely, practice," he said. "Tons of practice reps."

 

 Jake Ferguson, TE 

 Situation: Week 4, 2025 vs.  Green Bay Packers . Second-and-6 from Packers' 8 

 Ferguson might not have forgotten what it felt like to score a touchdown, but for him it felt like an eternity. He had gone 22 games since scoring against the Seattle Seahawks on Nov. 30, 2023. Part of his drought had to do with Prescott missing nine games in 2024 with avulsion of a hamstring.

 But it stretched through the first three weeks of the 2025 season.

 "It was a while," Ferguson said. "I remember, and the media didn't let me live it down."

 

 Lined up initially as a wing, Ferguson shifted a few yards to his left before the snap, putting cornerback Nate Hobbs in coverage. Ferguson was able to get inside of Hobbs at the goal line, using his body to shield the smaller corner and give Prescott an easy throw that gave the Cowboys a third-quarter lead.

 "When I caught it, it was like a huge weight off my shoulders," Ferguson said. "And I remember the guys coming up to me and [Prescott] came up to me very calm and was like, 'Welcome back,'" Ferguson said. "I was like, 'Thank you.' All I could say was, 'Thank you, thank you, thank you.'"

title: Inside Patrick Mahomes' remarkable return from knee injury
summary: On Dec. 14, Mahomes, after suffering the most significant injury of his career, vowed to be back for Week 1. Here's how he did it.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Positioned next to Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes , at the start of what would be a nine-month odyssey, was the MRI machine. The results of the scans that Dec. 14 day revealed the most significant injury of Mahomes' nine-year career: a torn ACL and LCL in his left knee.

 As the minutes passed, more people entered the room inside the Chiefs' training facility, located a few hundred feet from Arrowhead Stadium -- team head trainer Rick Burkholder; Mahomes' agent, Chris Cabott; Mahomes' wife, Brittany; coach Andy Reid; general manager Brett Veach; and club owner Clark Hunt. Together -- less than an hour after Mahomes had crumpled to the turf, grabbed his knee and screamed in pain -- the group began contemplating next steps.

 At one point, someone looked at the calendar. The first Sunday of the 2026 NFL season was scheduled for Sept. 13, 273 days away. While exploring surgical options, a phone call was made to Dr. Dan Cooper, the renowned Dallas Cowboys  head team physician who specializes in knee and shoulder injuries. Cooper presented a proposition to Mahomes: If he wanted to return to the field as soon as possible, giving himself a chance to be back in uniform for the start of the Chiefs' 2026 campaign, he would need to fly from Kansas City to Dallas the next morning to have surgery.

 

 "I'm willing," Mahomes responded, "to do whatever it takes."

 Throughout his rehab and recovery, Mahomes has said that same sentence many times. And his exhaustive, day-after-day actions have led to him achieving his mission -- one that began next to the MRI machine 274 days before Kansas City's season opener.

 When the Chiefs opened their season Monday against the Denver Broncos , Mahomes, 30, was available and started under center, tossing two touchdowns and running for another in a 31-10 victory.

 "It's incredible," Veach said. "That's a guy that defines what leadership and what the face of a franchise should look like. He gave up an entire summer. He just attacked [the rehab]. Everybody in the building sees it. The level of sacrifice is something that has been an example throughout the entire organization."

 Mahomes' injury punctuated Kansas City's disappointing 2025 season. Following the two-minute warning in the team's Week 15 game against the Los Angeles Chargers , Mahomes tried to rally the Chiefs to a game-winning drive. He scrambled out of the pocket, rolling to his right. With defensive end Da'Shawn Hand chasing him from behind, Mahomes threw the ball away. But a few steps later, Mahomes planted his left foot, which stuck into the turf, and hyperextended his knee, the knee bowing to the outside of his leg, which damaged his LCL.

 

 The Chiefs' 16-13 loss to the Chargers eliminated Kansas City from the playoffs, the team's first time missing the postseason since 2014.

 "I wasn't playing my best at the end of last year before I got hurt," said Mahomes, who rushed for a career-high 422 yards and five touchdowns last season. "I think I ran a little bit too much."

 One reason Mahomes and the Chiefs selected Cooper is his experience repairing two of the four main stabilizing knee ligaments 24 hours after injury, including reattaching the LCL.

 Aaron Borgmann, the founder of Borgmann Rehab Solutions and a former physical therapist and athletic trainer with the Chiefs, said most players wait a week or sometimes longer before having the surgery because of how much their knee has swelled. By having an expedited procedure, Mahomes avoided that wait. Also in his favor: He did not have any artery, nerve, joint surface or meniscal damage, according to Burkholder.

 "For [most people], it's 10 days for an MRI, it's another doctor's visit and then another week to schedule surgery and so on," said Borgmann, describing general practices involving a torn ACL. "But we're not professional football players. I stand on this: NFL players of today have the best medical care in the world due to our healthcare system and our availability of imaging.

 "We have more doctors associated with NFL teams than any other professional sport in the United States. It is the best medical care you can find in the world."

 Even before his surgery, Mahomes wrote on his social media accounts, vowing to not fail his expectations.

 "I [will] be back stronger than ever."

 

 

 AWAITING MAHOMES ON Day 1 of 274 was Julie Frymyer, one of the Chiefs' top assistant athletic trainers. In his first rehab session, less than 24 hours after the surgery, Mahomes gritted his teeth and grimaced in pain while Frymyer assessed his muscles and worked to make sure the knee didn't swell up.

 Mahomes and Frymyer had been through such a scene many times before for three other injuries over the quarterback's career.

 Since Mahomes became the Chiefs' starter in 2018, Frymyer has been one of the team's most sought-out trainers. Mahomes on numerous occasions has credited much of his success in recovering from injuries faster than the average player to Frymyer -- and not to the fan theory that he possesses healing powers similar to Marvel character Wolverine. Also helping him, according to Frymyer and various others in the Chiefs organization, is Mahomes' remarkable ability to tolerate pain, whether during a game or in the team's training room.

 

 Frymyer's first major assignment with Mahomes occurred Oct. 17, 2019, when Mahomes dislocated his right kneecap while attempting a quarterback sneak.

 "I remember going into that halftime and he's trying to talk me into [him] going back out and playing," Reid said of Mahomes. "That [mindset] is huge for that position. You've got a lot of eyes on you. Guys are going to watch how you go about your business."

 With Frymyer's help, Mahomes surprised the Chiefs by missing just two games, returning to the field 24 days later. Before his 2025 knee injury, that was the longest absence of his career. A few months later, Mahomes led the Chiefs to their first Super Bowl victory in 50 years. The following year, during the postseason, Mahomes returned seven days after sustaining a painful turf toe in his left foot -- while also having a concussion from the previous week. Back on the field, he excelled, leading the Chiefs to Super Bowl LV, where they were beaten by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers .

 Frymyer became well-known among Chiefs fans and trainers in the NFL after the 2022 postseason, when she administered almost around-the-clock treatment and therapy for eight consecutive days after Mahomes experienced a painful high sprain of his right ankle in a win against the Jacksonville Jaguars in the divisional round. Despite his limited mobility, Mahomes once again carried the Chiefs back to the Super Bowl, defeating the Philadelphia Eagles for the franchise's third championship.

 "I trust her so much," Mahomes said of Frymyer, who last year starred in a State Farm commercial alongside the quarterback and pop singer Meghan Trainor. "There's days you come in [and] you're tired. I mean, you're sore. But she makes sure I finish the entire workout -- and I'm going to do it the right way. She knows when to pull back on some days.

 "It lets me go out there and work and not have to think about if I'm doing too much [or] am I doing not enough."

 

 Unlike those previous, brief rehabs, Frymyer this time had to find the correct balance of when to motivate and when to encourage Mahomes through a monthslong process.

 The most grueling days were in late December, when he couldn't walk. While wearing a protective brace, Mahomes couldn't sleep with much comfort. Christmas Day was not ideal, either. Instead of playing with his teammates, Mahomes watched the Chiefs lose to the Broncos from a suite inside Arrowhead Stadium, his crutches nearby.

 "The toughest part was the beginning, not being able to get up and chase my kids around," Mahomes said. "I remember sitting at the [training] table and watching us play those last few [road] games and how much it…

title: Broncos face tough opening stretch, try to avoid slow start
summary: The Broncos are 4-8 in September under Sean Payton after Monday's loss to the Chiefs. And they now face five 2025 playoff teams in a row.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Stumbling out of the gate has been a theme for the Denver Broncos since Sean Payton was hired as coach prior to the 2023 season. And those slow starts are coming to the forefront again after Monday night's season-opening loss to the Kansas City Chiefs .

 The 31-10 meltdown at Arrowhead Stadium was the first game of a brutal opening stretch that could potentially put the Broncos in a big hole by mid-October if recent history repeats itself. Denver's next five games are against 2025 playoff teams that won at least 11 games last season. And two opponents in that stretch -- including the Jacksonville Jaguars , who the Broncos (0-1) will play in their home opener on Sunday ( 4:05 p.m. ET, Empower Field at Mile High, CBS ) -- scored 27 or more points in Week 1 victories.

 "We're kind of tired of these slow starts," said edge rusher Nik Bonitto in a sullen locker room as Monday night turned into Tuesday morning. "Coming out every year and not starting the way we want. I don't think it was a wake-up call; we've just got to execute better from everybody."

 

 Monday's loss dropped the Broncos to 4-8 in September under Payton. They've won only one of their past four openers and are trying to avoid their third 0-2 start in four seasons. Even last season, when Denver went 14-3 and advanced to the AFC Championship Game, started with two losses in the first three weeks. So, starting faster was a talking point throughout August, both publicly and behind the scenes.

 "I don't think we've really started fast here in my three years -- I'm pretty sure we haven't," Payton said just before the season began. "... I think that's going to be important."

 It could be vitally important to the Broncos' playoff pursuits given how frontloaded their schedule is this season. Next up are the Jaguars (1-0), who got four touchdown passes from Trevor Lawrence in their season-opening win over the Cleveland Browns . Jacksonville won the AFC South with a 13-4 record last season, which included a 34-20 victory in Denver last December that snapped an 11-game Broncos winning streak.

 That will be followed by a Sunday night home game against the preseason Super Bowl favorite Los Angeles Rams (0-1). Then the Broncos will hit the road to play the  San Francisco 49ers  (1-0) and Los Angeles Chargers (0-1). The tough stretch finishes with a short-week, Thursday night game at home against the  Seattle Seahawks (1-0).

 The schedule softens considerably after that point, as the Broncos face only one opponent that finished last season with a winning record in Weeks 7-15. But they know they can't afford to dig a massive hole before that.

 "I think everybody knows [Payton] has talked about a fast start," Broncos wide receiver Courtland Sutton said. "You go into every game thinking you want to get going early and you don't really think about anything more than the week in front of you. So, it's just like, if we start fast each week that's a fast start of a season."

 Monday's loss was particularly troubling, especially the run defense and quarterback Bo Nix 's unsettled play in Davis Webb's first regular-season game as the playcaller.

 Nix was sacked four times for only the second time in his three-year career. He fumbled three times (losing one) and threw an interception, finishing 17-of-28 with 131 passing yards with a touchdown and the interception. The Broncos gained only 176 total yards on a mere 47 plays (32 pass plays, 15 runs), with Payton saying the Broncos' game plan had "a lot of throws, not enough runs."

 

 The leaky run defense is a growing issue, as Monday was the third consecutive game (including playoffs) the Broncos had given up at least 141 rushing yards dating to last season. The Chiefs pounded out 220 rushing yards, 173 coming from running back Kenneth Walker III . Kansas City pointed its rushing plays toward the middle of the formation, often pinning linebackers Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad away from ball carriers. The Chiefs broke 19 tackles Monday, according to ESPN Research, with Walker breaking 11. The Broncos broke six as a team .

 "Coach had us in the right spot and we missed tackles and plays we were in the wrong spot," Singleton said. "... We're going to point the fingers at ourselves."

 Monday wasn't the fast start the Broncos hoped for, but they can take solace in being able to dig out of slow starts the past two seasons to make the playoffs. Denver started 0-2 in 2024 and was 5-5 in November before finishing on a 5-2 kick to reach the postseason. Last season's 1-2 start was erased by 13 wins in the Broncos' final 14 regular-season games. Even in 2023, when the Broncos' 0-3 start included an infamous 70-20 loss to the Miami Dolphins , Denver recovered and had a 6-5 record entering December before finishing 8-9.

 But that all seemed like ancient history as the Broncos quietly packed their gear to leave Arrowhead. Now they must find solutions on the practice field the rest of the week before they face the Jaguars in Game No. 2 of a rough six-week opening stretch.

 "We know this is not going to be the whole season for us," Nix said. "That's the first time since Baltimore [a 41-10 loss in Week 9 in 2024] that we've been beat pretty handily like that. ... I do think [Monday] was not a good representation of us as a team."

title: Packers' No. 1 task after loss: Protect Jordan Love
summary: Green Bay's offensive line has to improve after Love was pressured relentlessly by Minnesota's defense Sunday.
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- It wasn't just how many times Jordan Love got hit in the Green Bay Packers ' 39-22 loss to the Minnesota Vikings  on Sunday -- although even that number was more than originally believed -- it was how quickly the quarterback had defenders in his face.

 Ten times on Sunday, Love faced unblocked pressures -- the most of any quarterback in Week 1 and tied for the most in a game by any quarterback in the past five seasons, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.

 Among the 28 quarterbacks to be sacked in Week 1, Love's average time before being sacked was the fourth fastest (3.59 seconds).

 "What's disappointing is we had a few protection busts that absolutely should not and cannot happen," Packers coach Matt LaFleur said.

 According to the official game statistics, the Vikings registered 15 hits on Love.

 When asked what he told the offense after Love was hit 15 times, offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich replied: "18 times actually."

 LaFleur and his staff have a long list of things to fix before their Week 2 game at the New York Jets  ( 1:00 p.m. ET, Fox ). The offensive line -- and the entire blocking operation -- is at the top of that list.

 

 Perhaps the most telling breakdown of the game came with a little more than 5 minutes left. The Packers had just fallen behind 25-22 after leading 22-10, but they still had a chance if they could put a drive together. Instead, Love was sacked on consecutive plays, losing the second one and giving the Vikings the ball at the Packers' 1-yard line, where they put the game away.

 On the first sack, Minnesota's Dallas Turner was unblocked off the left edge despite having two players -- right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele and tight end Mark Redman -- lined up across from him. Neither blocked him, with Redman essentially knocking Bako-Bewele out of the way.

 "Yeah, that was a bust," LaFleur said.

 "I mean I think that's the type of team they are, so in order to combat that you gotta communicate, be on the same page, focus in," Bako-Bewele said. "I think in the second half, there were some miscommunications here and there that got us beat."

 

 In some ways, it should not have been a major surprise that there were issues with the offensive line. It was a game of musical chairs throughout training camp. One day, guard Aaron Banks would practice a little. The next day, he wouldn't practice at all. He rarely took any 11-on-11 snaps because of a lingering knee issue from last season. It was much the same for Bako-Bewele, who had offseason knee surgery.

 Still, the Packers thought Banks would be ready for the season opener but when he was a late scratch at the end of the week, they had a decision to make. Based on the way they practiced for six weeks in camp, it seemingly would have been a choice between playing rookie Jager Burton in Banks' place or putting Anthony Belton at right guard and moving Jacob Monk to left tackle. The problem was that Belton, who started six games at right guard last season, took most of his reps at right tackle in camp because Bako-Bewele was limited.

 They did neither.

 Instead, Donovan Jennings got the call because he had been better of late in practice, Stenavich said.

 With or without Banks, who is looking more and more like a bad signing after Packers general manager Brian Gutekunst gave him a four-year, $77 million contract as a free agent in 2025, the Packers appear to be open to some personnel changes up front.

 "We're gonna keep working that this week [now that] Zach [is] kind of more situated at tackle," Stenavich said Tuesday. "So we're gonna kind of rotate a few guys and just see what our best combination is for sure."

 The Packers can sit back and say that no other team is likely to blitz as much as the Vikings did. It's defensive coordinator Brian Flores' M.O., and he lived up to it. According to NFL Next Gen stats, the Vikings blitzed Love on 78.3% of his dropbacks -- the fourth-highest rate in any game since at least 2018.

 

 The Packers handled it in the first half -- 189 passing yards and two touchdowns against the blitz -- but melted down in the second, when the Vikings sacked Love four times and picked him off once while blitzing.

 That doesn't mean the Jets, or anyone else on the Packers' schedule, will scrap their usual style in favor of the Flores formula, but it might make them throw in a few extra pressures.

 The Packers were last in pass block win rate for Week 1 at 9%, according to ESPN Analytics. The next-worst team, the Cardinals, were 22%. Jordan Morgan , making his first start at left tackle, ranked dead last among all Week 1 tackles in pass block win rate. Bako-Bewele was 47th. Among guards, Monk ranked 55th and Jennings 56th. Sean Ryan ranked last (32nd) among centers.

 "I think there's some things that we definitely have to get cleaned up that we'll certainly see, I'm sure, this week," LaFleur said. "But that would be a wholesale commitment to go to that style of defense, you don't see a whole bunch of that in the league."

title: Could David Montgomery be key to unlock Texans' offense?
summary: Houston scored its most points in a season opener since coach DeMeco Ryans took over.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Throughout training camp for the  Houston Texans , newly acquired running back  David Montgomery  was adamant about his all-around ability .

 In his debut Sunday, he backed his talk -- finishing with the most touchdowns (two rushing and one receiving) in a Texan debut in franchise history. 

 Houston fell short 36-31 to the  Buffalo Bills  to foil Montgomery's day, but he had 79 total yards (60 rushing and 19 receiving) as Houston scored the most points in a season opener under coach DeMeco Ryans in his four years.

 Houston had a need at running back, so they traded for Montgomery with the Detroit Lions in March. The offense finished with 124 rushing yards on 32 carries, which helped take pressure off quarterback  C.J. Stroud  and helped open up passing lanes en route to a 287-yard passing day. 

 

 "That's going to be our identity," Montgomery said. "[Offensive coordinator] Nick Caley believes in that. Coach Ryans believes in that also. Me, [ Woody Marks ] whenever we get the balls in our hands, we want to make it a point to take it personal to ensure that they can lean on us when they need us."

 Ryans felt good about the execution from Houston's offensive line combination of left tackle Aireontae Ersery , rookie left guard Keylan Rutledge , center Evan Brown , right guard Ed Ingram and right tackle Trent Brown .

 If the offensive line can consistently pave running lanes for Montgomery, that'll create the foundation Ryans wants: Physicality.

 "David doesn't do a great job without talking about the offensive line," Ryans said. "I thought those guys controlled the line of scrimmage really well, especially in those short-yardage, critical situations."

 From an advanced metrics standpoint, Montgomery's day where he averaged 3.0 yards per carry could have been more efficient all-around. He had a 35% success rate, which ranked 27th among running backs with at least 10 carries in Week 1 according to Next Gen Stats, and Houston's run block win rate was 74% (16th). So there's room to grow.

 

 Montgomery called their offensive output "OK" -- which speaks to them not being satisfied. But his individual performance added him to an active two-player list of having a multi-rushing touchdown game with three different franchises ( Detroit Lions , Chicago Bears and Houston) joining his former teammate in quarterback Justin Fields (Bears, Pittsburgh Steelers , New York Jets ).

 Houston brought in Montgomery with hopes that he could be a true bell cow for an offense that ranked 22nd in rushing yards per game (108.9) and 29th in yards per carry (3.9).

 "I would've loved to give David a game ball," Ryans said. "Very impressive game by him. Really encouraged with what he brings. Guy who can be an explosive runner, physical runner, he was able to get positive yards -- even when the run may have been blocked for zero [yards], he was able to get four and five yards on runs."
